q: What is a food web?
e: A food web connects many tangled food chains together like a giant, busy neighborhood.

q: Which organ holds liquid urine until you go to the bathroom?
e: The bladder is like a stretchy little water balloon that stores pee until you reach the restroom.

q: What does an adult butterfly use its wings to do?
e: Colorful wings let butterflies flutter between sweet flowers to drink delicious nectar.

q: Which part of a sprouted seed grows upward toward the sunlight?
e: The eager stem stretches straight up, carrying tiny leaves to catch the warm morning sunshine.

q: Which of these parts is found in plant cells, but NOT animal cells?
e: Plants need a rigid cell wall for extra stiffness, while animals need soft, flexible cells.

q: What are the tiny openings on leaves that let gases in and out?
e: Stomata are microscopic mouth doors that open and close to breathe the outside air.

q: What hard parts in your mouth cut and grind food?
e: Your teeth chop and crush every bite of food so it is small enough to swallow safely.

q: At what stage do humans learn to speak in full sentences and start school?
e: In childhood, kids run, laugh, and head to school with brains buzzing with curiosity!

q: Where do plants get their energy to make food?
e: Green leaves soak up warm sunshine like tiny solar panels to cook their own leafy meals.

q: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make food?
e: Leaves breathe in carbon dioxide from the breeze, using it as a secret ingredient for sweet sugars.

q: How much of a healthy meal plate should be filled with fruits and vegetables?
e: Filling half your plate with colorful plants gives your body an awesome rainbow of vitamins and minerals.

q: What is an apex predator?
a: An animal with no natural predators
An animal that eats only seeds
e: Sitting proudly at the top, an apex predator rules the food chain without being hunted.

q: What did Gregory Mendel use to test genetic crossovers?
e: A curious monk grew thousands of garden peas to see how family traits like height and color pass along.

q: A bear does NOT defecate during hibernation.
e: During their super-long winter nap, bears shut down their tummies completely and never need a bathroom break.

q: What organelle aids in synthesis of DNA in cells?
e: Ribosomes are busy little cell factories that build the proteins needed to help make and copy DNA.

q: Which of these bones is hardest to break?
e: Your sturdy femur is built thick like a tree trunk, making this thigh bone the absolute hardest to break.

q: How many legs do butterflies have?
e: Like all proud insects, these fluttery garden dancers have six tiny legs for tiptoeing across sweet flower petals.

q: What is the name of a rabbit's abode?
e: Bunnies use their busy paws to dig a burrow, a cozy underground tunnel just right for snuggling.

q: Rhinoplasty is a surgical procedure on what part of the human body?
e: Just like a rhinoceros shows off its mighty snout, a rhinoplasty is a special operation to fix a human nose.

q: How many chromosomes are in your body cells?
e: Your body cells get 23 pairs of chromosomes, holding the wonderful instruction book that makes you unique.

q: Zebras are white with black stripes.
e: Underneath all that fancy dazzle, zebras actually have black skin and grow white stripes on top.

q: What is the thin, outermost layer of the Earth?
e: Just like a fresh loaf of bread, Earth is wrapped in a thin, rocky outer layer called the crust.

q: Celiac Disease is a disease that effects the heart, causing those effected to be unable to eat meat.
e: This tricky condition actually upsets your tummy whenever you eat gluten found in bread, not meat or your heart.

q: The biggest distinction between a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell is:
a: The presence or absence of certain organelles
The presence or absence of a nucleus
e: Eukaryotic cells keep their precious instruction manuals tucked inside a cozy room called a nucleus, while prokaryote cells let theirs float free.

q: 71% of the Earth's surface is made up of
e: Looking down from space, our planet wears a giant splash of blue because vast, rolling oceans cover most of its surface.

q: Kangaroos keep food in their pouches next to their children.
e: That is false! A kangaroo's cozy pouch is strictly a nursery for her baby, not a pocket for storing snacks.

q: The human heart has how many chambers?
e: Your marvelous heart is split into four little rooms, pumping blood in and out all day long.

q: How many bones are in the human body?
e: Inside you right now, 206 sturdy bones work together like a magical team to help you dance!

q: What is the powerhouse of the cell?
e: Mitochondria act like bustling little power stations, turning the food you eat into energy to keep your cells dancing!

q: What is the largest animal currently on Earth?
e: Gliding through deep blue seas, the mighty blue whale is bigger than any creature that has ever lived!

q: Which class of animals are newts members of?
e: Newts are proud amphibians, starting out swimming with tiny gills before happily exploring damp moss on land.

q: What is the collective noun for a group of crows?
e: When these clever birds gather together, people call the spooky crew a murder!

q: Which of the following bones is not in the leg?
e: Your radius actually lives in your lower arm, helping your wrist twist around whenever you wave hello.

q: What is an example of a bacterial pathogen?
e: Cholera is caused by sneaky bacteria lurking in dirty water that can make a person feel terribly sick.

q: The Kākāpō is a large, flightless, nocturnal parrot native to which country?
e: The delightfully pudgy kakapo parrot waddles through the mossy, quiet forests of New Zealand under the starry night sky.

q: What animal takes part in Schrödinger's most famous thought experiment?
e: A clever scientist imagined a curious cat hiding inside a closed box to show just how strange tiny particles can be.

q: About what percentage of the Earth's surface is water?
e: Looking down from outer space, sparkling blue oceans cover a whopping seventy percent of our watery planet.

q: Rabbits can see what's behind themselves without turning their heads.
e: With wide eyes set high on their heads, bunnies can spot sneaky visitors behind them without even turning around.

q: Cats have whiskers under their legs.
e: It is true! Sneaky kitties have special whiskers behind their front paws to feel moving critters when they pounce.

q: Hippocampus is the Latin name for which marine creature?
e: This charming sea creature got its Latin name because its curved little head looks just like a tiny horse underwater.

q: Which breed of dog is traditionally associated with firefighters?
e: Energetic, spotted Dalmatians used to run beside horse-drawn wagons, bravely clearing busy streets for firefighters.

q: A flock of crows is known as a homicide.
e: A big group of these clever black birds is famously called a murder, not a homicide.

q: Wombats are native to which Country?
e: These chubby, burrow-digging wombats waddle and play naturally across the grassy hills and wild bush of Australia.

q: How many teeth does an adult rabbit have?
e: Behind those famous bunny grins hide twenty-eight busy teeth, constantly grinding down tough hay and garden greens.

q: Rabbits are carnivores.
e: That is false! Fluffy bunnies are gentle plant-eaters that would much rather munch on sweet grass than eat meat.

q: Elephants are physically unable to jump.
e: It is true! These gentle giants are far too heavy and lack the springy ankles needed to jump into the air.

q: The Axolotl is an amphibian that can spend its whole life in a larval state.
e: This smiling underwater salamander chooses to never grow up, keeping its feathery baby gills for its entire happy life.

q: What is the scientific name for modern day humans?
e: Homo sapiens is our official scientific name, which means wise human in the grand story of life.

q: What produces the green colour of most plant leaves?
e: Leaves wear bright green coats because they are packed with chlorophyll, a little helper that catches sunshine to make food.

q: Which is the national animal of India?
e: With its fiery orange coat and mighty prowl, India chose the magnificent tiger to represent the whole nation's strength.

q: The Killer Whale is considered a type of dolphin.
e: Believe it or not, these giant ocean acrobats are actually the biggest, splashiest dolphins in the sea!

q: Rabbits can't vomit.
e: Bunnies have super-strong tummy muscles that keep everything locked inside, meaning they never burp or throw up.

q: What is Grumpy Cat's real name?
e: Behind that famous, adorable frown was a sweet little kitty named Tardar Sauce.

q: What name is given to all baby marsupials?
e: Whether it grows into a big kangaroo or a sleepy koala, every marsupial baby is warmly called a joey.

q: A slug’s blood is green.
e: This is true! Instead of red, a slug's blood turns a cool green color because it carries oxygen using copper.

q: The internet browser Firefox is named after the Red Panda.
e: Even though the browser logo looks like a fiery fox, a firefox is actually another name for the fluffy red panda.

q: Rabbits are rodents.
e: Bunnies might nibble like mice, but an extra pair of upper teeth makes them lagomorphs instead of rodents.

q: What colour is the female blackbird?
e: Lady blackbirds wear cozy brown feathers instead of black, helping them hide like little shadows while keeping their eggs safe.

q: What is the "powerhouse" of the Eukaryotic animal cell?
e: Mitochondria act like tiny, buzzing batteries, happily making all the energy your cells need to keep zooming around.

q: What is the fastest  land animal?
e: With paws built like race cars, the speedy cheetah can outrun every other creature sprinting on dry land.

q: The freshwater amphibian, the Axolotl, can regrow it's limbs.
e: These smiling little water dwellers possess real-life magic, easily regrowing lost legs without even leaving a scar!

q: A caterpillar has more muscles than humans do.
e: Tiny caterpillars wiggle along using thousands of bendy muscles, while humans only need about six hundred to jump and dance!

q: Snakes and lizards are known to flick their tongue, this behavior is to?
e: That tongue dances into the breeze to capture floating scent bits, helping the snake sniff out its neighborhood.

q: By definition, where does an abyssopelagic animal live?
a: At the bottom of the ocean
e: These mysterious creatures make their home at the bottom of the ocean, swimming happily in the chilly, pitch-black deep.

q: What color is a Steller's Jay?
e: This noisy forest acrobat shows off striking blue feathers below and a midnight-black hood on its clever head.

q: Which of the following blood vessels carries deoxygenated blood?
e: The pulmonary artery rushes tired, oxygen-hungry blood away from your heart straight to your lungs for fresh air!

q: What do you call a baby bat?
e: Even though they fly through the night sky, a cozy baby bat is affectionately called a pup.

q: Which is the longest bone in the human body?
e: Tucked inside your thigh, the mighty femur stretches from hip to knee, easily beating every other bone in length.

q: In 2016, the IUCN reclassified the status of Giant Pandas from endangered to vulnerable.
e: It is true! Thanks to protected bamboo forests, growing numbers helped these fluffy giant pandas move safely off the endangered list.

q: The shape of the Earth is a perfect sphere.
e: Our spinning world bulges around its middle like a chubby tummy, making it a slightly squished ball instead of a perfect sphere.

q: Which of these animals are not real?
e: While the others roam our wild world, the Nemean lion lives only in grand old storybooks from ancient Greece.

q: Human cells typically have how many copies of each gene?
e: You inherit two copies of each gene recipe—one lovingly gifted from your mom, and one from your dad!

q: Which of the following is NOT a rodent:
e: Even with their twitchy noses, rabbits are lagomorphs, not rodents, because they pack an extra pair of upper chewing teeth!

q: The action of the sodium-potassium pump is an example of which of the following types of transport?
e: Because this tiny cell pump must push substances uphill against the crowd, it burns energy, making it an active transport worker.

q: Which of the following North American spiders' bite could be fatal to humans?
e: Shy as it looks, the brown recluse packs venom so potent that its rare bite can actually be dangerous to humans.

q: Some bacteriophages [bak-TEER-ee-oh-fay-jez] do not immediately kill the bacteria that they infect; rather, they incorporate themselves into the host genome [JEE-nome]. What is the term for the incorporated virus?
e: When a sneaky virus tucks itself asleep inside a bacterium's DNA, scientists call this cozy little squatter a prophage!

q: Which of the following is the region of the body where the thyroid gland is located:
e: Right in your neck sits a little butterfly-shaped helper called the thyroid gland, quietly steering your daily energy.

q: Sharks have repeated rows of identical teeth that are shed throughout their lives. Which of the following best categorizes their teeth?
e: Because every single chomper in a shark's grin shares the exact same pointy shape, they are called homodont teeth.

q: Ubiquitin [you-BIH-kwih-tin] tags can be used to direct proteins to a proteasome [PRO-tee-uh-zohm]. What happens to the protein there?
a: It is sent to the nucleus
e: The proteasome acts like a hungry recycling machine, eagerly chomping tagged old proteins into tiny reusable scraps.

q: Which of the following would most likely contain an alkaloid?
e: Clever plants brew natural chemicals called alkaloids, using their bitter taste to send hungry bugs packing!

q: Arginine [AHR-juh-neen] is a positively charged amino acid in water. This amino acid is considered which of the following?
e: Arginine holds onto a positive charge in water, which proudly earns it a spot in the basic amino acid club.

q: Which of the following is a major function of the large intestine?
e: Think of your large intestine as a thirsty sponge, soaking up extra water so your body stays happily hydrated.

q: Which of the following makes 3-dimensional protein studies difficult?
a: Proteins never fold properly outside their native cell
Chaperonins are required for some proteins to fold
Proteins lose their 3D structure once you remove them from the cell
e: Studying folded proteins is tricky because some need tiny helper molecules called chaperonins to bend into shape.

q: Which of the following human organs has the largest mass?
e: Like two giant, spongy balloons filling your chest, your lungs weigh much more than smaller neighbors like the kidneys or pancreas.

q: Which of the following is a segmented worm:
e: Earthworms are built like bendy trains made of tiny ring segments, happily wiggling through the cool mud!

q: Which of the following organisms is known to only produce a small number of offspring at a time?
e: Instead of laying hundreds of eggs, a chimpanzee mom pours all her love into just one precious baby at a time.

q: Which of the following is the BEST description for the location in the human body of the esophagus:
a: behind the trachea connecting the mouth to the lungs
behind the trachea connecting the mouth to the stomach
in front of the trachea connecting the mouth to the stomach
in front of the trachea connecting the mouth with the lungs
e: Tucked right behind the trachea, your esophagus works like a food slide connecting your mouth to your stomach!

q: Before a protein can be made, a gene must first be transcribed into what molecule?
e: A gene passes its secret recipe to messenger RNA, sending this tiny courier off to build brand-new proteins.

q: Of the following, which is NOT considered a type of vascular tissue in plants?
e: Unlike vascular pipes that carry water, tough sclerenchyma is made for pure body support, not plumbing.

q: Ferns differ from gymnosperms and angiosperms in which of the following ways?
a: Ferns do not produce seeds, while gymnosperms and angiosperms do
The dominant life stage of ferns is haploid, while gymnosperms and angiosperms are diploid
Ferns do not have non-motile sperm, whereas angiosperms and gymnosperms do
Ferns do not have xylem or phloem [FLOH-em], whereas gymnosperms and angiosperms do
e: Ferns skip making seeds entirely. Instead, these ancient leafy greens spread across the forest floor by floating tiny spores into the wind.

q: Most nerves in mammals are covered with a sheath of myelin [MY-ah-lin]. Which of the following is the main function of this layer?
e: This cozy myelin blanket wraps around nerves like a slick slide, helping electrical messages zip across your body in a flash!

q: Which of the following reptiles is known as a living fossil?
e: Meet the tuatara, a reptile called a living fossil because its kind survived unchanged since the dinosaur days!

q: Which of the following terms is most often used to describe a biochemical reaction where the forward reaction is at the same rate as the reverse reaction:
e: When forward and backward changes march at the exact same speed, the reaction balances happily in chemical equilibrium.

q: The now extinct species "Thylacine" was native to where?
e: The striped thylacine, also known as the Tasmanian tiger, once roamed wild across the grassy hills of Tasmania, Australia.

q: Unlike other mollusks , cephalopods (read as: SEH-fah-loh- pohds) have which of the following characteristics?
e: Speedy octopuses pump their blue blood safely through tidy, closed pipes instead of letting it slosh around loosely.

q: Which of the following biological molecules make up the main part of the bilayer and hydrophobic region of the plasma cell membrane:
e: Phospholipids line up like tiny swimmers holding hands, tucking their tails away from water to build the cell's cozy, protective bubble!

q: Some scientists believe that humans have possibly caused the sixth mass extinction on Earth. Which of the following is a major consequence of mass extinction?
a: Stabilizing population flux within a specific environment
e: When a mass extinction strikes, countless species vanish forever, leading to a huge loss of Earth's marvelous biodiversity.

q: Which of the following structures in the chicken egg is analogous to the mammalian placenta?
e: Just like a placenta helps human babies, the allantois acts as a caring chick's nursery sack for breathing and holding waste.

q: Which of the following is NOT a mollusk [MOL-uhsk]?
e: Snails and squids belong to the mollusk family, but a monopod is just a one-legged camera stick, not an animal!

q: Carrots, parsnips, radishes, and beets are all examples of:
e: These crunchy, colorful veggies are actually roots, digging deep into the dirt to slurp up water and store yummy food!

q: The medial meniscus forms which part of what joint in the human body?
e: Your knee stays happy and bouncy thanks to the medial meniscus, a rubbery little cushion tucked inside.

q: Protist habitats are often characterized by the presence of which of the following?
e: Tiny protists love to splash, so they always look for damp, moist places where they can wiggle and swim around!

q: Cholesterol is responsible for altering membrane fluidity. In which of the following conditions would the presence of cholesterol have the greatest effect on the fluidity of the cell membrane?
a: When cholesterol levels increase and the membrane is at a low temperature
When cholesterol levels increase and the membrane is at a moderate temperature
When cholesterol levels decrease and the membrane is at a low temperature
Cholesterol has the same effect, regardless of the temperature
e: In the chilly cold, membranes want to freeze solid, but extra cholesterol squeezes between the parts to keep things fluid and moving.

q: Which of the following components in cell sap is responsible for the red and blue colors seen in many fruits and vegetables?
e: Anthocyanin pigments act like nature's magic paintbrush, splashing berries and veggies with brilliant reds, purples, and blues!

q: What do you study if you are studying entomology?
e: Entomology is all about exploring the buzzing, crawling, six-legged world of insects!

q: Which of the following best explains why there are no major populations of horse-donkey hybrids in the wild?
a: The geographic distributions of horses and donkeys do not overlap
Horses and donkeys have different mating rituals
Horse and donkey gametes [GAM-eets] cannot fuse
e: Mules are wonderfully tough, but because these hybrids are sterile, they cannot have babies to make their own wild herds.

q: Which of the following biomes, on average, receives the lowest amount of annual precipitation?
e: Even though it looks chilly, the tundra is actually a frozen desert that gets less rain and snow than almost anywhere else!

q: What is the collective noun for rats?
e: When a clever bunch of scampering rats huddle together, this playful squad is delightfully called a mischief!

q: Which of the following are NOT bryophytes (read as: BRY- oh-fyts):?
e: While tiny bryophytes hug the ground without tubes, ferns have hidden pipes to carry water and grow tall!

q: Which of the following cats is the largest?
e: The mighty Siberian tiger takes the crown as the biggest cat on Earth, prowling through snowy forests like a giant furry king!

q: Which of the following classifications would be inclusive of eucalyptus, cattails, duckweed and buttercups?
e: Even tiny duckweed and giant eucalyptus trees are angiosperms, because they all share a secret superpower: making blossoms to show off their seeds.

q: Which of the following organisms has spines?
e: A sea urchin protects its soft round body with a prickly coat of sharp, movable spines that ward off hungry neighbors!

q: Which of the following locations functions as the thermostat of the human body?
e: Your hypothalamus acts like your brain's cozy little thermostat, turning up the heat when you shiver and cooling you off when you sweat.

q: A newborn baby was found to have 47 chromosomes. What is the term for this disorder?
e: When a baby ends up with an extra chromosome instead of forty-six, scientists call this uneven count aneuploidy.

q: When basophils react to a foreign substance, they secrete a signaling molecule that causes blood vessels to dilate and leak fluid at the site of inflammation. What is this signaling molecule?
e: When trouble arrives, basophils sound the alarm by releasing histamine, opening blood vessels wide to rush in healing helpers!

q: Which of the following allows fungi to feed more efficiently?
e: Like an underground web of super-straws, mycelium spreads out wide to slurp up tasty nutrients from every corner of the soil!

q: Hydrogen peroxide is often used to clean wounds. It reacts with catalase to do which of the following?
a: Generate toxins that stop bacterial cell wall production
e: Catalase zaps hydrogen peroxide into harmless water and bubbles of pure oxygen that fizz right before your eyes!

q: Many diseases, including cystic fibrosis, are caused by recessive homozygosity [hoh-muh-zy-GOS-i-tee] of a particular gene. Since these diseases are caused by recessive genes, one might think that they should have been eliminated long ago. What is the leading theory on why diseases like cystic fibrosis still exist?
a: Individuals with the disease are able to have children before the effects of the disease emerge
A single recessive allele of the gene causing the disease may confer a selective advantage
Two copies of the recessive allele of the gene causing the disease may confer a selective advantage
Individuals that are heterozygous [het-er-uh-ZY-guhs] for the gene causing the disease are as healthy as normal individuals
e: Carrying just one copy acts like a hidden shield, secretly protecting people from other deadly sicknesses so the gene stays around.

q: In a worm, gene X regulates the phenotypic expression of gene Z. What type of inheritance pattern does gene Z demonstrate?
e: That is epistasis, where one bossy gene steps right in front of another, deciding whether its partner gets to shine or stay hidden.

q: Photosynthesis has both light and dark reactions. Which of the following occurs without the presence of light?
a: Water is split to produce oxygen
Carbon dioxide is transformed to sugar
e: Even when the sun goes to sleep, busy plants quietly knit carbon dioxide into sweet, energizing sugar.

q: What gene elements are removed from mRNA through the process of splicing?
e: Tiny cell scissors snip out introns like scrap paper, leaving behind only the most important pieces of the genetic message.

q: Which of the following hormones plays a major role in the male reproductive system?
e: Androgens are the busy chemical messengers that guide boys as they grow, building deeper voices and helping male bodies work properly.

q: Which of the following will most likely reduce genetic variation in a population?
e: Stabilizing selection loves playing it safe in the middle, trimming away unusual traits until everyone ends up looking remarkably alike.

q: A peptide sequence with the amino acid composition proline-glycine [GLY-seen]-glycine-tyrosine [TY-ruh-seen] would have what percentage of aromaticity?
e: Out of four building blocks lined up here, only tyrosine wears a special chemical ring, giving this chain exactly 25 percent ring power.

q: Which of the following is most directly responsible for the exchange of genes during meiosis:
e: During crossing over, friendly chromosomes hug and swap little pieces of themselves, mixing up traits like trading collectible cards!

q: A nonsense mutation is most likely to result in which of the following events?
e: A nonsense mutation shouts stop too early, cutting the growing protein short before it can finish its grand adventure.

q: What does "hippopotamus" mean and in what langauge?
e: Long ago, clever Greeks watched this gigantic swimmer splash in the water and named it "river horse."

q: Which of the following organisms is least likely to perform well in a hypoxic region of the ocean?
e: Blue marlins are speedy ocean sprinters that gulp tons of oxygen, so stuffy, low-oxygen water stops them in their tracks.

q: Polyp and medusa are two stages in the life cycle of which of the following?
e: Cnidarians are magical sea creatures like jellyfish that start planted like tiny flowers, then transform into floating, bell-shaped swimmers!

q: During which of the following phases of meiosis [my-OH-sis] do homologous [ha-MAWL-uh-gus] chromosomes break apart?
e: In Anaphase I, matching chromosome partners share a gentle goodbye tug and pull apart toward opposite ends of the cell.

q: In a bacterial culture, there are 2000 Escherichia coli per milliliter of tryptic soy broth. What is the term used to describe this number?
e: Density simply measures the crowd, counting how many tiny bacteria are packed together inside each single drop of liquid.

q: The name of Dr. Joseph Lister is most often associated with what?
a: Pioneering the development and use of vaccines
e: Dr. Lister became a hospital hero by washing tools clean, showing doctors how sterile habits stop sneaky germs from causing infections.

q: Introducing rabbits in Australia that eat the same food and use the same space for burrows as native marsupials is what type of species interaction?
e: When newcomers and locals tussle over the same cozy burrows and leafy snacks, that neighborhood rivalry is called competition.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about paper wasps?
a: Stinging workers do not survive the winter
A mature nest may have 20 to 30 adults
e: Unlike honeybees, busy little paper wasps have smooth stingers, meaning they can zap a pesky intruder again and again.

q: Which of these bones is fused in a bird's body?
e: A bird's wishbone is actually two collarbones, or clavicles, fused tight together to give its wings super flying power!

q: A geneticist studying fruit flies notices that flies with short wings also tend to have red eyes. She concludes that the genes for wing length and eye color may be which of the following?
e: When traits travel together like best buddies holding hands on a chromosome, we say their genes are linked!

q: Which of the following is an example of a biotic factor?
e: Biotic simply means alive, and a forest floor crowded with sprouting mushrooms is bursting with life!

q: Which of the following are the 3 basic organs of higher plants:
e: Every plant relies on roots to drink, stems to stand tall, and leaves to catch warm sunshine.

q: The most frequent subconscious activity repeated by the human body is blinking.
e: While your eyelids flutter a lot, your steady heartbeat and quiet breaths happen far more often each day.

q: Which of the following is an example of organisms found living next to hydrothermal vents.
e: Creatures living beside scorching, deep-sea vents are called extremophiles because they genuinely love thriving in Earth's wildest, harshest neighborhoods.

q: Name the tiny air sacs involved in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the lungs.
e: Millions of tiny alveoli act like microscopic balloons, happily trading fresh oxygen for carbon dioxide every time you take a breath!

q: Which of the following is the target of alkylating [AL-kil-lay-ting] agents, such as mustard gas?
e: These sneaky chemicals attack DNA, scrambling the precious recipe book inside our cells that tells our bodies how to grow.

q: Two species, A and B, have a predator-prey relationship. Which of following best describes the graphs of their populations vs. time?
a: When the graph of species A has a positive slope, the graph of species B has a positive slope
When the graph of species A has a positive slope, the graph of species B has a negative slope
When the graph of species A has a positive slope, the graph of species B is uncorrelated
When the graph of species A is at a maxima, the graph of species B is at a maxima
e: It is a wild see-saw dance: when hungry hunters multiply, their scurrying prey gets eaten and begins to dwindle.

q: Which of the following trees have simple, pinnate leaves:
e: Cherry and apple trees grow simple leaves with neat, feather-like veins branching from one central stem.

q: In which of the following environments are extremophiles most likely to be found?
e: Extremophiles love tough neighborhoods, happily splashing around boiling hydrothermal vents at the dark bottom of the ocean.

q: A series of amino acids joined together will make a:
e: When amino acids click together in a long chain, they fold into a hardworking protein ready to help your body.

q: Down Syndrome is usually caused by an extra copy of which chromosome?
e: Down syndrome happens when cells accidentally pack an extra third copy of little chromosome 21 into the suitcase of life.

q: Which of the following parts of a plant produces pollen:
e: The stamen is a flower's little pollen factory, dusting visiting bumblebees with powdery yellow grains.

q: Why do invasive species tend to outcompete native species?
a: Invasive species are better adapted to the area
Invasive species have no native predators
Invasive species remove competition from the area
Invasive species reduce predation pressure on other species
e: Without any local hunters around to stop them, these rowdy newcomers take over and crowd everyone else out.

q: Which of the following animals typically moves around through propagating rhythmic contractions known as peristalsis [peh-rih-STALL-sis]?
e: An earthworm travels underground by squeezing and stretching its squishy body in neat, rippling waves.

q: What part of the mammalian female reproductive tract is responsible for making gametes [GAM-eets]?
e: The ovary acts like a cozy cradle that carefully creates and protects precious egg cells.

q: Which of the classes of biomacromolecules has the highest energy density per unit mass?
e: Fats are nature's ultimate energy backpacks, cramming far more fuel into every tiny bite than proteins or carbs can.

q: Which of the following is the largest songbird in North America?
e: With glossy black feathers and a huge wingspan, the clever common raven towers over every other songbird in North America.

q: A plant produces small flowers that do not have a strong odor and are not brightly colored. The plant is probably fertilized by which of the following?
e: Without showy colors or sweet perfume to invite hungry bugs, this quiet bloom lets the playful wind carry its pollen across the meadow.

q: After a signaling molecule binds to a receptor, what enzymes often set off a cascade of phosphorylation [faws-four-il-AY-shun] events?
e: Kinases are like tiny helpers playing tag, happily passing phosphate tags from one protein to the next to wake up the whole cell!

q: Which of the following would be least likely to diffuse through the plasma membrane of a cell?
e: Fibrinogen is a gigantic, bulky protein, far too huge to squeeze through the cell’s tiny doorways without an official escort.

q: If you were to take a section of a leaf, which of the following statements correctly aligns the part of the leaf and its function?
a: Mesophyll (read as: MEH-zoh-fil): Opening through which air brings carbon dioxide
Epidermis: Region where most photosynthesis takes place
Stoma: Protect and support the leaf
e: Inside the leaf, tiny thylakoids act like solar panels, happily catching sunbeams to help make sweet plant food.

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of hydrolysis [hy- DROL-uh-sis] of a biomolecule?
a: Conversion of fats to fatty acids and glycerol [GLIS-uh-rol]
Conversion of proteins to amino acids
e: Hydrolysis breaks big molecules apart, but building DNA actually snaps small nucleotide blocks together into something brand-new!

q: Which of the following events is least likely to be associated with initiation of seed germination?
e: A waking baby seed needs lots of fresh oxygen, so restricting its breathing would keep the little sprout fast asleep.

q: Amylase starts the chemical reaction of breaking down starch in the mouth. In which of the following categories of proteins is amylase classified?
e: Amylase is an enzyme, a speedy little helper that chops giant bites of starch into sweet, tiny sugars in a flash.

q: Which of the following correctly describes the use of crystal violet in a biology lab?
a: Used to determine the absorption profile of a material
A staining agent to visualize bacteria
A standard cell used to compare the color of protein crystals
An electrode to use in protein chemistry experiments
e: Crystal violet paints see-through bacteria in bright, cheerful purple so scientists can easily spot the tiny critters under a microscope.

q: Which of the following animals does NOT have a four- chambered heart?
e: Unlike us, a little frog hops along with a three-chambered heart, mixing its blood in one cozy pump.

q: Gary the gardener raises a species of annual flowers that can produce pink or white flowers. Gary buys a pot of white flowers and plants them in his garden and each successive year saves only that year's generation of seeds to plant the next year. Over many generations of years of flowers Gary only ever sees white flowers. Which of the following is the BEST explanation for this breeding pattern:
a: the original plant was homozygous dominant
the original plant was homozygous recessive
the original plant was heterozygous for both colors
the original plant was homozygous but Gary cannot know for sure whether it is a dominant or recessive color
e: The plant was homozygous because it only made white seeds, but without pink flowers to compare, Gary cannot know which color dominates.

q: What is the part of the brain that is most directly involved in walking and coordination?
e: The cerebellum is your brain’s clumsy-busting dance master, coordinating your muscles so every step stays graceful and balanced.

q: Most scientists believe that protists evolved from which of the following?
e: Long ago, simpler prokaryote cells took a giant leap forward, growing bigger and more organized to become the very first protists.

q: Cheese, yogurt, apple cider, olives, and sauerkraut are all made with:
e: Friendly bacteria are tiny kitchen helpers that feast on foods, transforming milk into tangy yogurt and tasty cheese!

q: Which of the following animals has been observed to communicate via a dance language, including maneuvers such as the waggle dance?
e: To share the secret location of sweet flower patches, clever honeybees do a cheerful waggle dance for their buzzing hive mates!

q: Which of the following neurons would be capable of conducting an action potential more quickly than the rest?
a: A myelinated [MY-uh-luh-nay-tid] nerve fiber with a narrow diameter
A myelinated nerve fiber with a wide diameter
An unmyelinated nerve fiber with a wide diameter
An unmyelinated nerve fiber with a narrow diameter
e: A wide nerve fiber wrapped in a cozy myelin jacket lets electric signals zip through fast, just like a superhighway!

q: The act of girdling a tree would most likely be done by which of the following?
e: Hungry porcupines love munching on sweet inner bark, chewing a ring completely around the trunk for a tasty woodland snack.

q: Which of the following is considered the dominant generation in flowering plants:
e: The leafy green plant you see blooming outside is the sporophyte stage, ruling as the main, dominant form of a flower's life!

q: For what reason would a spotted hyena "laugh"?
e: That spooky chuckle is not a happy giggle; hyenas actually laugh when they feel nervous and stressed.

q: Rabbits eat grass and foxes eat rabbits. What role do foxes play in the food chain?
e: Grass is eaten first by hungry bunnies, which makes the sneaky fox a secondary consumer when it catches dinner!

q: Which of the following is the causative agent for some cases of familial fatal insomnia, Creutzfeld-Jacob disease, and kuru?
e: A prion is a misfolded protein that acts like a copycat bully, reshaping healthy brain proteins and causing serious disease.

q: A small population of native red-backed salamanders is migrating downhill towards a vernal pool. Along the way, half of the population is lost while crossing a road. This would possibly lead to which of the following outcomes?
a: More competition among members of the population
Stationary individuals that do not migrate to vernal pools
e: Losing salamanders to pure bad luck is genetic drift, which accidentally changes what family traits the survivors pass on.

q: Most of the growth in a plant is due to which of the following?
e: Plant cells stretch out like tiny green water balloons, making cell elongation the real secret to shooting up tall.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about leopards?
a: They are hybrids of lions and panthers
They can leap to the branch of a tree while holding an impala carcass in their mouths
They have a very broad diet
e: Leopards are their own unique wild species, not a mixed-up hybrid of lions and panthers like ancient storytellers once believed.

q: Where are DNA molecules located in prokaryotes?
e: Without a nucleus to tuck it into bed, a bacterium lets its DNA float freely in the soupy cytoplasm.

q: Which of the following is the scientific name for the knee cap:
e: Your knee hides a tough little bone shield called the patella, perfectly protecting every playful hop and skip.

q: The seeds of a certain plant are covered in tiny barbs. Which of the following is their likely mode of dispersal?
e: Those prickly seeds are clever hitchhikers, clinging onto furry animals to catch a free ride to a new home.

q: An adaptation is any kind of modification in bodily structure or behavior that increases an organism's chance of survival in their environment. Which of the following is NOT an example of an adaptation in an organism to its current environment?
a: The large eyes of an owl for improved night vision
The spines of a cactus for improved water retention
The appendix of a human for improved protein digestion
The jaws of a Venus Flytrap for improved ability to capture insects
e: Your appendix does not digest protein today, so it is just a quiet leftover rather than a helpful modern survival tool.

q: Which of the following organisms is not a eukaryote (read as: yuh-KEHR-ee-t)?
e: Tiny bacteria keep things super simple without a neat nucleus, so they are not eukaryotes like you or your houseplant.

q: Which of the following scenarios is the LEAST likely to result in allopatric [al-oh-PAT-trik] speciation?
a: Two species of wolves living on either side of a now-underwater isthmus
Two bird species living on nearby islands formed by rising sea levels
Two species of ground squirrels separated by a large canyon formed by an earthquake
Two species of fish moving back and forth across a tropical reef system
e: Fish swimming freely across a reef never get separated by a barrier, so allopatric speciation cannot keep them apart.

q: Which of the following organisms were the earliest life forms to evolve in the ocean?
e: Long before fins or claws, tiny bacteria were the very first microscopic pioneers exploring our ancient oceans.

q: Which of the following best describes the earliest fish in the fossil record?
e: The earliest fish were like tiny swimming knights, sporting tough armored bodies before anyone even invented jaws!

q: Some inhibitors, rather than competing with the substrate at the active site, bind to a distal site on the enzyme to inhibit activity. What type of inhibition is this?
e: In allosteric inhibition, a sneaky blocker taps a special side spot, gently changing the enzyme's shape so work quietly stops.

q: Spallanzani, Reti and Pasteur were all:
a: helpful in disproving the theory of spontaneous generation
scientists who supported the genetic work of Mendel
supporters of the work of Charles Darwin
e: These clever scientists showed that living things come from parents, not thin air, disproving spontaneous generation once and for all.

q: Which dog breed is named after a region in Croatia
e: These playful, spotty dogs get their name from Dalmatia, a sunny coastal region tucked away in Croatia.

q: Which of the following terms is MOST commonly used to refer to the copying of DNA during the cell cycle:
e: Before a growing cell divides, it photocopies its precious genetic recipe book through a process called replication.

q: You would like to evaluate the distribution of mRNA in a microbial population. Which method is likely to be most helpful to you?
e: Cells write messages using mRNA, and transcriptomics is the tool that lets us read those busy notes.

q: Which of the following is the general relationship between the availability of soil nutrients and bacterial populations?
a: Increased bacterial populations are predicted as soil nutrients increase
Decreased bacterial populations are predicted as soil nutrients increase
Bacterial populations are not impacted by nutrient availability
There are no bacteria in soil
e: When soil is loaded with tasty nutrients, hungry little bacteria throw a feast and multiply like crazy!

q: During which of the following parts of mitosis do kinetochores (read as: ki-NEH-toh-kohrs) begin to mature and attach to the spindles?
e: During prophase, the dividing cell gets ready as kinetochores wake up and grab onto the spindle ropes.

q: Imagine that you conducted an experiment where you tested the effects of different fertilizers on plant growth over the course of one month. You have to present your data in a graph. What variable would you plot on the y-axis?
e: Plant height climbs straight up the vertical y-axis, proudly showing off how tall your leafy buddy grew.

q: Which of the following organs is the first to lose its function under hypoxic conditions?
e: Your brain is an eager daydreamer that needs fresh air every second, so it dozes off first when oxygen runs out.

q: Which of the following would be the best outgroup when building a phylogenetic tree of cats?
e: While big cats all belong to one feline family, the wolf is a canine outsider, making it the perfect outgroup.

q: Which of the following compounds stimulates the generation of red blood cells, and is banned by most major athletic organizations?
e: Erythropoietin orders your body to make extra red blood cells, giving athletes an unfair boost of sneaky energy!

q: Which animal might live in a kelp forest?
e: Playful sea otters love kelp forests, wrapping themselves in giant seaweed blankets so they do not float away while napping!

q: In which of the following parts of the kidney does filtration occur?
e: The renal corpuscle acts like a tiny kitchen strainer, filtering waste out of your blood to keep you sparkling clean.

q: Which of the following describes the shape of a bacterial pilus:
e: A bacterial pilus acts like a super-thin hollow tube, reaching out like a tiny straw to grab onto things.

q: If an animal has 42 chromosomes in its normal, non-gamete or somatic cells, what term would be given to the gametes that have 21 chromosomes:
e: Carrying just half the usual recipe of chromosomes, these special little cells are known as haploid.

q: Which of the following are the sugar transporting cells of the phloem in flowering plants:
e: Sieve tube cells link together like living drinking straws, piping sweet sugary syrup from sunny leaves to feed the whole plant.

q: Which of the following is closest to the percentage of species that have lived on Earth that are now extinct?
e: Over time, ninety-nine percent of Earth’s ancient species have vanished, gently making room for new creatures to explore our world.

q: What organ in the human body is responsible for storing glucose in the form of glycogen [GLY-kuh-juhn]?
e: Your liver works like a faithful pantry, packing extra sugar away as glycogen until you need a burst of energy.

q: Andrew synthesizes some bacteriophage viral particles that contain biomolecules labeled with both phosphorus-32 and sulfur-35. He then infects some unlabeled bacteria with the viral particles. Which of the following observations would he NOT be able to make after the infection?
a: The original viral particles still contain sulfur-35-labeled molecules
If the bacteria are allowed to produce more viral particles, they will contain phosphorus-32-labeled molecules
e: Viruses leave their sulfur coats outside the bacteria like muddy boots, so you will never find sulfur inside!

q: In an amoeba, which of the following is the primary purpose of the pseudopods?
e: A squishy amoeba stretches out its pseudopods like little blobby feet, using them to crawl along and explore its puddle!

q: Which of the following is the most common energy intermediate that couples exergonic and endergonic reactions in living cells:
e: ATP acts like a rechargeable battery, happily passing energy between reactions to keep your cells buzzing with life!

q: A student puts an elodea plant into a test tube and adds water and baking soda. After putting the test tube under 24 hours of light, the student notices bubbles forming on the leaves. The bubbles are most probably which of the following?
e: Drinking in the bright light, the happy water plant makes food and burps out fresh oxygen gas bubbles!

q: Which of the following is most advantageous to plants that depend on insects for pollination:
e: Sticky pollen acts like tiny patches of Velcro, happily hitching a ride on fuzzy bee legs to visit neighboring flowers.

q: Which of the following parts of the brain is responsible for controlling heart rate and breathing?
e: Tucked low in your brain, the trusty medulla works quietly behind the scenes to keep your heart beating and lungs breathing.

q: Which of the following statements about Duchenne muscular dystrophy is NOT true?
a: It is a sex linked, inherited, muscle-destroying disorder
It involves degeneration of individual muscle fibers
It usually presents with an unequal weakness of voluntary muscles on both sides
It involves a progressive atrophy of skeletal muscle
e: This muscle disorder actually weakens both sides of the body equally, like matching shoes wearing down together, rather than unevenly.

q: Which of the following determines the sex of a turtle egg?
e: Warm, cozy sand tucks the turtle eggs in and tells nature whether to hatch baby girls or baby boys.

q: You are constructing a simple ecosystem model to predict microbial growth in a marine environment. Which of the following elements are you least likely to include in your model as a possible limiting nutrient?
e: The ocean is already swimming in tons of natural sulfur, so hungry microbes never have to worry about running out!

q: Which of the following is NOT part of the human respiratory system?
e: Your esophagus is a busy food slide heading straight to your tummy, so it belongs to digestion, not breathing.

q: Which of the following is the smallest object that a typical student compound light microscope is able to allow a person to see:
e: Tiny E. coli bacteria are just large enough for your school microscope to spot, while viruses and molecules are far too small.

q: In pea plants, the yellow seed trait is completely dominant over the green seed trait. Suppose you cross a pea plant that is heterozygous [het-er-uh-ZY- guhs] for the yellow seed trait with a pea plant containing green seeds. What colors of seed will the offspring have?
a: Half of the offspring will have green seeds and half will have yellow seeds
A seed color that is halfway between green and yellow
e: Since the yellow parent carries a hidden green recipe, half the baby seeds turn out green and the other half sprout yellow.

q: Which of the following is least likely to be found in a hot desert climate?
a: A plant with broad flat leaves
A plant with thick fleshy leaves
A plant with thin needle-like leaves
e: Broad, flat leaves lose water way too quickly under the scorching sun, so thirsty desert plants avoid wearing them.

q: Which of the following species thrives in a salt marsh?
e: Feisty blue crabs feel right at home paddling through the salty mud and hiding among the tangled marsh grasses.

q: Why is hair a good candidate for conducting sequencing of ancient DNA?
a: Keratin in hair protects DNA from degradation
The presence of melanin yields better sequencing data
DNA in hair is free from mutations
e: Tough keratin coats each hair like a shield of armor, safely locking delicate ancient DNA away from time and decay.

q: On an island, half of one species of birds has small beaks and the other half has large beaks. A tree with small seeds is very prevalent on the island; hundreds of years later, the small-beaked birds outnumber the large-beaked birds. According to the principles of natural selection, which of the following is the most likely explanation?
a: Birds with small beaks were better able to fight birds with large beaks
Large beaks gradually shrunk due to the smaller available food
Birds with small beaks were most likely to forage successfully, and were thus more likely to reproduce
Birds with large beaks are likely to have more offspring
e: Birds with small beaks gathered food easily, stayed healthy, and had lots of chicks that inherited those handy little beaks.

q: Which of the following is the best example of a vestigial structure on a marine organism?
e: Whales secretly carry tiny leftover hip bones from their land-walking ancestors, tucked away inside even though they do not need legs to swim!

q: Hormones regulate the concentration of glucose in the blood. Which of the following hormones is properly described by its role in this regulation?
a: Epinephrine [e-puh-NE-fruhn] suppresses release of glucagon [GLOO-kuh-gon] and insulin
Somatostatin [suh-mat-uh-STAT-in] enhances release of glucose from glycogen
e: Insulin acts like a gentle key, unlocking cells so sugar moves inside, which safely decreases blood glucose levels.

q: Finnish Lapphund dogs were used for herding reindeer.
e: Wearing warm fuzzy coats, these brave pups spent centuries helping people round up and guide reindeer herds.

q: Which of the following organisms contains the most chitin (read as: KYE-tin) by percent of body weight:
e: Mighty little ants wear their crunchy chitin like a full suit of armor, while big animals leave it out entirely!

q: Which of the following is a lipid:
e: Lipids are just slippery fats and oils, so golden corn oil fits right into this greasy little family.

q: Which of the following groups of animals shared the most recent common ancestor with birds?
e: Look closely at a tiny robin and you will see a dinosaur cousin; birds share their most recent family ancestor with prehistoric dinosaurs!

q: Which of the following is the BEST explanation for the function of nuclear pores:
a: to prevent damaging hydrogen peroxide from entering the nucleus
to prevent too much pressure from metabolism from building up in the nucleus
to allow the nucleus to sweat
to allow substances such as mRNA to leave the nucleus
e: These pores act like tiny doorways, letting important helpers like mRNA slip outside the nucleus to deliver instructions.

q: Unlike eutherians, both monotremes and marsupials are associated with which of the following?
e: Instead of staying tucked inside a mother's womb, these unique babies do their growing on the outside, in pouches or eggs.

q: What is the purpose of the lateral line in fish?
e: A fish’s lateral line acts like underwater tickle sensors, feeling hidden vibrations and ripples gliding through the water.

q: The human right lung has how many lobes?
e: With plenty of room on the right side, that lung neatly splits into three breezy lobes to catch your breath.

q: Which of the following does NOT characterize dicotyledon [dy-kot-l-EEd-n] plants?
e: Dicot leaves love branching out with webby patterns, leaving neat parallel lines to grass and other plant cousins.

q: Which of the following is NOT a difference between archaeans and eubacteria?
a: Archaeans have a nucleus, while eubacteria do not
Eubacteria have peptidoglycan [peptihdo-GLY-can] in their cell walls, while Archaeans do not
Archaeans can have introns, while eubacteria do not
Archaeans have several different RNA polymerases [paw-LIM-er-aces], while eubacteria have just one
e: Neither of these microscopic microbes has a nucleus, so having one isn't a difference between them at all.

q: Which of the following portions of the seed serves as the plant embryo's food supply until germination?
e: Think of the endosperm as a cozy packed lunch waiting inside the seed to feed the baby plant before it sprouts.

q: Sometimes, there is more of a particular ion inside of a cell than there is outside of the cell. Which of the following will a cell do if it requires even more of this particular ion?
a: Nothing, since the ions diffuse into the cell across the membrane
The lipid molecules of the membrane "flip" the ions across
The ions are transported into the cell via channel proteins
The ions are transported into the cell via transport proteins
e: Little transport proteins act like hardworking pumps, using energy to haul even more ions inside against the crowded flow.

q: It is generally believed that most of the oxygen in the air today came from:
a: oxidation of carbon molecules containing oxygen
release of oxygen from volcanic vents
e: Tiny plants soaked up golden sunshine and breathed out fresh oxygen through photosynthesis, filling the sky just for us!

q: Which of the following is NOT made primarily out of glucose?
e: While cotton and starch are built from sweet glucose sugars, little silkworms spin their shiny silk threads using strong proteins instead.

q: The process of Gram straining bacteria can be used to classify bacteria based on the structure of which of the following organelles?
e: The colorful stain hugs the bacteria's tough cell wall, revealing whether this tiny traveler wears a thick coat or a thin jacket.

q: Which of the following has been most greatly and directly altered by human activity in the biosphere?
e: By burning fuels and farming, humans have drastically stirred up Earth's natural chemical cycles of carbon and nitrogen.

q: Sea stars, velvet worms and northern shrike birds - all three are examples of:
e: These sneaky critters might look completely different, but each one is a hungry predator hunting down other creatures for dinner!

q: About how much of their body weight in food do sea otters eat every day?
e: To stay warm in chilly ocean waves, a fuzzy sea otter must gobble down a whopping 25 percent of its body weight daily!

q: Which organism existed over 3.5 billion years ago and is considered a living fossil?
e: Long before dinosaurs stomped around, tiny microbes built rocky homes called stromatolites, and these ancient wonders are still growing today!

q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of microevolution?
e: When creatures pick partners completely at random, gene mixes stay nicely balanced instead of shifting over time.

q: A plant cell containing 0.1 molar sucrose and 0.2 molar glucose is placed in a 0.3 molar solution of sucrose. What type of solution is this?
e: Both sides hold the exact same amount of sugar! Because everything is perfectly balanced, this peaceful solution is called isotonic.

q: Which of the following do clams use as an anchor to fix themselves into the sand:
e: A clam stretches out its squishy muscular foot to dig deep into wet sand and anchor itself safely from rolling waves!

q: What will occur to an animal cell if it is placed in a hypotonic environment?
e: Water rushes into the thirsty cell like an overfilled water balloon until pop, it explodes!

q: What is the term for the site on an enzyme that a substrate binds to?
e: An enzyme's active site is like a special VIP parking spot, perfectly shaped for just one helper molecule to click right in.

q: The echidna is a monotreme.
e: This spiky little marvel belongs to the monotreme family because it lays eggs instead of giving live birth.

q: Chemoreceptors [KEE-mo-receptors] would likely be involved in sensing which of the following?
e: Chemoreceptors act like tiny chemical sniffers, perfectly designed to catch invisible scent messages called pheromones floating through the air.

q: In which of the following areas of the human body is the ileum bone found:
e: Your pelvis features the wide, curving ilium bone, proudly helping your hips hold up the rest of your body.

q: What type of cellular receptor is the most common and is characterized by 7 alpha helices [HEEL-ih-seez]?
e: GPCR receptors are nature's most popular lookouts, weaving back and forth seven times across the cell to catch incoming signals.

q: Which of the following instruments did Louis Pasteur use in dispelling the theory of spontaneous generation:
a: swan necked flasks with boiled and unboiled broth
open and closed jars with rotting meat
flasks of amino acids and other organic molecules exposed to electric charges
e: Those curvy swan-necked flasks let fresh air inside while trapping sneaky germs in the bend, proving soup cannot create life alone.

q: Which of the following is the most important function of fiber tracheids [tray-key-ids] in woody plants?
a: Absorption of nutrients from the soil
e: These sturdy plant fibers act like wooden beams inside a house, keeping giant trees standing tall and proud!

q: The average lifespan of a wildcat is only around 5-6 years.
e: That statement is false because tough wildcats can happily prowl the forests for ten to fifteen long years.

q: Which of the following is not considered a plant organ?
e: Roots, stems, and leaves are giant whole organs, but sieve-tube elements are just tiny straw-like cells working together inside them.

q: Which of the following best describes the role of NADPH in the process of photosynthesis?
e: NADPH acts like a generous helper, donating high-energy electrons as a reducing agent to help assemble sweet plant sugars.

q: In a human heart, through what structure does oxygenated blood first pass?
e: Fresh, oxygen-rich blood takes its very first step into the heart's left atrium before going anywhere else.

q: The development of polyploidy in plants plays the most direct role in which of the following?
e: In sympatric speciation, plants duplicate their DNA sets and instantly blossom into brand-new species right beside their plant neighbors.

q: A plant produces flagellated sperm and the dominant stage in its life cycle is haploid. Which of the following plants best fits this description?
e: Velvety green moss spends most of its life as a haploid plant, sending tiny swimming sperm on wet puddle adventures.

q: In a population of colorful parakeets, hunters often only kill the red parakeets because they are so easy to spot. What type of selection pressure does this illustrate?
e: Directional selection steers the whole flock in one path, favoring duller colors as bright red parakeets get spotted and picked off.

q: Which of the following statements it true about pollen?
a: Pollen must be transferred between plants by insects
Pollen travels through the style and directly fertilizes the ovule
Either before or after arriving on the stigma, each pollen grain undergoes a mitotic cell division producing two sperm
e: Each pollen grain divides into two tiny sperm cells, eagerly packing its bags to help make a brand-new seed.

q: Which of the following is the most detrimental type of point mutation?
e: A frameshift mutation scrambles a cell's whole recipe by shifting every letter, causing the most damaging genetic chaos!

q: What type of mammalian muscle is under voluntary control?
e: Whenever you decide to dance or wave, you are bossing around your skeletal muscles, which happily obey your commands.

q: From what source does the energy required for photsynthesis come?
e: Green leaves soak up warm sunlight like golden blankets, using that bright energy to cook up sweet plant food.

q: Lipids will dissolve best in which of the following:
e: Greasy fats and water just refuse to get along, but chloroform welcomes oily lipids with open arms and dissolves them easily.

q: Liver tissue in a monkey would be expected to be structurally most similar to which of the following tissues?
e: Since both do the same clever cleaning job in close primate cousins, monkey liver tissue looks just like human liver.

q: Which of the following is the BEST example of a heterozygous condition:
a: the matching alleles for a certain physical characteristic are different
one of a pair of chromosomes is lost
e: A heterozygous trait means having two different genetic instructions, like getting one brown-eyed allele and one blue-eyed allele.

q: Which of the following fish exhibit protandry and are all male when hatched?
e: Every baby clownfish hatches as a boy, but the bravest leader of the reef can transform into a female later!

q: Which of the following can be found in eukaryotes [YOU-care-ee-oats], but not in prokaryotes [PRO-care-ee-oats]?
e: Eukaryote cells have tiny, bustling powerhouses called mitochondria to make energy, but simpler prokaryotes must live without them.

q: Which of the following is true regarding viruses and viroids?
a: Viroids contain RNA; viruses do not
Viruses contain RNA; viroids do not
Viroids contain protein; viruses do not
Viruses contain protein; viroids do not
e: Sneaky viruses bundle up in protective coats made of protein, but tiny viroids wander around completely naked.

q: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells both contain:
e: Every single cell, tiny or grand, wraps itself in a soft cell membrane to keep its precious insides safe.

q: Which of the following animals would you have to eat in order to ingest a potentially lethal dose of tetrodotoxin [te-troh-duh-TOK-sin]?
e: Round little puffer fish carry dangerous tetrodotoxin inside their bellies to keep hungry sea critters from taking a bite!

q: Pollination of flowering plant species is carried out primarily by which of the following?
e: Hardworking insects, like buzzy bees and beetles, do the heavy lifting by delivering most of the plant world's pollen.

q: Which of the following plants is sometimes called a fiddlehead when it is immature:
e: Before it unfurls into leafy fronds, a young fern curls up tight like a violin neck called a fiddlehead.

q: What cell organelle is known as "the powerhouse of the cell?"
e: Mitochondria work like tiny, buzzing power plants, turning your snacks into all the energy you need to zoom around!

q: What effect does the wobble position in a codon have on protein synthesis?
a: The 2nd base can change and have no effect
The 3rd base is an absolute determinant
e: Think of the third letter as a goofy little dance partner who can wobble around without changing the cell's recipe at all!

q: To which of the following categories of living organisms does E. coli belong:
e: E. coli is a tiny, single-celled bacterium bustling inside our tummies to help digest our food.

q: Plasma is the part of human blood that consists mostly of which of the following?
e: Plasma is a swirling, golden river made mostly of pure water, carrying blood cells like merry little rafts on a journey.

q: Which scientist is credited with discovering cells?
e: Robert Hooke peeked through his microscope at cork and discovered tiny empty rooms he named cells!

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of bacteria?
e: Little bacteria keep their DNA floating freely inside because they do not have a cozy home called a nucleus.

q: Which of the following best describes a bacteriophage:
a: a stage in the development of most bacteria
the release of disease-causing bacteria from a host organism
e: A bacteriophage is actually a sneaky little virus that hunts down bacteria like a tiny space lander!

q: Feather color in chickens can be a codominant trait. You cross a white chicken with a black chicken. Which of the following phenotypes will you see in the first generation of chicks?
a: All of the chicks will be gray
The chicks will be more black than white
Each of the chicks will be black and white in about equal proportions
The chicks will be more white than black
e: Since both feather colors want to shine, each chick ends up delightfully speckled with black and white in equal parts!

q: Which of the following kingdoms contains organisms that directly produce methane as a byproduct of metabolism?
e: Ancient, tough little microbes called archaea love burping out stinky methane gas as they turn their food into energy!

q: What biome is dominant in sub-Saharan Africa and characterized by the dominant plants being fire resistant:
e: The sun-drenched African savanna is home to brave, fire-resistant trees that happily survive sweeping wildfires.

q: The oxygen released into the air as a product of photosynthesis comes from what?
e: When thirsty plants drink water, sunlight snaps those water drops apart to set fresh oxygen free into the air!

q: Which of the following is NOT a member of the order Cetacea?
e: Gentle, slow-swimming manatees are sirenians related to elephants, not cetaceans like speedy dolphins and whales.

q: Which of the following molecules gives carrots their orange color?
e: Carotene works like a tiny paintbrush dipped in sunshine, dressing up carrots in their bright orange coats.

q: Most extremophiles belong to which group of organisms?
e: Archaea are nature's toughest little adventurers, happily living in boiling hot springs and extreme places where nothing else survives.

q: Stamen is to anther as carpel is to:
e: Just like an anther crowns the stamen, a cozy ovary rests safely inside the carpel to protect baby seeds.

q: Which of the following is NOT an autoimmune disease?
e: Unlike autoimmune mix-ups where your body fights itself, shingles is actually caused by a sneaky chickenpox virus waking up.

q: Blood is classified as what type of body tissue?
e: Blood is connective tissue because it flows like a busy river, visiting and connecting every single neighborhood in your body!

q: What phase is the stage of the cell cycle in which proteins are made in preparation for DNA replication?
e: In the G1 phase, a growing cell stretches its legs and cooks up proteins to prepare for copying its DNA.

q: If a person has cyanosis, what color is his or her skin?
e: When blood runs low on fresh oxygen, cyanosis paints the skin a chilly shade of blue!

q: Which of the following are not considered to belong to the bryophyte [BRYE-oh- fite] group?
e: Mossy bryophytes stay tiny and hug the ground, but fancy ferns grew hidden plumbing pipes to carry water up high!

q: Which of the following biomes takes up more square area of the world than any other biome:
e: The vast taiga wraps around our world like a giant blanket of evergreen trees, covering more land than any other biome!

q: In which of the following areas of the human body is the frontal bone found:
e: Your frontal bone sits right at the front of your head, making up your forehead to protect your brilliant, daydreaming brain!

q: Which part of a dicot [DYE-kawt] seed has the greatest concentration of carbohydrates?
e: The endosperm acts like a cozy pantry packed with sugary carbohydrates, feeding the baby plant until it wakes up.

q: Which of the following anatomical structures is missing in the hagfish:
e: The slimy, ancient hagfish never grew a jaw, so it slurps its meals with a round, toothy mouth instead.

q: For which of the following situations would active transport be required?
a: Movement of ethanol across a cell membrane
Releasing carbon dioxide produced by respiration
Moving molecules against a concentration gradient
e: Active transport spends precious energy to push molecules uphill, forcing them against their natural crowd flow.

q: What do we call the evaporation of water from plants that occurs chiefly while their stomata are open for the passage of carbon dioxide and oxygen during photosynthesis (read as: fe-te-SIN-teh-sis)?
e: Transpiration is like plant sweat, where thirsty leaves breathe out water droplets into the sunny sky.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of heterokonts?
e: Heterokonts love living everywhere, thriving in fresh lakes and damp soil just as happily as in salty ocean water.

q: Which of the following best explains why most food chains have fewer than five organisms in them?
a: Energy is too complex to cycle through multiple steps
The amount of energy at the producer level can only support a limited number of consumers
There is only enough room on Earth for a certain number of animals, and they are divided into food chains
Ecosystems can only support a certain number of organisms, and they are divided into food chains
e: Plants only catch so much sun, so energy runs out before it can feed more than a few hungry creatures.

q: In birds, which of the following is the correct order of organs in digestion?
e: A bird stores seeds in its crop, softens them in the stomach, grinds them in the gizzard, and digests them in the intestine.

q: Which of the following plant cell components is responsible for making a connection between the cytoplasm of adjacent cells?
e: Plasmodesmata are like tiny secret doorways between plant cells, letting friendly neighbors share messages and sips of water.

q: Which of the following eukaryotic organelles contains digestive enzymes at maturity?
e: A lysosome is the cell's tidy recycling bin, packed with digestive enzymes to melt down old leftovers.

q: Which of the following kinds of microscopes typically is used to view the surface of objects ranging in size from cells to small insects like fleas to reveal minute surface details:
e: A scanning electron microscope bounces beams of tiny particles off flea coats to reveal unbelievable, 3D surface details!

q: Which of the following is closest to the length of time it takes for a typical human cell to complete mitosis:
e: Making a brand-new copy is a big job, taking a busy human cell about one whole day to divide!

q: Antibiotics are completely ineffective at treating the causative agent of which of the following diseases?
e: Antibiotics only defeat bad bacteria, so they are totally helpless against influenza, which is caused by a sneaky virus.

q: Which of the following structures is too small to be seen reliably with a basic light microscope with a 400-times objective?
e: A viral capsid is so teeny-tiny that regular light microscopes cannot spot it without special superpower lenses.

q: Scientists are using genetic engineering to develop a wheat crop that is resistant to a particular kind of moth. How would they determine if the plants are moth resistant?
a: Determine the length of the moth reproductive cycle in normal wheat
Monitor moth populations in separate fields planted with control and experimental wheat crops
Monitor numbers of moth species infesting normal wheat
Determine whether moths in test wheat can be controlled with chemical sprays
e: Scientists compare moth numbers between fields of regular wheat and experimental wheat to see if the new plants truly repel bugs.

q: Cartilage belongs to which of the following animal tissues types:
e: Cartilage is connective tissue because it acts like trusty glue, cushioning and linking your bones together with bouncy flexibility.

q: Ornamentation often contributes to the mating behavior and choices of animals. Male elks are highly ornamented. Which of the following types of mating system would you expect?
e: Bull elk show off giant antlers to win a whole herd of female admirers, a grand family style called polygyny!

q: Bacteria are commonly used to produce which of the following?
e: Helpful little bacteria brew vinegar by munching on alcohol and magically turning it into sharp, tangy liquid!

q: Which of the following is the organ mainly responsible for producing digestive enzymes and insulin:
e: Your pancreas is a multitasking hero, whipping up digestive enzymes for your food and insulin to balance your sugar.

q: Into which of the following does a typical fern spore most directly develop:
e: When a tiny fern spore lands, it sprouts directly into a little heart-shaped gametophyte to start the next generation.

q: In which of the following locations does the Calvin cycle take place?
e: Plant leaves make sweet sugar right in the stroma, the cozy fluid-filled kitchen inside chloroplasts.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about the Iberian lynx?
a: It is one of the most endangered cat species in the world
It can leap more than 19 feet horizontally and more than 9 feet vertically
It has a characteristic beard around its face
e: While this bearded wildcat is a champion hopper, leaping nineteen feet is a superpower meant for snow leopards, not the lynx.

q: Which of the following is true of virus genomes [JEE-nomes]?
a: They are always composed of DNA
They may be composed of either DNA or RNA
e: Tiny viruses pack light for their adventures, carrying an instruction book made of either DNA or its cousin, RNA.

q: What is the medical term for low blood sugar?
e: Hypoglycemia happens when your body's fuel tank runs low on sugar, leaving your energy engines feeling sleepy.

q: Organisms of the same class would also share which of the following?
e: Think of a phylum as a giant family tree branch, so any critters sharing a class must sit together on that same branch.

q: Which of the following organisms has an archegonium:
e: Tiny green moss hugs the forest floor, using little flask-shaped homes called archegonia to keep its precious eggs safe and snug.

q: Which of the following is LEAST likely to be found in or on a root of a flowering plant:
e: Roots work in the dark underground, so they do not need stomata, which are tiny mouth-like breathing pores on sunny leaves.

q: Which of these is NOT a bone found in the human arm?
e: Your arm bones love waving hello, but the sturdy tibia lives way down in your lower leg!

q: Which of the following biomes would be characterized by a large proportion of coniferous trees, populations of hibernating mammals, moraine lakes, and bogs?
e: Bundle up in the snowy taiga, a wonderland packed with cone-bearing evergreen trees and sleepy creatures snoozing through the cold winter!

q: Adipose tissue stores mostly:
e: Adipose tissue acts like a cozy squishy blanket, packing away energy in the form of rich lipids, or fats.

q: Given no other information, which of the following nutrients would you expect to be in highest abundance in a field planted entirely with red clover?
e: Clever clover plants team up with friendly root bacteria to pull rich nitrogen from the air, happily feeding the soil beneath them.

q: Homo sapiens is the scientific name for which of the following?
e: Look right in the mirror! Homo sapiens is simply the fancy scientific name for curious, story-telling human beings like you and me.

q: In photosynthesis, during which of the following stages is oxygen released as a byproduct?
e: Photosystem two cracks open water droplets with sunlight, puffing out fresh oxygen like a tiny breath of fresh air for the world!

q: Which of the following factors does NOT affect the rate of photosynthesis?
e: Plants make their food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide, so outside free oxygen doesn't change their cooking speed.

q: Which of the following enzymes most likely catalyses the removal of electrons:
e: An oxidase enzyme is a busy little helper that loves to pluck electrons away from other molecules during chemical adventures.

q: The exchange of gases between blood and the tissue occurs normally in:
e: Teeny-tiny capillaries have walls so thin that fresh oxygen can easily hop out of the blood and give nearby tissues a hug.

q: Which of the following human diseases is dominant?
e: Huntington's disease is dominant because just a single copy of that bossy gene is enough to cause the illness.

q: Which of the following pairs of structures can be considered homologous [hoe-MAWL-uh-gus]?
e: A human hand and a cat paw share the exact same bone blueprint, like secret family cousins wearing different gloves.

q: Which of the following BEST describes muscle tone:
a: length versus width of a muscle
average energy use or oxygen use of a fully contracted muscle
amount of tension or contraction of a resting muscle
e: Even when you are snoozing, your muscles keep a tiny bit of tension called muscle tone so they are always ready to spring into action.

q: The difference between xylem [ZY-luhm] and phloem [FLOH-em] is which of the following?
a: Xylem transports water and dissolved nutrients, while phloem transports dissolved organic materials in an aqueous solution [AK-wee-uhs]
Phloem transports water and minerals, while xylem transports sugars
Phloem is not found in plants, while xylem is only present in plants
Xylem is not found in plants, while phloem is only present in plants
e: Xylem sips water upward from thirsty roots, while phloem delivers delicious, sugary snacks to every corner of the plant.

q: Chromosomal polyploidy results in which of the following phenotypic differences in fruits and vegetables?
e: Packing extra sets of chromosomes makes plant cells puff up like balloons, adding serious weight to your favorite juicy fruits.

q: What is the scientific name of the Common Chimpanzee?
e: Pan troglodytes is the special scientific name given to our clever, fruit-loving chimpanzee cousins.

q: The tracheal system in insects includes many small external openings on the sides of their bodies. What function does this system serve?
e: Bugs use these tiny side doorways to breathe, sending fresh air straight to their wiggling muscles.

q: Which of following correctly pairs a monomer with one of its corresponding polymers?
