q: Which of the following birds dives below the ocean surface to find fish?
e: Petrels bravely plunge beneath the rolling waves, using their wings like underwater flippers to chase down slippery fish!

q: Which of the following is a phylum of plants that is characterized by naked or uncovered seeds?
e: Gymnosperms, like pine trees, proudly show off their naked seeds out in the open without any cozy fruit covers!

q: Which of the following is an example of a multiple fruit?
e: A pineapple is actually a big party of dozens of little flowers, all fusing together to make one yummy multiple fruit!

q: Which of the following is NOT an effect of the sympathetic nervous system?
e: In fight-or-flight mode, your body widens your eyes to spot danger, so constriction of pupils is not part of the rush.

q: A scientist performs a Gram stain on an unknown strain of bacteria and observes that the bacteria are stained purple. What does this indicate about the bacteria?
a: Their nuclei are high in collagen
Their cell walls contain large amounts of peptidoglycan
Their cell walls are surrounded by lipotoxins
e: That lovely purple color means these tiny critters wear thick jackets made of peptidoglycan, soaking up dye like a sponge.

q: Exopolymeric substances, or EPS, are exuded by microorganisms during times of environmental stress. Which of the following is NOT a function of EPS?
e: This gooey slime shields germs from drying out, but it cannot feed them, so it offers no protection against starvation.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the bald eagle?
a: They have both binocular and peripheral vision
They only eat animals they capture themselves
They are thought to mate for life
They tend to construct their nests near water
e: Majestic bald eagles love easy meals, happily snatching snacks from other birds or scavenging leftovers instead of always hunting fresh prey.

q: Which of the following plants traps and digests insects:
e: A sundew plant sparkles with sweet, sticky drops that trick curious bugs, gluing them tight so it can digest them.

q: What part of the brain takes its name from the Greek for seahorse?
e: Tucked inside your brain, the memory-making hippocampus curls up looking just like a tiny seahorse, which is what its name means!

q: An amphibian species is on the verge of being lost from all ecosystems in which it previously lived. Which term best describes this species?
e: When these amphibians are dangerously close to vanishing from the world forever, they are called endangered so we can rush in to protect them.

q: The haploidy [HAP-loy-dee] of gametes [GAM-eets] supports which of Gregor Mendel's laws?
e: Gregor Mendel's law of segregation explains how gene pairs split up, ensuring each gamete carries just one copy instead of two.

q: Which of the following is the hormone produced by the human body to control blood sugar and when not produced in sufficient amounts is the cause of some forms of diabetes:
e: Insulin is the body's friendly helper that controls blood sugar, making sure your cells get fuel so diabetes does not stop the fun.

q: The suffix, "wort," is commonly found in the names of which of the following?
e: Long ago, gardeners used the friendly word wort as an old-fashioned nickname for helpful, leafy herbs.

q: Within the land plants, which of the following groups has the greatest number of species?
e: With hundreds of thousands of colorful cousins blooming everywhere, flowering plants easily outnumber all other plant families on land.

q: Which of the following types of plant cell tissue is considered the least specialized?
e: Parenchyma cells are like a plant’s all-purpose handymen, doing everyday chores without needing any fancy, specialized upgrades.

q: A carnivorous animal eats flesh, what does a nucivorous animal eat?
e: Just like a busy squirrel packing its cheeks for winter, a nucivorous creature loves crunching on tasty nuts.

q: What is the largest part of the brain?
e: The cerebrum is the big, wrinkly brain boss, taking up the most space to handle all your brilliant thoughts and daydreams!

q: What is the colour of unoxidized blood?
e: Even when it is resting and low on fresh oxygen, your blood is always a cozy, deep red shade.

q: What is the term for the process of programmed cell death that helps structures develop shape during development?
e: Apoptosis is nature’s master sculptor, gently telling extra cells when to disappear so your fingers can neatly separate!

q: Indoleacetic acid is the most common of what group of hormones?
e: Indoleacetic acid belongs to the auxin family, the plant whisperers that tell growing green stems to reach for the sun.

q: Which of the following terms is used to describe the extra copy of a chromosome synthesized during S phase prior to mitosis?
e: When a chromosome makes an identical twin copy of itself, that shiny new partner is called a sister chromatid.

q: Which of the following is least likely to be impacted by decreased environmental pH?
e: While acidic water dissolves chalky shells, tough little diatoms build their homes out of sturdy glass and stay perfectly safe.

q: Which of the following has the steps of mitosis placed in the correct order?
e: Cells divide in an orderly dance: prophase packs up, metaphase lines up, anaphase pulls apart, and telophase builds two new homes!

q: Which of the following animals best exhibits aposematic [ap-oh-seh-MAT-ik] coloration as a defense mechanism?
e: With bright yellow and black stripes, a bee wears bold warning colors to tell hungry predators, 'Watch out, I sting!'

q: Which of the following accurately matches the part of the flower and its description?
a: Top part of the stamen that produces and bears pollen - sepal
Swollen base of the flower than attaches it to the stem - carpel
Sticky part of the flower's carpel that traps pollen grains - stigma
Part of the flower containing the ovules that later develop into seeds - anther
e: Like a sweet little landing pad, the stigma stays super sticky so it can trap passing grains of pollen!

q: Hirudinea [HEER-oo-din-ee-ah] is a class that contains which of the following organisms?
e: Leeches belong to the Hirudinea family, squirming through the water like little stretchy ribbons looking for a warm snack.

q: Which of the following elements is found in DNA?
e: Phosphorus acts like the sturdy glue in DNA's backbone, holding the steps of your body's instruction book safely together.

q: Integral membrane proteins are firmly associated with the cell membrane lipid bilayer and are only removable by agents that interfere with what type of interactions?
e: These proteins nestle deep inside the oily membrane, held tightly by hydrophobic bonds that love hiding away from water.

q: As an adaptation to arid environments, Crassulacean [kras-uh-LAY-shuhn] acid metabolizing (CAM) plants open their stomata during the night and close them during the day. Which of the following is a CAM plant?
e: Pineapples are clever desert survivors, holding their breath during the blazing day and opening up at night to save precious water!

q: Pellagra [puh-LAG-ruh] results from a deficiency of what?
e: Our bodies need vitamin B3 to stay energized, so missing this vital nutrient causes an uncomfortable illness called pellagra.

q: Which of the following chemical bonds is most important in DNA secondary structure?
e: Gentle hydrogen bonds hold DNA's twisting ladder together, acting like tiny magnetic hands that can unzip and zip right back up!

q: What is the name of the respiratory disease that is categorized by the inflammation of the mucus membrane?
e: When your breathing tubes get irritated and swollen with sticky mucus, doctors call that grumpy chest tickle bronchitis.

q: Which of the following blood vessels carries oxygenated blood?
e: Fresh off a visit to your lungs, the pulmonary vein happily rushes back to the heart loaded with crisp, clean oxygen.

q: Which of the following terms is used by microbiologists for a bacterium with a rod shape:
e: Meet bacillus, a tiny rod-shaped germ that looks just like a microscopic hot dog rolling around under the microscope!

q: What is the greatest source of organic material that reaches the sea floor?
a: Minerals dissolved in superheated water from hydrothermal vents
e: Trillions of tiny dead phytoplankton drift down like underwater snowflakes, making a delicious feast that covers the ocean floor.

q: Cyamids, commonly known as whale lice, are tiny crustaceans that live on the skin of whales. Cyamids obtain nutrition from the whale by feeding on dead skin and algae that grow on the whale's body; it is believed that whales are not helped or harmed by their presence. This type of biological relationship can best be described as which of the following?
e: In commensalism, tiny whale lice hitch a free ride and snack, while the giant whale does not mind a bit!

q: Which of the following breeds of dogs would be least likely to be trained as a seeing eye dog?
e: Chinese shar-peis have deep, wrinkly folds around their eyes, making it tricky for them to see clearly enough to guide someone!

q: Within which of the following tissues would one find the largest number of reticulocytes [reh-TIK-yoo-loh-sites], which are immature red blood cells?
e: Inside your bones, a bustling factory works non-stop to build brand-new baby red blood cells called reticulocytes!

q: In which of the following environments would a thermophilic bacteria most likely evolve:
e: Thermophilic bacteria adore bubbling heat, making a cozy hot spring their absolute favorite place to grow and thrive.

q: The evolution of flowers in many plants is believed to have depended most directly on the presence and evolution of which of the following:
e: Flowers dressed up in bright colors and sweet smells so hungry insect pollinators would visit and help them reproduce!

q: Which of the following is the plant hormone MOST directly responsible for plants growing towards a light source:
e: A clever plant helper named auxin stretches the shady side of a stem, gently bending the sprout toward the warm sun.

q: Plants are comprised of three main non-reproductive organs. Which of the following choices correctly summarizes these three organs?
e: Long before making flowers, every plant relies on thirsty roots below, strong stems to stand tall, and green leaves soaking up sunshine.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of regular echinoids (read as: i-KY-nohids)?
e: Spiky regular echinoids are round and five-sided, leaving fancy branched tentacles to their sea cucumber cousins instead.

q: What is the study of the cells and tissues of plants and animals?
e: Histology is the wonderful science of peering through a microscope to explore the cozy neighborhoods of plant and animal tissues.

q: Which of the following is the BEST explanation why fruit flies are popular experimental organisms in genetic studies:
a: they are true breeding with almost no mutations and have only two chromosomes
they are cheap to maintain, produce many offspring, and have a short time between generations
they are very safe, carry no human diseases, and have only two chromosomes
their genes are extra-sensitive to mutation-causing substances, which makes them excellent to observe evolving under stress
e: Fruit flies are tiny science champions because they grow up fast, cost pennies, and quickly welcome hundreds of babies.

q: Epiphytes [EP-uh-fyts] primarily obtain water and nutrients through what?
e: Living high up on tree branches, epiphytes drink rain and catch nutrients directly through their thirsty leaves.

q: Which of the following groups of organic compounds in the human body are the most diverse in size, shape, and function?
e: Proteins are nature's ultimate shapeshifters, folding into endless forms to tackle almost every job in your body!

q: A glacier splits a population of rabbits in two. Which of the following best describes what might happen in the two populations over a long period of time?
e: When an icy glacier separates rabbit families, allopatric speciation takes over as the two groups slowly evolve into different species.

q: FAD [F.A.D.] is a cofactor derived from what vitamin?
e: Vitamin B helps build busy molecules like FAD, working inside you to turn yummy lunch snacks into pure playground energy!

q: Myopia is the scientific term for which condition?
e: Myopia is shortsightedness, making distant trees look blurry while a cozy book up close stays crystal clear.

q: Which of the following is the longest snake alive today?
e: Stretching out longer than two tall adults lying head to toe, the reticulated python wins the crown for the longest snake!

q: Which of the following terms best describes the inheritance of the A and B antigen genes in human blood?
e: In co-dominance, genes A and B team up as equal partners, both proudly showing their faces on your red blood cells!

q: Which of the following is closest, in days, to the average red blood cell's circulation lifetime?
e: Each hardworking little red blood cell zooms through your body for about 120 days before retiring from its wild circulatory ride!

q: Which of the following infectious diseases cannot be cured with current antibiotics:
e: Antibiotics only zap pesky bacteria, so they cannot cure influenza, which is caused by a sneaky virus instead.

q: As a tree ages, which of the following BEST describes what happens to the secondary phloem:
a: it accumulates in large quantities into the xylem
it is crushed between each year's xylem
it is lost as part of the bark and does not accumulate in great quantities
e: As a growing tree gets wider, its older phloem is pushed outward, flaking away as bark instead of piling up inside!

q: Unlike eukaryotes [yoo-KAR-ee-ohts], prokaryotes [proh- KAR-ee-ohts] typically have only one chromosome. Which of the following is a unique characteristic of prokaryotic [proh-KAR-ee-oht-ik] genomes?
e: While our DNA stretches out like shoelaces, tiny bacteria connect their single chromosome into one continuous circle.

q: Which of the following phenomena does NOT contribute to water's ability to move against gravity through a plant's vascular system?
e: While xylem pulls water upward, phloem pressure is busy sending sugary snacks downward, so it cannot lift water up tall trees.

q: What is the collective noun for bears?
e: A cozy group of sleepy bears lumbering together through the woods is delightfully called a sloth.

q: You press down on your arm and feel a pulse beating. From which of the following types of blood vessels is the pulse originating?
e: Every heartbeat sends a powerful rush of blood through your stretchy arteries, which you can feel dancing right under your fingertips!

q: Which of the following statements about wood in a tree is NOT true?
a: Wood is made of secondary xylem [ZY-luhm] and fibers
The oldest wood is at the center of the tree while younger wood is towards the periphery
Annual rings consist of both early (spring) wood and late (summer) wood
True wood is only found in monocots, while dicots do not produce true wood
e: Monocots like grasses and palms cannot make true wood; that sturdy trick belongs to dicots like oak trees and conifers.

q: Which of the following structures do bacteria use to transfer DNA during conjugation?
e: Friendly bacteria reach out with tiny, hair-like bridges called pili to pass genetic recipes to their neighbors!

q: For reasons known only to her, Susie wants her houseplant Reggie the Radish to make as much oxygen as possible. Which of the following should Susie do to increase Reggie's rate of oxygen production?
a: Bring in more plants to reduce the levels of carbon dioxide in the room
Put the plant in the corner of the room where there is less light present
Put a humidifier next to the plant
Set the thermostat to the lowest temperature possible in the room
e: Humid air keeps leafy pores wide open without drying out, letting the plant happily photosynthesize and release more oxygen.

q: In mammals, what teeth are evolved primarily to function in gripping and tearing:
e: Pointy canine teeth act like sharp little hooks, perfectly shaped for gripping and tearing into tasty food!

q: What is the location of the biceps femoris muscle?
e: Tucked along the back of your thigh, this powerful muscle helps bend your leg for every joyful jump!

q: What is the joint that is formed by the articulation of the tibia, fibula, and femur?
e: Your knee is the wonderful hinge where your long thigh bone meets the two lower leg bones to keep you running!

q: Which of the following is the best reason that snakes do not reproduce with worms?
e: Mechanical isolation simply means their body parts do not fit together, like trying to plug a garden hose into a keyhole.

q: Which of the following is NOT a main class of connective tissue in humans?
e: While every tissue is packed with cells, cellular is just a description, not a main connective tissue group like bone or cartilage.

q: What is the purpose of the Eustachian tube [yoo-STAY- shuhn]?
a: It improves outer ear transmission of sound
It improves vibration of the malleus
It clears mucous from the middle ear into the throat
e: This clever little hallway acts like a drainage pipe, sweeping sticky mucus safely out of your middle ear into your throat.

q: Amylase [AM-il-ace] catalyzes the digestion of starch into sugars. The presence of high amounts of amylase in the blood is likely to be associated with dysfunction of which of the following organs?
e: Your pancreas is the hard-working chef that cooks up amylase, so too much in your blood means it needs help.

q: The cancer that is frequently associated with asbestos exposure is which of the following?
e: Breathing in sharp asbestos dust can harm the chest lining, leading to a serious illness called mesothelioma.

q: Which of the following types of plant cell tissue is considered most important for structural support?
e: Sclerenchyma cells build extra-tough, woody walls, acting like sturdy wooden beams that keep tall plants standing proud against the wind.

q: What is the innermost layer of the root cortex?
e: Deep inside the root cortex, the endodermis forms the innermost ring, acting like a gentle security gate for water.

q: What structures are responsible for delivering amino acids to the ribosome [RYE-beh-sohm]?
e: Meet tRNA, the bustling delivery scooter that zooms over to the ribosome factory with fresh amino acid building blocks.

q: A photosynthetic cell might have more of what organelle than a non-photosynthetic cell?
e: Sun-loving plant cells stay extra busy making food, so they need more peroxisomes to tidy up chemical messes.

q: You catch a common cold from one of your Science Bowl teammates. Which of the following would be LEAST effective for treating your symptoms?
e: Colds are caused by sneaky viruses, so antibiotics cannot help you because they only battle bacteria!

q: Which of the following processes represents asexual reproduction in bacteria?
e: When a tiny bacterium wants to start a family, binary fission lets it simply pop right in half to make an identical twin!

q: Which of the following are the result of the 5' to 3' [5-prime to 3-prime] directionality of DNA polymerase [POL-uh-muh-rays]?
a: Degradation of the 3' to 5' strand of parental DNA
e: Because the copier can only build in one direction, it makes the backwards strand in short puzzle pieces called Okazaki fragments.

q: Human pregnancy tests detect levels of which of the following hormones?
e: Pregnancy tests look for chorionic gonadotropin, a special chemical hello that a brand-new, growing baby whispers into Mom's body.

q: Which of the following statements about pancreatic cancer is NOT true?
a: Early pancreatic cancer usually does not cause symptoms
Pancreatic cancer often remains contained within the pancreas
Smoking is a risk factor for pancreatic cancer
Pancreatic cancer is difficult to cure
e: Pancreatic cancer is sneaky and rarely stays put. Instead of remaining contained, it loves to wander off and spread to other organs.

q: You are looking through a microscope at an unlabeled sample of human tissue. You notice the tissue is multinucleated, and contains striations. What tissue are you examining?
e: Striped and packed with many nuclei, skeletal muscles are the mighty tissue helping your bones run and jump!

q: Which of the following is likely to occur when applying water or heat from an iron to reversibly straighten hair?
e: Warm water or a hot iron gently unzips weak hydrogen bonds holding hair keratin together, letting bouncy curls relax flat.

q: Charles Darwin used what process to illustrate the mechanisms of natural selection?
e: Darwin pointed to artificial selection, showing how pigeon breeders pick their favorite birds, to reveal how nature gently does the same.

q: The majority of ocean organisms living in hydrothermal vents are believed to be which of the following?
e: Down in the pitch-black deep sea, trillions of super-tough bacteria happily feast on hot chemicals where almost nothing else can survive.

q: Honeybees and other pollinators transfer pollen from the:
a: Anther to the Stigma of the Flower
Stigma to the Anther of the Flower
Filament to the Sepal of the Flower
Sepal to the Filament of the Flower
e: A busy bee dusts yellow powder off the flower's pollen-packed anther and delivers it straight to the sticky stigma next door.

q: Which of the following organisms exhibits radial symmetry?
e: Shaped like a living wheel, a sea star's matching arms spread outward in a circle from its center.

q: Which of the following processes is directly related to coral bleaching?
e: When ocean waters get too warm, stressed corals lose their colorful algae roommates, called zooxanthellae, turning ghostly white.

q: Which of the following is the most specific place where the subunits of ribosomes are made in eukaryotes?
e: Deep inside the nucleus sits the nucleolus, a cozy, bustling workshop dedicated to assembling the pieces of shiny new ribosomes.

q: What is the limiting factor for phytoplankton productivity in the tropical open ocean?
e: Even under warm sunny skies, floating plankton cannot grow big and strong without tasty mineral nutrients to feed on.

q: Which portion of the Marijuana plant produces the psychoactive substance known as THC?
e: The plant makes THC mainly inside its sticky female flowers, using tiny glittering glands to create the powerful chemical.

q: What stage of development do the majority of eukaryotic cells remain in for most of their life?
e: Cells spend most of their cozy lives in interphase, happily growing, eating, and prepping before ever dividing.

q: Which of the following neurotransmitters is utilized at all vertebrate neuromuscular junctions?
e: Whenever your brain tells a muscle to move, acetylcholine is the busy chemical messenger that rushes over to trigger the twitch.

q: How does coral reproduce?
a: It is pollinated by other fish
Eggs and sperm are released in the open water
Male and female coral attract each other
e: Corals throw a giant underwater blizzard party, releasing millions of eggs and sperm to meet and float together on ocean currents!

q: Which of the following is TRUE regarding the differences between RNA and DNA?
a: RNA is used as a catalyst, while DNA is not
RNA cannot be replicated, but DNA can
RNA is always single-stranded, while DNA is always double-stranded
RNA is more stable than DNA
e: While DNA sits quietly guarding the cell's blueprints, energetic RNA rolls up its sleeves to speed up chemical reactions as a catalyst.

q: How many net molecules of ATP does glycolysis [gly- KOL-uh-sis] produce?
e: Glycolysis spends two tiny energy coins to break down sugar and earns four back, leaving a neat profit of 2 ATP.

q: Which of the following terms is used to define benthic organisms that live in the spaces between particles of sediment?
e: Meiofauna are teeny-tiny critters small enough to play hide-and-seek between individual grains of sand on the seafloor.

q: In which of the following types of interspecific interaction is there no negative effect on either species involved?
e: In commensalism, one creature gets a sweet perk while its partner is not bothered at all, so nobody gets harmed.

q: What type of virus has the Food and Drug Administration recently approved to be sprayed on certain foods as a preservative against bacterial contamination:
e: A bacteriophage is a tiny viral hero that only hunts sneaky bacteria, keeping our favorite foods fresh and safe to eat.

q: When you have the flu, what part of the nervous system is responsible for elevating your body temperature?
e: The hypothalamus is your brain's trusty thermostat, cranking up the heat to bake away pesky flu bugs.

q: A cell is undergoing mitosis and has its paired chromatids [CROW- mah-tids] aligned at the center of the cell. In what stage of mitosis is the cell?
e: During metaphase, eager little chromosomes line right up across the cell's middle, like dancers ready for their big split!

q: Which of the following is a reason why a prion is different from a virus?
a: Viruses are not alive and do not have genomes
Viruses are much smaller than prions
Prions do not contain nucleic acids
Prions are always enveloped, while only some viruses are
e: Viruses carry suitcases of genetic instructions, but mischievous prions are just folded proteins traveling with no nucleic acids at all.

q: If birth and death rates are equal and a population is growing, what is the most likely relationship between immigration and emigration?
a: The same amount of immigration as emigration
e: When births match deaths, a population grows only when immigration brings in more new neighbors than emigration takes away.

q: Which of the following mutations in a coding region would cause the LEAST damage to the rest of the translated protein?
e: Because the cell reads letters in threes, adding three bases slips in one extra part without scrambling the rest of the protein.

q: Mercury and some other toxins have the ability to bioaccumulate in higher trophic levels. This is partially due to the fact that these toxins are soluble in which of the following?
e: Sneaky toxins melt right into an animal's body fat, hiding there safely instead of washing away.

q: Which of the following is the site where small and large subunits of ribosomes (read as: RY-boh-sems) are assembled?
e: Deep inside the nucleus sits the nucleolus, a cozy little factory where protein-making ribosome parts are carefully snapped together.

q: Which of the following is the best explanation as to why germs that infect a certain family of animals will often NOT be able to infect a different family of animals:
a: different metabolic pathways exist in different animals
germs gain entry into cells by binding to receptors which are often specific to certain groups of organisms
the immune systems of different animals prevents infection of unusual diseases
germs reproduce only when genes in a cell allow them
e: Germs carry special keys that only fit the receptor locks on cells of certain animal families.

q: A blood cell is placed into a salt solution and is observed to shrink. What type of solution was the blood cell placed in?
e: In a hypertonic solution, extra salty water outside lures moisture out of the cell, leaving it shriveled like a sad raisin.

q: Pampas, steppes, and savannas are all different types of:
e: Pampas, steppes, and savannas are all giant grasslands, rolling like endless seas of waving green across our wide world.

q: Which of the following accounts for the largest increase in cancer death rate in the USA between the years 1900 and 1990:
e: As smoking became very popular during the twentieth century, lung cancer tragically saw the biggest rise in deaths.

q: Which of the following exhibits quaternary [QUAH-tur-nairee] protein structure?
e: Hemoglobin has quaternary structure because four protein teammates clasp together like a squad to carry oxygen through your blood.

q: In a heart transplant patient, which of the following cells causes transplant rejection by attacking the heart?
e: Overprotective T cells spot the borrowed heart, mistakenly see it as an enemy invader, and launch an attack.

q: Which of the following animals possesses a lateral line?
e: A clever fish uses its lateral line like an invisible superpower, feeling every ripple and wave tickling through the water.

q: The "mountain chicken" is a chicken.
e: Nature loves surprises; the mountain chicken isn't a feathered bird at all, but a giant, croaking frog!

q: The Axiom of Preventive Medicine states that people with ___ risk for a disease should be screened and we should treat ___ of those people.
e: This rule focuses on helping everyone in the low risk group, since tiny helps across whole communities prevent the most illness.

q: Most of the wood in a typical 100 year old oak tree is made of which of the following cells?
e: A grand old oak builds its sturdy wood out of xylem, trusty little water pipes that banded together over decades.

q: Which of the following are not found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes?
e: Tiny prokaryotes are far too simple to hold mitochondria, those bustling little powerhouses found only inside complex eukaryote cells.

q: Which of the following patterns of inheritance are NOT correctly paired?
a: Red, pink, white color in flowers - sex-linked inheritance
e: Pink snapdragons come from incomplete dominance, not sex-linked traits, blending mom and dad's colors like wet paint.

q: A textbook picture shows two magnified images of different organelles. Image A shows the first organelle magnified 18,000 times. Image B shows the second organelle magnified 350 times. Both look the same size on the page. Which organelle is smaller?
a: They are both the same size
You can't tell from the information given
e: Organelle A is much smaller because the microscope had to zoom in eighteen thousand times just to show its tiny face.

q: Which of the following would be most effective for treating a human collagen deficiency?
e: Your body needs vitamin C like a cheerful master builder, using it to glue your tissues together with strong collagen.

q: While dissecting a plant in your botany class, which of the following tissues would you NOT see?
e: You will not spot ectoderm in a plant because that special outer layer belongs strictly to growing animal embryos.

q: The difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, is that prokaryotic cells lack what organelle?
e: Prokaryotic cells let their DNA wander freely, because they never built a cozy nucleus room to hold it.

q: What is the name for the microscopic pores on the surface of leaves and stems in plants through which gas exchange occurs ?
e: Stomata are like millions of microscopic green mouths on leaves, opening wide to take deep breaths of air.

q: What are rhino's horn made of?
e: That impressive horn is not bone at all, but tightly packed keratin, the very same stuff that makes your fingernails!

q: In which of the following classifications is a bacteriophage?
e: A bacteriophage is actually a sneaky little virus, shaped like a tiny moon lander that infects unsuspecting bacteria.

q: Which of the following types of joints can be found in the knuckles of a human index finger?
e: Your index knuckle is an ellipsoid joint, letting your finger happily wave up, down, and side to side.

q: Which of the following properties of water allow tall trees to transport water to the canopy?
e: Water molecules hold hands tightly and cling to tree walls, helping them climb all the way to the tippity-top leaves!

q: During what period are the first reptiles thought to have emerged?
e: In the swampy, giant-tree forests of the Carboniferous period, the very first scaly reptiles made their grand entrance onto land!

q: Which of the following terms refers to signals that are secreted by glands into the bloodstream, and have effects on distant organs?
e: Endocrine signals are like messages floating down a bloodstream river, traveling far away to whisper instructions to distant organs.

q: Which of the following is the BEST explanation for what would happen to a red blood cell if it were placed in a 25% sugar solution:
a: it would lose salt to the sugar solution and gain sugar and remain the same size
it would gain salt and swell
it would lose water to the sugar solution and gain salt and remain the same size
it would lose water to the sugar solution and shrink
e: Surrounded by thick, thirsty sugar water, the red blood cell loses its own water and wrinkles up like a tiny raisin.

q: Which of the following statements is TRUE?
a: the human y chromosome has hundreds of known genes
mutations are changes in the genetic code found in DNA
humans have the largest brains per body size than any other animal that has ever lived on Earth
all infectious agents are caused by some sort of living organism
e: DNA is a wonderful instruction manual for life, and mutations are simply little typos that change the code.

q: What structures on the outside of bacteria are MOST typically associated with the ability of bacteria to control their movement:
e: Flagella act like little motorboat propellers, spinning around to steer a tiny bacterium on its grand adventures.

q: The ocean's distinct smell comes from dimethyl [dy-METH- uhl] sulfide (DMS), which is released upon the death of what ocean organism?
e: That salty seaside smell comes from tiny phytoplankton, microscopic ocean drifters that release a puff of scent when they die.

q: Which of the following organisms is NOT a thallophyte (read as: THAH-loh-fyt)?
e: While thallophytes are simple plant-like algae, Entamoeba is a squishy microscopic amoeba that belongs to the protozoan family instead.

q: Which of the following characteristics is NOT true of the herbicide Paraquat?
a: It is non-selective, killing a wide range of annual grasses and broad-leaved weeds
It is linked to the development of Parkinson's disease
It remains biologically active in the soil for approximately 60 days
e: Paraquat loves soil so much that dirt hugs it tight, putting its weed-fighting powers to sleep almost immediately instead of lasting sixty days.

q: Which of the following is the BEST example of how evolution progresses:
a: animals learn to survive through experience and teach their offspring
certain mutations improve an organism's offspring's chances to survive and reproduce in different environments
animals develop certain strengths and weaknesses through experience and pass the knowledge down by example
an animal that is successful at hunting will be more likely to survive
e: Helpful genetic changes give baby creatures special superpowers to survive tough challenges and pass those gifts to their own young!

q: The Latin phrase in vitro now commonly means what?
e: In Latin, this phrase means in glass, describing cozy science experiments bubbling safely inside artificial lab dishes instead of living bodies.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about botulism?
a: It is caused by a virus
Food-borne botulism can thrive in raw honey
Its toxin can be used to reduce severe underarm sweating
e: Botulism is not caused by a virus, but by a crafty little bacterium that makes a powerful toxin.

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
e: An octopus has three big hearts beating together, working as a team to pump blue blood through its chilly ocean home.

q: Which of the following is the LEAST likely method a maple tree uses to regulate water:
a: opening and closing stomata in stems and leaves
e: A tree's heartwood is its sturdy, retired center, happily holding the trunk up while younger outer wood does all the heavy water lifting.

q: Which of the following vitamins is produced by bacteria in the human colon?
e: Friendly little gut bacteria work like tiny chefs, busily cooking up vitamin K to help your scrapes form helpful scabs!

q: Which of the following is NOT found in prokaryotes:
e: Tiny prokaryote cells pack super light, skipping fancy packaging centers like the Golgi apparatus to keep their miniature lives simple.

q: Fingernails can reveal much about a person's overall health. Which of the following nail appearances corresponds to liver disease?
a: Half of the nail is pink and half of the nail is white
The nail is yellowish, with a slight blush at the base
e: When a tired liver needs help, fingernails can lose their cheerful pink blush and turn ghostly white to tell the tale.

q: A sea star would NOT be found in which of the following marine environments?
e: Sea stars love crawling on solid ground with tiny tube feet, so you will never catch them floating adrift in the open pelagic sea!

q: Which of the following best explains why estrogen in the blood is typically found attached to globular [GLAW-byoo-lur] proteins?
a: It needs to be transported in an inactive form
It is quickly broken down when unbound
It is produced attached to these proteins
e: Estrogen is oily and hates swimming in watery blood, so it hitches a ride on friendly protein rafts to travel across your body.

q: What characteristic is most likely to identify two organisms as the same species?
a: All of their physical characteristics are very similar
They fill the same role in the ecosystem
They are of similar size and shape
e: When two creatures have babies that can grow up and have babies of their own, that proves they belong to the same species.

q: What is the average lifespan of a domestic rabbit?
e: With plenty of crunchy greens and love, pet bunnies happily thump along for eight to twelve years.

q: Which of the following processes represents the restoration of severed appendages?
e: Like a salamander regrowing a lost tail, regeneration is nature's magic trick where brave little cells rebuild a missing part from scratch!

q: The human disease malaria is caused by which of the following types of pathogen?
e: Sneaky single-celled protists hitchhike inside mosquito bites, slipping right into our bodies to cause the feverish illness called malaria.

q: Thigmotropism [thig-moh-TROHP-ism] in vines can allow them to wrap around other branches to grow higher. This form of taxis occurs in response to which of the following stimuli?
e: Curious climbing vines love a gentle hug, using the sense of touch against a sturdy neighbor to guide their journey skyward.

q: Hemophilia is an X-chromosome-linked recessive trait. Which of the following percentages is the probability that the daughter of a male with the disease and a female carrier is a hemophiliac?
e: Dad always passes along his affected gene, leaving a fifty-fifty coin-flip chance that mom passes hers too, giving their daughter the condition.

q: Barr bodies are produced as a result of which of the following?
e: Inside female cells, one X chromosome curls up for a permanent nap through X-chromosome inactivation, turning into a tiny resting spot called a Barr body.

q: Which of these constitutes a correct DNA base pairing?
e: Inside our DNA ladder, base A always reaches across to lock hands perfectly with its favorite partner, T.

q: Which of the following is an example of a change in the primary structure of a protein?
a: A protein folding into a beta sheet
e: A protein is like a beaded necklace, so swapping just one amino acid bead changes its original chain pattern.

q: Which of the following best describes the pathway of aerobic respiration?
a: Glucose is oxidized and oxygen is reduced
Oxygen is oxidized and glucose is reduced
Both glucose and oxygen are oxidized
Both glucose and oxygen are reduced
e: Your busy cells break down sweet glucose by oxidizing it, while trusty oxygen scoops up electrons, getting reduced to spark energy.

q: One of the types of finches Darwin observed is the warbler finch, which has a long, sharp, and narrow beak. What type of food does the warbler finch primarily consume?
e: With a beak like tiny, pointy tweezers, this little bird is built just right for snatching up sneaky, wiggling insects.

q: Prokaryotic cells divide by the process of:
e: Simple prokaryotes make new friends through binary fission, copying their insides and neatly pinching into two identical twins.

q: In bean and corn seeds, the food supply that is used by the seed to germinate and grow is in which of the following:
e: Think of the cotyledon as a cozy lunchbox, packed with tasty snacks to help a sleepy baby seed sprout.

q: Which species of tuna is in immediate danger of extinction due to overfishing?
e: Fast-swimming southern bluefin tuna are so heavily fished that these majestic ocean speedsters are in danger of disappearing completely.

q: Which of the following is an example of a plant with bulb stems?
e: Underground, an onion wraps its food in snug, juicy layers around a short stem, making it a true bulb.

q: Forest fires are important in some ecosystems for all of the following reasons except:
a: They create a warmer climate, increasing precipitation
They thin understory, making way for increased growth
They help clear dead and dying organisms
They can remove non-native, non-fire-resistant species
e: Wildfires clear out old clutter so baby trees can sprout, but they cannot magically change the climate to bring extra rain.

q: Which of the following animal products has NOT been correctly paired with the animal that produces it?
e: Woolly sheep make soft, waterproof lanolin wax to keep their coats dry, not goats!

q: Chromosomes are composed of:
e: Chromosomes are neat little packages where your long recipe of DNA stays tidily wrapped around spools of protein.

q: Which of the following statements best describes the histone code?
a: DNA transcription is regulated by chemical modifications of histone tails
Chromatin is tightly coiled around histone proteins forming nucleosomes
The number of histone proteins per cell correlates directly with transcriptional activity
Histone euchromatin is characterized by highly repetitive sequences
e: Little chemical tags decorated onto histone protein tails act like a secret code, telling the cell when to read its DNA recipes.

q: Which of the following is the location of the patella bone:
e: Your patella sits right on your knee, acting like a sturdy little shield to protect your leg as you run!

q: Which of the following is a central mechanism for homeostasis in which the product of a metabolic or physiological pathway regulates its production by inhibiting an earlier step in its own production?
e: Like a smart heater clicking off when a room gets warm, negative feedback stops a pathway once enough is made.

q: Phylogenetic systems of classifying organisms into various groups are mostly based on:
e: Scientists group living things by their evolutionary history, sketching a grand family tree that shows who shares ancient ancestors.

q: Plasmodium falciparum [plaz-MOH-dee-uhm fal-see-PUH- room] is one of four causative agents of malaria in humans and, like the other three, is which of the following?
e: This sneaky malaria germ is a protozoan, a tiny one-celled critter that hitches a ride inside mosquitoes to cause trouble.

q: In eukaryotic cells, which of the following portions of an mRNA molecule is translated?
e: Cells snip away the extra pieces, keeping only the exons to be translated into the wonderful proteins you need.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a tundra?
e: Even in the chilly tundra, flocks of traveling animals migrate in for summer, so they are definitely not absent!

q: Angiosperms [AN-jee-uh-spurms] are plants that do what?
e: Angiosperms are the showstoppers of the plant world, blooming with colorful flowers and wrapping their seeds inside yummy fruits!

q: A periwinkle is what type of organism?
e: A periwinkle is actually a tiny sea snail, happily scooting across rocky shores inside its sturdy little spiral shell.

q: What is the Linnean name of the domestic apple tree?
e: Scientists gave the sweet domestic apple tree the fancy, ancient name Malus pumila to officially identify this crunchy orchard favorite.

q: Assuming that the following structures are unlabeled and unstained, which would be least likely to be visualized using a light microscope with the standard resolution of 0.2 microns?
e: Ribosomes are far too teeny for standard light microscopes to spot, hiding like microscopic specks inside the cell.

q: The extinction of large hooved mammals from Central America has been implicated in the reduction of what types of plants, which relied on them for seed dispersal?
a: Plants with pods, such as peas
e: Ancient giant beasts were the only critters big enough to gulp down massive avocado pits and plant them everywhere.

q: Which of the following genetic disorders results from a dominant allele?
e: It only takes one bossy gene copy from a parent for Huntington's disease to take charge, making it dominant.

q: Which of the following is an example of anaerobic respiration?
a: Yeast performing fermentation to release ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide
A rose using carbon dioxide to produce glucose in the Calvin cycle
A mouse cell using one molecule of glucose to produce 36 ATPs
A plant performing photosynthesis to produce energy for storage
e: Hungry yeast can feast without any oxygen, burping out alcohol and carbon dioxide through anaerobic fermentation.

q: A biker falls and now has trouble balancing. Which of the following structures is likely damaged?
e: Inside your inner ear, tiny fluid-filled loops called semicircular canals act like liquid compasses to tell your brain which way is up.

q: What is the world's longest venomous snake?
e: The king cobra can stretch longer than a whole minivan, reigning as the longest venomous snake on the planet!

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about the kingdom Fungi?
a: Fungi are more closely related to plants than animals
Fungi are not dependent on light
Fungi can grow in any direction
Fungi usually reproduce by wind-disseminated spores
e: Believe it or not, mushrooms are actually closer cousins to you and your pets than they are to green plants!

q: Although not scientifically verified, which of the following plant communities has been hypothesized to utilize allelopathy?
e: Tough chaparral shrubs might use allelopathy, leaking secret chemicals into the dirt to stop neighboring seeds from crowding their sunny space.

q: The malleus, incus, and stapes [STAY-peez] are small bones that play a role in which of the following functions?
e: These three teeny ear bones dance together, bouncing sound vibrations deep inside so you can hear every lovely song!

q: Mammals became dominant after a mass extinction at the end of what period?
e: When the Cretaceous period ended with a giant asteroid splash, the big dinosaurs bowed out, letting our fuzzy mammal ancestors take center stage.

q: How many pairs of chromosomes do human somatic cells have?
e: Inside your cells, you carry 23 cozy pairs of chromosomes, like matching socks packed with all the secret recipes that make you, you!

q: Which organism has a lateral line system?
e: Sharks have a nifty lateral line running down their sides that feels every sneaky ripple in the water like built-in underwater radar.

q: Which of the following fix nitrogen in soil?
e: Friendly legumes team up with helpful root bacteria to turn air into rich soil food!

q: Which of the following is typically the most detrimental type of point mutation?
e: A frameshift mutation shifts the whole genetic message over by one letter, scrambling every single word that follows into total nonsense.

q: Which of the following groups of organisms is responsible for most of the photosynthetic activity in the oceans?
e: Tiny drifting protists like algae soak up ocean sunshine, making most of the sea's food and giving our whole planet fresh oxygen to breathe!

q: What organism acts as the vector of malaria in humans?
e: The Anopheles mosquito accidentally carries the malaria parasite from person to person when it stops by for a sip.

q: Muscle cells in our heart are constantly working. Which of the following organelles would they have in larger quantities than other cells in the body?
e: Because your heart beats non-stop, its cells are packed with extra mitochondria, the bustling power plants making endless energy!

q: Which of the following statements about flatworms is NOT correct?
a: Flatworms have no true body cavity and an incomplete digestive system
Flatworms do not have a respiratory system
There are true blood vessels present in the flatworms
The flatworms have a ladder-like nervous system with a distinct head region that includes nerve cells and sensory organs
e: Flatworms are so wonderfully flat that they absorb oxygen right through their skin, meaning they have no need for any blood vessels at all.

q: In what state will a plant cell be if placed in a hypotonic [high-poh-tawnic] environment?
e: Water rushes inside like air into a balloon, puffing the plant cell up nice and firm in a state called turgor.

q: Standardized terms are used to describe locations on an organism's body. Which of the following terms refers to the region of the body with the stomach?
e: Scientists use the fancy word ventral to describe your belly side, where your tummy happily rumbles whenever lunchtime rolls around.

q: Many antibiotics inhibit bacterial protein synthesis, but not eukaryotic [YOU-care-ee-AW-tic] protein synthesis. Which of the following best explains why?
a: The antibiotics cut up bacterial mRNA, but not eukaryotic mRNA
Eukaryotes [YOU-care-ee-oats] have enzymes to destroy the antibiotics, but bacteria do not
Eukaryotes can export the antibiotics, preventing them from damaging the cell
The antibiotics affect bacterial but not eukaryotic ribosomes
e: Antibiotics target the tiny protein factories, or ribosomes, in bacteria, but leave ours alone because our cell factories are built differently.

q: You are using a dichotomous key to identify a leaf you have picked up. You observe that you have a leaf with several main veins of about equal size, all of which extend from a common point at the base of the blade. Your leaf could be from which of the following trees?
e: Maple leaves spread their big veins from one base like open fingers waving hello to the sky.

q: A small human lymphocyte and a red blood cell are both about how many micrometers across:
e: At eight tiny micrometers wide, these hardworking cells are just the right size to squeeze through your skinniest blood vessels.

q: Which of the following techniques was used by Meselson and Stahl to separate samples of DNA that contained different amounts of DNA labeled with a heavy isotope and a light isotope of nitrogen in their experiments on DNA replication:
e: Centrifugation spins the DNA on a super-fast merry-go-round, separating the heavy pieces from the lighter ones.

q: Which of the following best describes why humans are unable to digest cellulose?
e: Our stomachs simply lack the special chemical scissors, called enzymes, needed to chop tough plant cellulose into tiny bites.

q: Which of the following pathways harvests the largest number of ATP molecules per molecule of glucose?
e: By breathing in oxygen, aerobic respiration squeezes a massive treasure chest of energetic ATP from each sweet glucose treat!

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about most carp?
a: They have teeth on their inferior pharyngeal bones
They are highly tolerant of salt water
They have a wide geographical range
e: Carp love splashing in cozy fresh rivers and lakes, so salty ocean water is definitely not for them.

q: When larvae emerge from fruit fly eggs, where do they tend to feed?
a: Near the surface of the fermenting fruit
In the non-fermenting portion of the fruit next to the overripe portion
e: Hungry baby fruit flies stay right near the surface so they can munch soft fruit while breathing fresh air.

q: Which of the following is a major reason for "dead zones" in the ocean?
e: Farm fertilizers wash out to sea, feeding huge algae parties that gobble up all the water's oxygen when they decay.

q: What do mad-cow disease, hantavirus, and malaria all have in common?
a: They all affect the nervous system
They all have mortality rates of 100%
They are diseases that primarily affect people living in tropical environments
They are all passed from animals to humans
e: All three of these sneaky illnesses make the leap into people by hitching a ride straight from animals.

q: When present in large numbers, which of the following can cause red tides?
e: When billions of tiny dinoflagellates gather together for an ocean party, their reddish bodies paint the water into a red tide!

q: Which of the following nitrogenous bases is the most structurally similar to guanine?
e: Guanine and adenine are purines, sharing a two-ring structure that makes them look like close chemical cousins.

q: Which of the following is NOT true of the plasma membrane:
a: it is made partly of lipids
it contains proteins imbedded in the lipid bilayer
it is rigid and helps maintain a definite shape for the cell
e: A cell membrane is actually squishy and flexible like a soap bubble, rather than stiff and rigid.

q: According to the botanical definition, examples of fruits include which of the following?
a: Tomato, coconut, acorn, celery, and garlic
Orange, cantaloupe, acorn, tomato, bell pepper
e: Because they all grow from flowers and protect seeds inside, science happily calls every one of them a fruit!

q: Which of the following is not a succulent plant?
e: Eucalyptus is a tall, woody tree instead of a succulent that packs extra water inside puffy leaves.

q: Which of the following organisms has a carapace [KAR-uh- pays]?
e: A crayfish wears its carapace like a tough little suit of armor across its back for protection.

q: An octopus can fit through any hole larger than its beak.
e: With no bones inside, an octopus is delightfully squishy and can squeeze through any space bigger than its hard beak.

q: Which of the following types of microscopes passes negatively charged particles guided by magnetic lenses through a very thin specimen, all in a partial vacuum, to produce an image at high magnification:
e: A transmission electron microscope shoots tiny beams straight through super thin slices, revealing secret worlds hidden deep inside cells!

q: During photosynthesis, for every molecule of glucose that is made, how many molecules of carbon dioxide and water are consumed?
a: six carbon dioxide molecules and six water molecules
four carbon dioxide molecules and four water molecules
twelve carbon dioxide molecules and twelve water molecules
six carbon dioxide molecules and twelve water molecules
e: To bake one sweet glucose molecule, a plant mixes six sips of water with six puffs of carbon dioxide.

q: Which of the following is the least likely to be a characteristic of an invasive species?
a: It will only survive under a narrow range of environmental conditions
It will have a longer reproductive cycle than native species
It will do economic and/or environmental harm in a new environment
e: Invasive invaders love exploring everywhere, so they rarely limit themselves to a fussy, narrow set of living conditions.

q: Which of the following plant structures is most closely associated with land plants?
e: Pollen grains drift through breezy air like tiny spaceships, helping land plants reproduce without swimming through water.

q: The first evidence that nitrogen-fixing bacteria populations have become too low in a terrestrial biome would be a decline in which of the following populations?
e: Plants are producers that crave nitrogen, so without helpful bacteria around, our leafy green friends dwindle first.

q: A tick sucks blood from a cow. Which of the following is this species interaction?
e: In parasitism, a greedy little tick steals a blood meal from an unlucky cow, helping itself while harming the cow.

q: Which of the following would be an example of a mycorrhizal [my-kuh-RY-zuhl] symbiosis?
a: A parasitic wasp laying eggs on a caterpillar
The bacterium Rhizobium [ry-ZOH-bee-uhm] infecting the roots of a peanut plant
Ants living in Acacia [uh-KAY-shuh] thorns and protecting the host plant
Ants that harvest honeydew from aphids [AY-fids] feeding on plants
e: Friendly Rhizobium bacteria cuddle into peanut plant roots, sharing nutrients like best pals so both can grow strong underground.

q: When was the first mammal successfully cloned?
e: Back in 1996, scientists made history by welcoming Dolly the sheep, the very first cloned mammal!

q: Which of the following best portrays an example of evolution by natural selection that has been directly observed in modern times?
e: Clever bacteria quickly learn how to survive our medicines, showing us natural selection and evolution happening right before our eyes!

q: Which of the following is the most common source of energy for brain cells in humans:
e: Your busy brain runs almost entirely on glucose, a sweet simple sugar that fuels every brilliant thought you dream up.

q: Which animal was part of an Russian domestication experiment in 1959?
e: Russian scientists gently picked the friendliest wild foxes, discovering that sweet pups soon grew floppy ears and wagging tails!

q: In the human skull, which of the following sinuses sits most posteriorly?
e: Tucked deep behind your eyes and nose, the sphenoid sinus sits the furthest back in your skull.

q: Which of the following populations of cells is likely to be most dramatically reduced in the brain of a patient with Parkinson's disease?
e: In Parkinson's disease, dopaminergic brain cells fade away, leaving the body without the chemical messages it needs to move smoothly.

q: When compared to animals, plants rank second in total numbers of species. Which of the following groups of animals is itself more diverse than plants?
e: From shimmering beetles to busy bees, insects rule the animal kingdom with more species than all the plants combined!

q: Which of the following is NOT a source of food for polar bears in the wild?
e: Polar bears hunt up north in the chilly Arctic, while emperor penguins waddle safely half a world away in Antarctica.

q: Root nodules are commonly found in legumes. Which of the following types of plants is an example of a legume?
e: Soybeans are pod-bearing legumes that team up with friendly soil bacteria inside little round root bumps.

q: Hyenas are more closely related to cats than to dogs.
e: Believe it or not, it is true! Beneath that dog-like laugh, hyenas actually belong on the cat branch of nature's family tree.

q: In a population of giraffes, giraffes with longer necks are more able to reach food sources, while incurring no negative fitness effects. Which of the following types of selection will take place in this population?
e: Because towering necks help giraffes reach yummy treetop leaves, directional selection nudges the whole population to grow taller over time.

q: Of the following, which level of taxonomic classification is the most specific?
e: Out of this group, a family is the tightest circle of relatives, sorting living things far more specifically than orders or classes.

q: Which of the following complexes breaks the central dogma of molecular biology?
e: Nature usually copies DNA into RNA, but reverse transcriptase is a cheeky rulebreaker that rewrites RNA backwards into DNA!

q: Which of the following characteristics will NOT help distinguish monocots from dicots [DY-kots]?
e: While petals and leaf veins give secrets away, middle leaf mesophyll looks too similar in both plants to help tell them apart.

q: Hormones released by the posterior pituitary control numerous emotions, drives, and autonomic functions. In which of the following locations are those hormones actually produced?
e: The wise hypothalamus acts like a master chef, whipping up hormones before sending them to the pituitary for delivery.

q: Which of the following groups of organisms is most commonly associated with the ability to fix nitrogen:
e: Tiny bacteria are the soil's secret superstars, magically turning air into nitrogen food that plants crave!

q: Pyrimidines are important components in nucleic acids, vitamins, drugs, and many other compounds. Which of the following nucleotide bases is NOT a pyrimidine?
e: Adenine is a double-ringed purine, standing tall beside the smaller, single-ring pyrimidines like a proud big brother.

q: Which of the following is the most distinguishing characteristic of all vertebrates adapted to life on land from amphibians:
a: presence of a coelom (read as: sil-OHM)
e: Land critters lay special amniotic eggs with their own private water bubbles, keeping babies cozy and moist far away from ponds!

q: Plants evolve adaptations to help them survive in different environments. One adaptation is an alternative pathway for photosynthesis. Which of the following is a Crassulacean [kras-uh-LAY-shuhn] acid metabolism (CAM) plant?
e: Spiky pineapples are smart CAM plants that hold their breath all day, sipping cool night air so they never dry out in the heat.

q: Which of the following parts of a cell is most directly responsible for synthesizing proteins:
e: Think of ribosomes as bustling little factory workers, stitching tiny parts together to assemble all the cell's essential proteins!

q: If you touched a crawfish, you would notice that its body is hard. That is because the crawfish:
e: A crawfish wears its hard bones on the outside like a crunchy suit of knightly armor, called an exoskeleton.

q: Which of the following are generally unable to generate organic carbon from inorganic carbon?
e: Unlike sunny plant chefs, hungry fungi cannot make food out of thin air, so they must munch on leftovers from the forest floor.

q: Which of the following is the most basic function of human eye lashes:
a: to shade the eye from bright sun
to prevent small particles from entering the eyes
to help disperse tears when blinking
e: Your eyelashes are like tiny broomsticks, standing guard to sweep away flying specks of dust before they tumble into your eyes.

q: Which of the following cell types undergo meiosis?
e: A primary spermatocyte gets ready to make future sperm by dividing through meiosis, shuffling genes into brand-new cells.

q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
e: Tucked deep inside your ear sits the tiny stapes, a stirrup-shaped bone smaller than a rice grain that dances to sound waves!

q: Which of the following is NOT an accurate representation of cladograms?
a: They emphasize the sequence in which derived characteristics arose
They illustrate the benefits provided by the derived characteristic
They visually organize the relationships between organisms that share characteristics
They can be constructed for any group of organisms
e: Cladograms map out how cousins are related, but they don't explain whether a trait actually helps a creature survive.

q: Sexual reproduction allows the rearrangement of alleles and the production of individuals with new or differing genotypes. Which of the following processes is a source of new genetic variation?
e: Shuffling genes just rearranges old traits, but a mutation creates totally new genetic ingredients from scratch.

q: Which of the following is the most common term biologists use to indicate that an enzyme has lost its normal 3-dimensional shape:
e: When a folded enzyme gets too hot, it unravels like a dropped ball of yarn, becoming completely denatured and unable to work.

q: Vestigial (pronounced VES-ti-gee-al) structures:
a: have no known function in their present owners
function in an analogous fashion in all species
e: Like an old toy left in the attic, vestigial parts are leftover body bits that do not have a real job anymore.

q: Looking at a picture of all of the chromosomes in a cell can help in the identification of mutations and abnormalities. What is this type of picture called?
e: A karyotype is like a neat family photo of all your chromosomes, lined up together so doctors can spot any mixed-up pieces.

q: The reactions that the cell uses to harvest energy from sugars can be classified as what?
e: Cells harvest sweet energy by passing electrons back and forth like a hot potato during redox reactions.

q: How many teeth does the average adult mouth have (except for wisdom teeth)?
e: A full adult smile lines up thirty-two handy teeth, working like a team of little chompers to crunch your food!

q: In plants, what cells secrete the waxy cuticle that protects plants from water loss?
e: Hardworking epidermal cells on a leaf's outer skin polish the plant with a shiny waxy jacket, keeping every precious drop of water inside.

q: If an order of plant has floral parts usually arranged in multiples of 4 or 5, it would most likely have:
a: vascular bundles arranged in a ring and a taproot
diffuse or fibrous root system and 2 cotyledons
e: These pretty blooms belong to dicots, plants that anchor down with a sturdy taproot and organize their stem pipes in neat rings.

q: Which of the following is NOT a venomous snake?
e: Instead of using venom, the reticulated python is a mighty hugger that wraps around its dinner with pure muscle power.

q: Which of the following is the most common term biologists use for the molecule that an enzyme will act on:
e: A substrate is the special puzzle piece that clicks into an enzyme's waiting hands, ready to be snipped or snapped together!

q: Which of the following best characterizes the material that is presented by antigen-presenting cells to T cells?
e: Scout cells chop invader proteins into tiny bite-sized peptide snippets, waving them like little warning flags to alert the brave T cells.

q: Which of the following is a club fungus?
e: Toadstools are club fungi because they sprout microscopic, club-shaped parts underneath their charming little forest umbrellas.

q: During the life-cycle of amphibians, which is not a means through which respiration can occur?
e: Air bladders are just handy pool floaties for fish, so frogs breathe through their skin, lungs, and gills instead.

q: In which ocean zone would coral reside?
e: Corals love sunbathing in the shallow neritic zone, where bright coastal waters give their tiny algae partners plenty of sunshine.

q: Which of the following is the primary function of vascular tissue in plants:
e: Plant vascular tissue works like a bundle of drinking straws, happily carrying water and sweet juices up and down.

q: Which of the following is NOT found in an animal cell?
e: Animal cells stay squishy and flexible so creatures can move, leaving rigid cell walls to the stiff stems of plants.

q: Which of the following types of enzymes would most likely be involved in adding a water molecule to a substrate?
e: With hydro right in its name, hydrolase is the tiny helper that happily splashes a water molecule onto its chemical friend.

q: Which of the following is NOT true of sister chromatids [CROW-mah-tids]?
e: Sister chromatids are identical biological twins made from the same recipe, so they always share the exact same matching alleles.

q: When uncoagulated whole blood is placed in a tube and centrifuged, it separates into two layers. The red opaque layer at the bottom of the tube is composed of the cellular components of the blood. What is the light yellow layer of clear fluid at the top of the tube fluid called?
e: Plasma is the golden, watery river that floats to the very top, gently carrying busy red blood cells on their journey.

q: Which of the following has the function of modifying, sorting, and preparing substances for use within the eukaryotic [yoo-KAR-ee-oh-tik] cell or for transport outside of the cell?
e: Think of the Golgi apparatus as a bustling post office, neatly wrapping and addressing packages before shipping them across the cell.

q: Which of the following cytoskeletal [SIGH-toh-skeletul] components has the largest diameter?
e: Even with micro in their name, microtubules are the biggest, thickest structural pipes holding the whole cellular house upright.

q: Which of these organisms get energy directly from the Sun?
e: Tiny cyanobacteria are brilliant little sunbathers, using sunlight to make their own food just like green plants do.

q: Which of the following is common to both bacteria and viruses?
e: Both of these tiny travelers carry nucleic acids, the secret instruction manuals of DNA or RNA that hold their life recipes.

q: At which of the following pH values would pepsin be most active?
e: Pepsin loves living in your sour, acid-filled stomach, where a super low pH of two lets it chop up proteins best.

q: Osmosis is:
a: the movement of water through a permeable membrane
the movement of salts through a semi-permeable membrane
the movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane
the pressure exerted by water through a semi-permeable membrane
e: Osmosis happens when water tiptoes across a semi-permeable barrier, sneaking through tiny gates to balance things out.

q: Of the following, which is true of type I diabetes?
a: It most often occurs later in life
It is characterized by the inability of receptors to recognize insulin
It is characterized by the inability of the pancreas to produce insulin
It is most often due to unhealthy lifestyle choices
e: In type one diabetes, the pancreas stops making insulin, the trusty little key needed to unlock sugar for our cells.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the functions of water in photosynthesis?
a: Donates electrons to replace those removed from chlorophyll in photosystem II
Donates H+ that will be used to generate a proton gradient to drive the synthesis of ATP from ADP
Provides H+ to reduce NADPH to NADP+
e: Water happily helps create NADPH instead of tearing it down, so it never turns NADPH back into NADP+.

q: Which of the following is a sex-linked trait in humans?
e: Color blindness hitches a ride on the X chromosome, making this colorful vision mystery pass down through our sex chromosomes.

q: Which of the following amino acids must we obtain in our diets?
e: Our bodies cannot make leucine from scratch, so this essential little building block must be invited in through the foods we eat.

q: Which of the following muscles is NOT considered a principal muscle for facial expression?
e: While other muscles help you smile and frown, the hyoglossus works behind the scenes down in your tongue.

q: Which of the following is NOT a commonly-used model organism?
e: Scientists study living creatures in the lab, but ancient Homo habilis vanished long ago and only left behind dusty old fossils.

q: In terms of available energy, why would low biomass be expected for any tundra biome?
a: Plants are not able to grow in the cold temperatures
High wind speeds remove the nutrients needed by plants
There is little sunlight to provide the initial energy
There are few top predators, so little energy is needed
e: The sleepy tundra sun barely peeks over the horizon, so plants starve for light and cannot grow into a big, bustling crowd.

q: Consider a cross of a pea plant having white flowers with a pea plant having red flowers. Of 50 seedlings from this cross, 25 produce white flowers and 25 produce red flowers. If white is dominant, which of the following is the BEST description for the genetic makeup of the white flowering parent plant:
e: Since half the baby plants bloomed red, the white parent must have carried a secret red gene alongside its white one, making it heterozygous!

q: Marsupials are far more abundant and diverse in Australia than in North and South America. Which of the following best explains why only three families of marsupials are found outside the Australian region?
e: Divergent evolution let ancient pouch-wearing cousins branch out in isolated Australia, happily growing into wonderfully different creatures over time.

q: Which of the following traits would you expect an ornithopod [AWR-nuh-thuh-pod] dinosaur to have?
e: The word ornithopod secretly means 'bird foot,' so these prehistoric giants stomped around on bird-like toes!

q: If a DNA template has the sequence TAC-ACA-GGG, which one of the following would be the correct messenger RNA codon sequence?
e: Messenger RNA trades DNA letters for their matching partners, swapping T for A, A for U, and G for C to make AUG-UGU-CCC.

q: If a flower is said to be incomplete and perfect, which of the following would apply?
e: A perfect flower keeps both its male and female parts, but it becomes incomplete when it skips wearing showy petals.

q: What is the name for the large green complex organelles that perform photosynthesis and are typically found in plant cells and algae?
e: Chloroplasts act like tiny green solar kitchens inside plant cells, happily cooking up sweet food using rays of sunlight!

q: When you are sick with a virus, your body builds up a defense system by making antibodies against it. Why, then, do we need to get flu shots every year?
a: Antibodies are usually only effective for a few months
We need antibiotics to combat the flu
We could be flu carriers even if we are not sick
The flu virus mutates every year
e: Sneaky flu viruses love wearing new disguises, mutating each year so your body needs a fresh wanted poster to spot them!

q: Which of the following compounds is found in the greatest abundance in animals?
e: Animals are basically wonderful, walking puddles, because everyday water makes up most of their bodies!

q: Which of the following statements is true regarding thymine [THIGH-meen], cytosine [sigh-toh-seen], and uracil [YUR-ah-sil]?
a: They can all be found in RNA
They can all be found in DNA
e: Cytosine, thymine, and uracil are all pyrimidines, sharing a neat, single-ring shape to help spell out genetic messages.

q: Babies cannot walk well. As they grow older, which of the following parts of their nervous systems will interact with their muscles, allowing for increased coordination?
e: The somatic nervous system acts like a cheerful coach, sending signals to your muscles so you can practice those brave first steps.

q: You can tell the age of a ladybird by counting the spots on his back.
e: Those cute polka dots reveal what kind of beetle it is, not how many birthdays it has celebrated.

q: A macrophage [MACRO-fayj] engulfs a bacterial cell and then creates molecules that trigger itself to migrate to the lymph node. What type of signaling is this?
e: Since auto means self, a brave cell giving itself marching orders uses autocrine signaling to get moving!

q: The oxygen released by plants and other autotrophs (read as: AW-toh-trefs) comes from which compound?
e: Plants take a sip of water and split it apart, keeping the hydrogen and puffing out fresh oxygen for us to breathe!

q: Which of the following is the location of the human thymus gland:
e: Tucked right behind your breastbone in your upper chest, this cozy little gland trains brave defender cells to protect you.

q: Which of the following is least likely to threaten biodiversity?
e: Ecotourism invites nature lovers to gently admire wild creatures without wrecking their homes, keeping animal families safe and thriving.

q: What is the common term for bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE)?
e: This brain sickness makes cattle wobble and act strangely, earning it the famous everyday nickname Mad Cow disease.

q: Which component of the cytoskeleton is actively involved in lining the chromosomes up at the cell equator in preparation for cell division?
e: Tiny, hardworking microtubules act like microscopic ropes, gently tugging chromosomes into a neat line right across the cell's belly.

q: Which of the following processes is NOT classified as passive transport?
e: Unlike passive drifting, endocytosis takes lots of cellular energy to wrap its membrane around a big gulp of food.

q: Which of the following is NOT a monomer?
e: Monomers are single building blocks, but maltose is a double scoop made of two sugar units holding hands.

q: In order to begin the digestive process, which of the following menu items would require the most salivary amylase?
e: Your mouth drools happy amylase bubbles to break down all the cozy starches packed inside a big bowl of yummy spaghetti.

q: Which of the following amino acids is NOT made by the human body?
e: Our bodies cannot build phenylalanine from scratch, so we must happily welcome this essential building block through the foods we eat.

q: Which of the following pairs is NOT a correct matching of an organism with its external symmetry classification?
e: Lobsters have matching left and right halves, which makes them bilateral, not biradial like comb jellies.

q: Which of the following statements about thermophiles in Yellowstone National Park is NOT true?
a: Many thermophiles live in hot pools of water
Studies of thermophiles have been helpful to the process of DNA fingerprinting
Most thermophiles are in the kingdom Eubacteria (read as: juh-bahk-TIR-ee-ah)
e: These heat-loving little daredevils actually belong to an ancient family called Archaea, not Eubacteria, while soaking in their sizzling hot spring spas.

q: Plant cells differ from animal cells in that only plant cells possess:
e: Plant cells wear a crunchy, boxy cell wall like a suit of armor to stand tall without needing any bones!

q: Keratins are considered structural proteins. This is because they are most often arranged in which of the following shapes:
e: Keratins twist into long, thin fibers, like microscopic ropes braiding together to make tough hair and strong fingernails.

q: Which of the following is the BEST description for the location of the human spleen:
a: lower right abdomen just above the hip bone
upper right abdomen just under the lower right ribs
lower left abdomen just above the hip bone
upper left abdomen just under the lower left ribs
e: Your trusty spleen stays snug and safe, tucked right inside your upper left belly just beneath your lower ribs.

q: Which of the following cells stimulate macrophages, B cells, and T cells?
e: Helper T cells act like cheerful team captains, rallying macrophages, B cells, and other T cells to join the big germ-fighting squad.

q: Which of the following is an example of a protist?
e: Kelp might look like an underwater tree, but this leafy organism is actually a massive protist dancing in the sea.

q: Which of the following leukocytes [LOO-kuh-sits] occurs in the LEAST abundance in the healthy human body?
e: Basophils are the rarest defenders in your bloodstream, making up less than one percent of your whole white blood cell team.

q: Which of the following choices does NOT represent a benefit of Mycorrhiza (read as: my-koh-RY-zah)?
e: These friendly underground fungi share lots of water and snacks, but helping roots grab nitrogen is just not their special job.

q: A Gram stain would be most useful in distinguishing organisms from which of the following groups?
e: A Gram stain acts like colorful magic paint, helping scientists tell tiny bacteria apart by turning their jackets purple or pink!

q: Which of the following will most likely occur for a bacteria that is an obligate or strict anaerobe (read as: an-AYE-robe) when grown in a test tube of nutrient agar that remains undisturbed :
a: the bacteria only grow against the walls of the test tube
the bacteria only grow at the top of the test tube
the bacteria only grow at the bottom of the test tube
e: These shy germs run away from fresh air, nestling down at the very bottom of the tube where no oxygen can bother them.

q: Which of the following is the primary excretory organ of the grasshopper:
e: Tiny Malpighian tubes work like little cleanup crews inside a grasshopper, sweeping away waste so it can keep hopping happily!
