q: Humans have a gene, called LCT, which encodes lactase. In most of the world, LCT is active in young children but is turned off in adults. However, northern Europeans and three different tribes of African pastoralists carry a mutation that permits it to be expressed in adults. The mutation is different in each of the four cases, indicating the mutation is an example of:
e: Different groups developed the same milk-drinking superpower independently, which is what convergent evolution is all about!

q: Which of the following is the enzyme that maintains chromosomal stability by protecting chromosome ends?
e: Telomerase works like the plastic tip on a shoelace, protecting chromosome ends from unraveling over time.

q: SNPs [snips] are used in DNA fingerprinting to distinguish individuals from each other. Which of the following events most likely precipitated the generation of a SNP [snip]?
e: A point mutation simply swaps out one single genetic letter, creating a unique little spelling difference called a SNP.

q: The water-proof layer within the endodermis of the root that filters substances entering a plant is called the:
e: The Casparian strip acts like a waxy raincoat, stopping water so the root can carefully inspect what enters.

q: Which of the following is an example of a protein with quaternary structure?
e: Hemoglobin has four protein buddies teaming up together into one big super-squad to carry oxygen everywhere!

q: Which of the following enzymes would be required for the formation of cDNA, a genetic transcript from eukaryotic cells that has had the introns removed?
e: Reverse transcriptase loves reading RNA messages backward to build shiny new strands of DNA.

q: The movement of cells from G-1 in the cell cycle into S-phase is mostly under the control of:
a: the availability of purines and pyrimidines
ubiquitin (read as: you-BIK-qui-tin) and proteosomes (read as: PRO-tee-oh-somes)
e: Cyclins and kinases team up like traffic controllers, waving a green flag when the cell is ready to copy its DNA.

q: Nematocysts (read as: NEHM-aht-oh-sists) are typically found in which of the following groups?
e: Cnidarians like jellyfish pack tiny, spring-loaded nematocysts in their tentacles to catch lunch with a quick zap!

q: Which of the following is NOT true of micro RNA in eukaryotes:
a: they target homologous sequences in mRNA
they are transcribed by RNA polymerase two
e: MicroRNAs never code for proteins themselves; instead, they act like quiet supervisors telling other messages to hush.

q: Which of the following is not a behavior generally associated with cancerous cells?
a: They cannot proliferate when not adherent to substrate
e: Cancer cells are rowdy rule-breakers that float freely, happily multiplying even when they have nothing to hold onto!

q: Which of the following traits does NOT make Eukarya distinct from Archaea and Bacteria?
a: Use of methionine [meth-eye-oh-neen] as initiator tRNA
e: Both Eukarya and Archaea use methionine to start building proteins, so it does not set Eukarya apart.

q: Helicobacter pylori [HEEL-ik-oh-bak-tur pie-LOR-ee] is associated with which of the following disorders?
e: This sneaky little tummy bug burrows right through your stomach's protective lining, causing painful sores called ulcers.

q: A pigeon is placed in a box. Sooner or later, the pigeon accidentally presses a button or lever that releases food. Eventually, the pigeon learns how to press the button whenever it wants food. This kind of learning is called:
e: In operant conditioning, a clever bird learns that pressing a button earns a tasty reward!

q: Which of the following portions of a gene could ultimately be translated to protein?
e: Exons are the superstar parts of the gene recipe that actually get used to build amazing proteins.

q: Which of the following would you NOT expect to experience during fasting or starvation?
a: Decrease in plasma fatty acid levels
Increased use of ketones for ATP production in the brain
e: When you are hungry, your body unlocks stored fat for energy, so fat in your blood actually goes up, not down!

q: A mutation that produces a dominant allele (read as: ah-LEEL) would:
a: Give the bearer a selective advantage
Result in the death of the bearer
Be expressed as an observable phenotype in a heterozygous organism
e: Like a bold singer taking the stage, a dominant gene shows off its trait even when paired with a different, quieter gene.

q: Which of the following disorders is due to a dominant trait?
e: Sometimes nature generously adds a spare digit! An extra finger or toe needs just one copy of the gene to show up.

q: Which of the following structures is referred to as our body's internal gyroscope?
e: Deep inside your ears, tiny fluid-filled loops swirl to tell your brain which way is up whenever you spin!

q: Which of the following is NOT a widely-conserved element of the mollusk body plan?
e: While most mollusks build hard homes, sneaky cousins like octopuses tossed away their shells to dance freely through the ocean.

q: During Western blotting, a blocking solution is often prepared. What is the primary function of the blocking solution?
e: This cozy liquid coats empty sticky spots on the membrane so roaming antibodies only cling to their true protein friends.

q: Animals excrete various forms of nitrogenous [ny-TROJ-uh- nuhs] wastes that are mainly the result of the catabolism of which of the following?
e: When cells break down proteins and DNA, they sweep away leftover nitrogen pieces like crumpled paper scraps after an art project.

q: Which of the following is the most superficial layer of the epidermis?
e: Like an invisible suit of armor, the stratum corneum sits on the very outside of your skin to protect you.

q: What are the most important sensory receptors for the monitoring and regulation of blood pressure in mammals?
e: Baroreceptors act like tiny pressure gauges in your blood vessels, gently alerting your brain whenever blood pushes too hard or too soft.

q: A man with an X-linked dominant trait has children with a female who is homozygous [hoh-muh-ZY-guhs] recessive for the trait. Which of the following proportions of his offspring will be affected by the trait?
a: All of his children, male or female
e: Dads always pass their only X chromosome to their daughters, meaning every single girl receives his dominant trait!

q: Which of the following trace nutrients is most important for proper function of cytochrome c [SY-tuh-krohm C]?
e: Cytochrome c holds a shiny speck of iron at its heart to catch and pass buzzing electrons like hot potatoes.

q: Restriction endonucleases [en-duh-noo-klee-AY-sis] are found in bacteria and are thought to provide protection from viruses by cutting viral DNA into small fragments. Molecular biologists have used these enzymes to do which of the following?
a: Clone specific genes into plasmids for expression by bacteria
Restrict the production of telomeres in yeast
Amplify desired DNA molecules in a controlled reaction
e: Scientists use these microscopic scissors to snip helpful genes and paste them into bacteria, creating clever little microscopic factories!

q: Which of the following best demonstrates paracrine [para-krin] signaling?
a: A tumor cell creates its own growth factors
An allergen results in localized histamine release
The pituitary gland secretes vasopressin [VAY-zoh-pressin] in response to thirst
The pancreas produces insulin after a meal
e: When pollen tickles your nose, nearby cells quickly whisper a sneeze alert by releasing histamine just to their next-door neighbors.

q: Some plants are able to adapt to normally toxic levels of metals in soil by absorbing and storing high concentrations of the metals within themselves. By doing this, these plants are able to detoxify the surrounding soil. Restoration ecologists use these plants as a form of:
a: Bioremediation, to remove harmful substances from the environment
Bioremediation, to add helpful plant life to the environment
Biological augmentation, to add helpful plant life to the environment
Biological augmentation, to remove harmful substances from the environment
e: Clever plants slurp up toxic metals from dirt to heal damaged earth, a green cleanup rescue called bioremediation!

q: Which of the following correctly describes the path of a newly synthesized secreted protein?
a: Rough endoplasmic reticulum [en-duh-PLAZ-mik ri-TIK-yuh-luhm], vesicles[VES-i-kuhls], Golgi apparatus, vesicles, plasma membrane
Golgi apparatus, vesicles, rough endoplasmic reticulum, vesicles, plasma membrane
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, vesicles, Golgi apparatus, plasma membrane
Golgi apparatus, vesicles, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, plasma membrane
e: Proteins get made in the rough ER, ride bubble carts through the Golgi packing plant, and ship out!

q: What is the term for the phenomenon by which antibodies binding to antigens on the surface of a bacterium promotes phagocytosis of that bacterium?
e: During opsonization, antibodies coat a sneaky germ like tasty sprinkles, making it irresistible for hungry defender cells to gobble up!

q: Which of the following is NOT an evolutionary adaptation of plants to arid climates?
a: Carbon incorporation and the Calvin cycle are separated
e: Desert plants actually open their breathing pores on cool nights to capture air safely, rather than keeping them closed!

q: Which of the following plant hormones plays the largest role in the germination of a seed?
e: Gibberellins ring like a tiny alarm clock inside a sleeping seed, happily telling it to wake up and sprout!

q: In which of the following organelles does transcription NOT occur?
e: Because peroxisomes do not carry any DNA recipe books, they cannot read or copy instructions like other busy organelles do.

q: Which of the following is LEAST accurate regarding human genetics:
a: genes from gametes are typically unchanged during their passage to the zygote
the zygote gets 1 allele from each parental gene pair
the number of copies of a particular gene can vary among individuals
e: Genes sitting close together on the same chromosome often travel hand-in-hand, so they do not always separate independently.

q: Which of the following MOST closely represents the location of the temporal bone in humans:
a: cheek or lateral border of the eye
e: Just tap your cheek right beside your eye. That cozy helmet of bone guarding your ear and cheek is your temporal bone!

q: Through what anatomical feature does water exit a sponge?
e: After slurping up dinner, a sponge happily squirts the leftover water out through a giant chimney at the top called an osculum!

q: Which of the following terms is used to describe the center of the field of vision?
e: Right in the middle of your eye's cozy camera sits the fovea, giving you the sharpest, clearest view of the world!

q: Which of the following occurs in meiosis but NOT in mitosis:
a: chromosomes line up at central area of cell
e: In meiosis, chromosome pairs hug and swap tiny pieces of themselves during crossing over, mixing up traits so you are completely unique!

q: Insects that eat solid food would likely have a gut with all of these properties, EXCEPT:
a: Sections which narrow to provide filtration
e: Chewing crunchy solid snacks needs grinding power, not tight filters that would cause a messy tummy traffic jam!

q: Which of the following is a major muscle of the back?
e: Your trapezius drapes across your upper back and shoulders like a trusty superhero cape, helping you shrug and steer your head.

q: Which of the following is NOT properly matched with its function or operation:
a: conjugation and transfer of genetic material between bacteria
F plasmids and reversible incorporation into bacterial genome
e: Transposons are just jumping bits of DNA that hop around on their own, not little partners trading genes back and forth.

q: Relating to photosynthesis, which of the following is not a direct product of light reactions?
e: Sunlight helps plants make energy and fresh air, but rubisco is just the hardworking enzyme helper waiting in the kitchen!

q: Which of the following is true of enzymes?
a: They increase the activation energy of metabolic reactions
They have active sites that bind to specific substrate molecules
They are made of chitin [KY-tin] protein
They generally act on a variety of substrate molecules
e: Each busy enzyme has a specially shaped pocket called an active site, waiting for the perfect puzzle piece to snap inside!

q: Which of the following is NOT a symptom or sign of a person suffering from diabetes mellitus ?
a: Decrease in the amount of urine production
e: With diabetes, the body flushes extra sugar with gallons of water, so people actually pee a whole lot more, not less!

q: When a gene is duplicated within an organism to generate a second copy of that gene, what term in genomics would describe the relationship between the genes?
e: When a gene accidentally makes an identical twin inside the same creature, scientists call these copycat partners paralogous genes.

q: Coronaviruses are positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses. Which of the following describes how their genetic material is processed after entering a cell?
a: Transcribed to mRNA with RNA-dependent RNA polymerase [pah-LIM-er-ace]
Reverse transcribed to DNA with reverse transcriptase
Translated after assembly of viral ribosomes
e: This sneaky virus looks just like an ordinary recipe card, so the cell's tiny ribosome chefs start reading and building it immediately!

q: When actin reaches its steady state in a cell, which of the following is occurring?
a: The actin filament is no longer adding new subunits or losing existing subunits
The actin filament is constantly adding new and losing existing subunits
The actin filament forms new disulfide bonds within itself
The actin filament forms new alpha helix structures to maintain its shape
e: Like a moving treadmill, the actin filament stays the same length by snapping new blocks onto one end while dropping old ones!

q: Photosynthesis requires water as a reactant. Oxygen atoms from the water end up in which of the following product molecules?
e: When thirsty plants split apart water molecules to capture energy, the leftover oxygen floats into the air for us to breathe!

q: Which of the following ions is NOT directly involved in setting the voltage of a cell membrane?
e: While lively sodium, potassium, and calcium buzz across cell borders to set electrical voltage, calm magnesium stays out of the game.

q: A deficiency of what trace element can result in goiter?
e: Your neck's little thyroid gland needs iodine to build hormones, and without it, it swells into a goiter asking for help!

q: Bungarotoxin [bung-garoh-TOK-sins] is a fast-acting lethal toxin that is the primary component of venom from the South Asian snake called a krait. It blocks nerve transmission at cholinergic [koh-luh-NUR-jik] synapses by competing with acetylcholine [uh-seet-l-KOH-leen] to bind irreversibly at the acetylcholine receptor. Which of the following would be LEAST LIKELY to also impact nerve transmission at the cholinergic synapses?
a: A drug floods the synapse with a molecule that resembles acetylcholine and is able to bind at the acetylcholine receptor, but cannot be recognized by acetylcholinesterase [uh-seet-l- KOH-leen-STUH-rays]
A chemical covalently binds to the acetylcholine receptor and is not easily inactivated
A chemical covalently bonds acetylcholinesterase at the enzyme active site
A drug increases the level of acetylcholinesterase present at the synapse
e: Adding more cleanup enzyme simply sweeps messages away faster, instead of permanently jamming the nerve's locks like deadly toxins do.

q: Which of the following molecules do methanogens (read as: meth- AN-oh-gens) most often use as their final electron acceptor in their generation of energy:
e: These tiny swamp microbes breathe in carbon dioxide to power their day, happily burping out methane gas as their grand finale!

q: Which of the following is a group of about 20 proteins that aid in the attraction and phagocytosis of microorganisms by macrophages:
e: Like a friendly rescue squad, the complement system tags invading germs so hungry defender cells can easily gobble them up!

q: Your teacher has a passion for studying human immunoglobulins, but they have to be dimers. What immunoglobulin does your teacher study?
e: IgA antibodies love teaming up in twos, holding hands as pairs to protect your nose and tummy from sneaky germs!

q: Which of the following types of microscopy require the specimen to be subjected to a vacuum?
e: Tiny electrons need an empty, airless vacuum to zoom straight through a sample without bumping into bouncy air molecules!

q: Which of the following best describes blood?
a: It is a specialized type of cell found in blood vessels
It is a type of cell formed in the bone marrow
It is a kind of connective tissue in which red and white blood cells are suspended in plasma
It is a kind of epithelial tissue [ep-uh-THEE-lee-al]
e: Blood is actually a connective tissue, acting like a warm river where busy red and white cells float through liquid plasma!

q: Which of the following is most likely to cause sympatric speciation?
e: When a plant doubles its chromosomes through polyploidy, it instantly becomes a new species right beside its family without ever moving away!

q: G-protein-coupled receptors and receptor tyrosine [TIE-row-seen] kinases are typically found on which of the following structures?
e: These clever sensor proteins sit right on the cell's outer plasma membrane, like little doorbells waiting to catch messages from outside!

q: The drug Digoxin from the Digitalis plant slows the reuptake of calcium by the sarcoplasmic reticulum (read as: ri-TI-kyuh-luhm). What is the effect of this on the strength and rate of heart contractions?
e: By trapping extra calcium inside, this medicine gives heart muscles a mighty squeeze, creating stronger beats while gently slowing down the rhythm.

q: Which of the following is the most similar to the ecosystem type that would be found at 4000m elevation in the Andes?
e: Way up high in the chilly clouds, freezing winds make the mountaintop feel just like the icy, treeless tundra!

q: Which of the following occurs during synapsis of meiosis:
a: non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes cross over
sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes cross over
non-sister chromatids of non-homologous chromosomes cross over
sister chromatids of non-homologous chromosomes cross over
e: Matching chromosome partners hug tightly, letting non-sister arms swap little pieces of recipe code to make you wonderfully unique!

q: Enzyme A has a high Km value and low Vmax value relative to Enzyme B. This means Enzyme A, relative to Enzyme B has which of the following?
a: Higher substrate affinity and a lower reaction rate
Lower substrate affinity and a higher reaction rate
Higher substrate affinity and higher reaction rate
Lower substrate affinity and lower reaction rate
e: A high Km means this enzyme struggles to grab its targets, while a low Vmax means it finishes the job much slower.

q: Which of the following best describes the way in which the summation of action potentials from a motor neuron can bring a muscle fiber to the maximal level of contraction?
e: When nerve signals zap so quickly that a muscle never rests, it locks into one steady, powerful squeeze called tetany!

q: What was the name of the Ethiopian Wolf before they knew it was related to wolves?
e: Long before tests proved its wolf heritage, folks looked at this red mountain hunter and called it the Simien Jackal.

q: Which of the following reactions is incorrectly matched to its enzyme?
a: Kinase: catalyzes the removal of a phosphate group from a molecule
Isomerase [eye-SOM-uh-rays]: catalyzes the rearrangement of bonds within a single molecule
Synthase: condenses two smaller molecules together
Protease [PROH-tee-ays]: breaks down proteins by hydrolyzing bonds between amino acids
e: Kinases do not remove anything; they love sticking shiny phosphate tags onto molecules like cheerful gift wrappers!

q: Which of the following is an example of an ectoparasite [ek-toh- PAR-uh-syt]?
e: Because ecto means outside, a sneaky louse clings to the surface of hair rather than living deep inside the body!

q: Which of the following is NOT a result of parasympathetic nervous system stimulation?
a: Stimulation of glucose release by the liver
e: Parasympathetic nerves help you rest and digest, so releasing rush-hour sugar from the liver belongs to scary emergencies instead!

q: In DNA replication, which of the following components is necessary for the synthesis of the lagging strand but not the leading strand?
e: Because the lagging strand is built in tiny backward puzzle pieces, trusty ligase must tape them all together!

q: Which of the following tissues would contain a chondrocyte?
e: Chondrocytes are cozy cartilage cells, living happily inside the smooth, bendy hyaline cushions that pad your joints!

q: Which of the following plants is most distantly-related to the tomato?
e: Tomatoes share traits with fellow broadleaf flowering plants, while corn is a monocot grass from a completely different green branch!

q: If a single nucleotide is inserted into the middle of the protein coding sequence of a gene, which of the following is the likely outcome?
a: A frameshift mutation that leads to multiple missense and/or nonsense mutations
A single codon will have a missense mutation
One codon will have a missense or nonsense mutation, and the another nucleotide [NOO- klee-uh-tyd] will be deleted
A frameshift mutation that is silent
e: Slipping in one extra letter shifts the whole reading frame, scrambling every word after it into mixed-up nonsense!

q: Injury to cranial nerve III would result in an inability to do which of the following?
a: Feel pain in the eye area
e: This busy nerve steers several eyeball muscles, so hurting it means your eye cannot make that turn to the left!

q: Which of the following phases is typically the longest in a normal cell's life cycle?
e: Interphase is the long, cozy time when a cell grows, eats, and copies blueprints before the quick division party!

q: Which of the following is NOT a common method by which ion channels are gated?
e: Ion gates open for electrical zaps, gentle stretching, or special chemical keys, but osmolarity does not trigger their latches.

q: Which of the following medications would likely be most effective in treating a human patient with influenza?
e: While bacteria flee from antibiotics, sneaky flu viruses need a special trap, and zanamivir stops them right in their tracks!

q: In which of the following aquatic ecosystems would you expect dissolved oxygen concentrations to be so high that they are supersaturated with respect to the atmosphere?
e: Chilly, crystal-clear oligotrophic lakes have so few messy plants and bacteria eating oxygen that the crisp water stays delightfully packed with it!

q: During embryogenesis, which of the following is MOST accurate concerning the blastopore:
a: it does not exist in protostomes
it originates before the blastula stage
it forms the anus in deuterostomes (read as: DOO-ter-oh-stomes)
it is the hollow center of the gastrula
e: In deuterostomes like us, early development builds the back exit first, turning that tiny starter dimple straight into the creature's anus.

q: Bacteria at deep sea vents obtain energy by oxidizing hydrogen sulfide. They would be classified as which of the following?
e: Far below where sunlight fades, chemoautotrophs cleverly whip up their own meals using deep-sea chemicals as their kitchen fuel!

q: With which of the following are cyclin-dependent kinases most directly involved:
e: Cyclin-dependent kinases act like tiny traffic cops, waving a green flag to tell growing cells when to safely divide.

q: Which of the following human diseases is associated with flaviviruses?
e: Yellow fever is the fiery tropical illness caused by the flavivirus family, which hitches rides inside buzzing mosquitoes.

q: The type of muscle that is in the walls of human arteries is:
e: Smooth muscle quietly lines your artery walls, gently squeezing without you even thinking about it to keep blood flowing peacefully.

q: What is the average amount of chinchillas born into a single litter?
e: Mother chinchillas usually welcome a cozy pair or trio of fluffy babies, making two to three the typical litter size.

q: Which of the following glia are normally only found in the peripheral nervous system?
e: Schwann cells live out in your limbs, wrapping cozy little blankets around peripheral nerves to zip messages back home!

q: The antiviral drug remdesivir [rem-DES-ih-veer] is metabolized within cells into a nucleotide analog that inhibits RNA-dependent RNA polymerases [pah-LIM-er-aces]. Which of the following viruses would be LEAST likely to be susceptible to remdesivir?
e: Remdesivir targets a specific copying machine, but HIV cleverly uses reverse transcriptase instead, slipping completely past the trap.

q: What genetic disease is caused by having an extra Y chromosome (XYY)?
e: When a boy is born with an extra Y chromosome in his genetic blueprint, doctors call it Jacob's syndrome.

q: Moths are nocturnal, have a good sense of smell, and are also pollinators of a variety of plant species, many of which have evolved to better suit the needs of their primary pollinators. Which of the following traits would you expect to find in flowers of moth-pollinated plants?
e: Flying in the dark, hungry moths follow their super noses toward flowers pumping out heavy, musky perfumes!

q: Which of the following epithelial [ep-uh-THEE-lee-uhl] tissues is NOT correctly matched to its location in the human body?
e: The busy rectal lining actually needs tall column-shaped cells to protect it, not little simple cuboidal cubes!

q: Tunicamycin [too-ni-kuh-MY-sin] is a drug produced by some bacteria. It is used as a tool by molecular biologists because it induces eukaryotic [yoo-KAR- ee-oh-tik] cells to arrest at the G1 checkpoint of the cell cycle. Using this information about tunicamycin and your knowledge of the cell cycle, which of the following would you expect to observe in a tunicamycin-arrested cell?
e: Frozen at the G1 gate, this arrested cell never begins copying DNA, leaving active APC proteins standing watch inside.

q: In 1937, a medicinal elixir produced by a pharmaceutical company killed 71 adults and 34 children because the solvent for the drug was diethylene [dy- E-thi-leen] glycol, a chemical used now as antifreeze. Diethylene glycol is toxic because it is converted to oxalic acid by alcohol dehydrogenase [dee-HY-druh-juh-nays] and other enzymes, which damages the kidneys and brain. If given early enough, ethanol is a treatment for this poisoning. Which of the following reasons is the most likely explanation for why ethanol is an effective treatment?
a: Ethanol is an allosteric inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase
Ethanol is a more competitive substrate for alcohol dehydrogenase than diethylene glycol
Diethylene glycol has a stronger affinity for ethanol than for alcohol dehydrogenase
Ethanol cleaves the diethylene glycol molecule through an electrophilic attack on the alpha- carbon of diethylene glycol
e: Ethanol acts like the enzyme's favorite treat, competitively distracting it so the dangerous antifreeze chemical cannot do harm!

q: Which of the following is NOT true regarding vertebrate muscle contractions?
a: Tropomyosin (read as: tre-poh-MY-oh-sin) binds the calcium ions and exposes the myosin binding sites on actin filaments
The H zone and I band become shorter
T Tubules spread action potentials into the muscle fiber
The contraction is terminated when calcium ions are taken up by the sarcoplasmic reticulum
e: Troponin is the actual helper that grabs calcium, while tropomyosin merely slides away so muscle fibers can pull together!

q: Which of the following planes splits the human body into right and left halves?
e: Imagine a neat line slicing straight down your nose, dividing you into matching right and left halves: the sagittal plane!

q: Which of the following best describes the flow of energy in an ecosystem?
a: Sun heterotroph autotroph (read as: Sun to heterotroph to autotroph)
Chemotroph autotroph heterotroph (read as: chemotroph to autotroph to heterotroph)
Detritovore autotroph heterotroph (read as: detritovore to autotroph to heterotroph)
Sun autotroph heterotroph (read as: Sun to autotroph to heterotroph)
e: Golden sunshine fuels hardworking plants, which then become delicious meals for hungry animals higher up the food chain.

q: What is the predicted size in billions of base pairs of the woolly- mammoth genome?
e: Much like their living elephant cousins, these shaggy giants carried about four billion genetic letters in their ancient recipe book.

q: White-nose fungus is rapidly spreading across the United States. Which of the following events is least likely to occur as a result of its spread?
e: Without cave bats dropping tasty snacks, fragile cave critters called troglobites struggle to survive instead of happily multiplying!

q: A population of actively dividing cells contains, on average, 30 femtograms of DNA per cell. After some period of time, you make another measurement and observe that the cells now have 60 femtograms of DNA per cell. Which of the following is the most reasonable conclusion to make about these cells?
a: They are going to perform meiosis [my-OH-sis]
They are going to perform mitosis
e: In the busy cell factory, S phase is copycat time, where the cell dutifully photocopies all its DNA to have twice as much!

q: Which of these animals belongs in class Chondrichthyes?
e: Instead of hard bones, the great white shark has bendy cartilage, placing it squarely in the class Chondrichthyes.

q: Which of the following statements about the Calvin cycle is NOT true?
a: It is an important step during photosynthesis
During the Calvin cycle, the simple inorganic molecule of carbon dioxide is used to make a complex organic molecule
The compound that begins the Calvin cycle is glyceraldehydes [glis-uh-RAL-duh-hyd]-3- phosphate
The energy needed for the Calvin cycle is provided by the light reaction
e: The Calvin cycle actually builds G3P at the very end like a sweet sugary treat, so it cannot start with it!

q: Operant and classical conditioning are both examples of which of the following forms of learning?
e: Both tricks are associative learning because a clever brain connects two things together, like hearing a bell and expecting a tasty treat.

q: Which of the following best explains why a Gram-negative bacterial infection would be more difficult to treat than a Gram-positive one?
a: The cell membrane of Gram-positive bacteria functions as an endotoxin
Gram-positive bacteria have a cell membrane and a secondary lipopolysaccharide layer (read as: lip-e-pahl-i-SAHK-ah-ryd)
Gram-negative bacteria have a cell membrane and a secondary lipopolysaccharide layer
e: Gram-negative bugs wear a tough outer shield of lipopolysaccharides, acting like a slippery raincoat that keeps helpful medicines from getting inside.

q: Which of the following is a monosaccharide?
e: Galactose is a monosaccharide because it is a proud little sugar building block standing entirely on its own!

q: Mistletoe is a vascular plant that imbeds root-like structures into the limbs of a tree, robbing it of moisture and nutrients. The mistletoe provides no resources to the tree on which it depends. The ecological relationship between the mistletoe and the tree is an example of which of the following?
e: Sneaky mistletoe acts as a parasite, stealing water and food from its tree host while offering nothing back in return.

q: In humans, hyperfunctioning of the thyroid gland can result from which of the following conditions?
e: In Graves' disease, the body mistakenly sends signals that boss the thyroid gland into working way too hard!

q: What is the term for deposition of solid matter composed of mineral substances and salts, formed in any portion of the human body, such as kidney stones?
e: When minerals bunch together like tiny stubborn pebbles inside your body, doctors call that tough little stone a calculus.

q: All of the following are major metabolic consequences of obesity except:
a: Decreased lipid storage in the liver
e: With obesity, the liver gets packed with extra fat, so fat storage definitely goes up rather than decreasing.

q: Which of the following receptors could NOT be found on the surface of a cell?
e: Cells have lots of clever surface doorbells, but a laminar receptor is made up and nowhere to be found!

q: The bones of a human forearm are homologous to all of the following structures except for a:
e: While whales and bats share our cozy bone skeleton, a fly wing is built from light bug armor without any bones!

q: A child who excretes black urine is born to two normal parents. The child has a recessive homozygous genotype. What is the most likely explanation for the genotype?
e: When parents share family ancestors, consanguinity makes it much easier for rare, hidden genetic instructions to match up in their baby.

q: The thumb's opposability can be attributed to what type of synovial joint?
e: Your thumb sits comfortably in a saddle joint, rocking back and forth just like a happy rider on a pony!

q: Which of the following compounds would one use to detect the presence of protein in a polyacrylamide gel?
e: Coomassie Blue loves hugging hidden proteins, painting them a bright blue so scientists can easily spot them.

q: A student wants to know if drinking caffeinated coffee before an exam increases performance. To test this hypothesis, the student gives half the class caffeinated coffee and half of the class decaffeinated coffee. What is the independent variable?
e: Caffeine is the independent variable because the student chooses who gets it, testing if that coffee buzz changes exam scores.

q: Amanda graphs the relationship between environmental temperature and metabolic rate for different animals, where temperature is plotted on the x-axis and metabolic rate is plotted on the y-axis. For the interval from 10 to 20 degrees Celsius, which of the following animals would Amanda expect to have the largest positive slope?
e: As chilly air warms up, a cold-blooded iguana perks up fast, sending its engine speed climbing quicker than warm-blooded pals!

q: In the lab, you engineer a gene so that it is specifically expressed in pancreatic cells. Which of the following aspects of the gene did you likely adjust?
e: The promoter acts like a customized ignition switch, choosing to fire up the gene only inside pancreatic cells.

q: Which of the following is the primary difference in regulation between the lactose and tryptophan operons:
a: tryptophan activates its repressor and lactose leads to an inactive repressor
when tryptophan is present, the repressor is inactive and the opposite is true for allolactose in the lac operon
allolactose is considered a co-repressor whereas tryptophan is actually an inducer
when tryptophan is not present, the co-repressor is able to inactivate the promoter directly
e: Tryptophan wakes up its repressor to halt production, while lactose happily turns its repressor off so work can begin!

q: In which of the following does the RUBISCO enzyme play a central role:
e: In the Calvin cycle, busy worker RUBISCO grabs carbon right out of thin air to help make food for plants!

q: The triple response in a growing seedling is typically triggered by which of the following stresses?
e: When a brave little sprout bumps its head against a stubborn pebble, it thickens up and bends to sneak safely around.

q: The 'Islets of Langerhans' is found in which human organ?
e: These tiny cellular islands live inside your pancreas, working like little factories to help balance your blood sugar.

q: Which of the following best describes the result of the first step of glycolysis [glye-KAWL-eh-sis] in a fibroblast?
a: Glucose-6-phosphate is fully committed to the glycolysis [glye-KAWL-eh-sis] pathway
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate [biss-FAWS-fate] is split into two three-carbon sugars
Glucose-6-phosphate can no longer exit the cell
e: Giving sugar a tiny chemical tag locks the door, trapping it inside the cell so it cannot sneak back out.

q: Photosynthesis requires water as a reactant. In which of the following product molecules do the oxygen atoms from the water end up?
a: C6H12O6 [C- six H- twelve O- six]
e: When thirsty plants crack open water drops for energy, they happily puff out the leftover oxygen gas for us to breathe!

q: Which of the following proteins makes up intermediate filaments in the cytoskeleton?
e: Tough keratin weaves sturdy ropes inside cells to keep them strong, just like it does in your hair and fingernails.

q: Symmetry in animal taxonomy describes which of the following?
a: Similarities in anatomy of different species
How the parts of an animal are arranged around a point or an axis
e: Symmetry is nature's lovely balance trick, showing how an animal's body parts neatly line up around a center point.

q: Salmon dine on smaller fish like tiny herring, thus acquiring the energy in the herring's meat. The herring ate a lot of food energy over its lifetime that was not transferred to the salmon, however. What happened to that energy?
a: The energy was destroyed by electrical impulses
The herring converted the energy to oxygen
The herring converted the energy to carbon dioxide
The herring used the energy of its food for metabolic processes and entropy
e: The little herring burned most of that energy to swim, breathe, and live its busy daily life, losing heat along the way.

q: With which of the following is protein binding to a TATA [TAH-tah] box activity associated?
e: Clamping onto this special DNA signpost tells the cell it is finally time to start reading and copying the genetic recipe.

q: Which of the following is NOT true regarding human myoglobin [my-uh-GLOH-bin]?
a: It exhibits higher affinity for oxygen than hemoglobin
It exhibits a sigmoidal [SIG-moid-uhl] saturation curve
It is primarily an oxygen storage protein
e: Unlike its team-playing cousin hemoglobin, solo myoglobin grabs oxygen right away in a smooth curve instead of an S-shaped one.

q: Which of the following pollinators is a member of the order Lepidoptera [lep-i-DOP-ter-uh]?
e: Lepidoptera means scaly wings, making fluttering fritillary butterflies the true members of this colorful insect family.

q: . In which of the following female cervids [SUR-vids] would you find antlers?
e: While other deer moms go bareheaded, girl reindeer proudly wear their own magnificent sets of snowy antlers!

q: Neurons can communicate with each another at synapses via synaptic vesicles. Which of the following does NOT participate in communication at these sites?
e: Neurons whisper across gaps using chemical notes and speedy gates, leaving slow ATP-powered channels out of the chat.

q: Which of the following reagents is NOT required to perform a polymerase chain reaction?
e: PCR only needs starters, building blocks, and copiers, so chemical cutters like restriction enzymes stay in the drawer.

q: Which of the following human cell types is MOST directly responsible for the secretion of antibodies:
e: B cells are the body's busy defense factories, happily cranking out tiny antibody shields to tag sneaky germs.

q: Which of the following techniques would you use to determine the 3-D structure of a protein?
e: By bouncing bright X-rays off crystallized proteins, scientists capture a brilliant 3D picture of their secret twists and folds.

q: A diploid cell has 32 chromatids in the G2 phase of the cell cycle. If you examine the cell in Prophase II you would find 2 cells each containing which of the following?
e: After dividing the cell's genetic treasure in half, each new cell steps into prophase two holding sixteen DNA molecules.

q: Which of the following animals would have the highest levels of myoglobin [my-uh-GLOH-bin] in their muscle?
e: Diving deep under Antarctic ice, Weddell seals pack their muscles with oxygen-holding myoglobin for extra-long underwater adventures.

q: In humans, which of the following structures is NOT derived from myeloid [MY-uh-loid] stem cells?
e: While most blood buddies grow from the myeloid branch, clever lymphocytes hatch from their very own lymphoid family tree.

q: Which of the following structures does dynein [dye-neen] travel along?
e: Dynein acts like a tiny hiker with little feet that march along microtubule highways to deliver cargo inside the cell.

q: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is involved in controlling which of the following?
e: Tucked inside the brain, this tiny master clock tracks the sun to run your natural daily sleep and wake rhythms.

q: Chaperonins [shap-ur-OH-ninz] are involved in which of the following processes?
e: Think of chaperonins like tiny helpers, gently tucking and folding floppy new proteins into their perfect shapes.

q: Sap that is used in making maple syrup is transported by what organ?
e: Deep inside the tree trunk, tiny straw-like tubes called xylem carry sweet, watery sap up toward the sunny branches!

q: Which of the following monomers CANNOT be converted into an intermediate that can be used for cellular respiration?
e: While your cells happily burn other snacks for fuel, nucleic acids are kept safe as precious blueprints instead!

q: Which of the following is NOT true about vaccinations:
a: they were first developed against viral infections such as small pox
they allow the immune system to respond more quickly and effectively on exposure to the disease causing agent
they will typically protect the person from infection within 24 hours after vaccination
they often require adjuvants which are nonspecific irritants for best results
e: Your body's tiny superhero defenders need a week or two to study up and build armor, not just twenty-four hours!

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about lichen [LY- kuhn]?
a: It is composed of algae and moss
e: Lichens are actually cozy partnerships between fungi and algae, leaving moss out of this woodland friendship completely.

q: Which of the following genetic disorders is caused by an aneuploidy of the sex chromosomes?
e: In Turner syndrome, a girl is born missing one of her two sex chromosomes, carrying just a single X.

q: If you were to selectively extract protein molecules from the H- zone of a sarcomere [SAHR-kuh-meer], which of the following would be found in the extract?
e: Right in the sarcomere's center stripe, thick little motor proteins called myosin stand all by themselves without actin.

q: According to the Hardy-Weinberg Law, from generation to generation, gene frequencies and genotype frequency in a randomly-breeding population are:
e: Without any sneaky surprises or changes, nature keeps the population's gene pool perfectly constant and steady over time.

q: Which of the following hormones is primarily responsible for maintaining pregnancy in most mammalian species?
e: Progesterone acts like a warm, loving blanket, keeping the womb safe and calm so a baby can grow!

q: Down syndrome is caused by:
a: A contagious disease passed from mother to fetus
e: Down syndrome happens when cells pack an extra copy of chromosome twenty-one, giving three instead of two.

q: Which of the following molecules does NOT act as an electron shuttle?
e: Electron shuttles zip around carrying sparks, but pyruvate is just a bite-sized piece of food waiting to be broken down.

q: MRSA [mirsa] is an infection-causing bacteria. Which of the following best describes why MRSA is especially difficult to treat relative to many other human pathogens?
a: It can evade the immune system
It is resistant to many antibiotics
e: MRSA is a tricky little troublemaker because it wears clever armor that shrugs off many common antibiotic medicines.

q: Which of the following branches of science deals with study of the life and phenomena of inland standing waters, especially lakes and ponds?
e: Limnology is the wonder-filled science of exploring quiet inland waters, peeking into the secret lives of lakes and ponds.

q: In a landmark 1958 study by researchers Meselson and Stahl involving nitrogen isotope labeling, which of the following important DNA replication mechanisms was supported by their data?
e: When DNA unzips to make copies, each new spiral keeps one trusted old strand, making it semiconservative!

q: Which of the following basic tastes is NOT recognized by a G-protein-coupled receptor?
e: Sour flavors sneak right through tiny ionic gates on your tongue, skipping those fancy receptor proteins entirely.

q: Which of the following statements about monocots and dicots is NOT correct?
a: Monocots have three holes in their pollen, while dicots only have one
Monocots have scattered vascular bundles, while dicot bundles are in a ring
Monocots lack a pith region in the stem, while dicots have a pith
Monocots have parallel venation in their leaves while dicots have netted veins
e: That statement is backwards! Monocot pollen actually has just one little groove, while dicots show off three.

q: Which of the following is an example of a negative chemotactic response in bacteria?
a: Marine bacteria that use carbon dioxide as a nutrient are able to sense the concentration and move toward more highly-concentrated areas
Bacteria being viewed under a microscope move away from the light
In a petri dish, E. coli will move away from concentrated areas of acetate
Photosynthetic bacteria will move towards the light in a gradient
e: Negative chemotaxis means swimming away from bad vibes, just like bacteria steering clear of harsh acetate!

q: Some transposons in bacteria carry genes for proteins as well as the gene for transposase. These proteins often benefit the bacteria by imparting:
e: These jumping genes carry special shield instructions that help bacteria survive medicines through antibiotic resistance.

q: Which of the following is LEAST accurate regarding Avian migratory patterns:
a: migration of birds from the tropics to the northern latitudes is typically endogenously controlled
the migratory timing of many birds is being affected by global change
both large and very small birds migrate long distances
breeding in most birds is timed to be when fewest predators are present
e: Birds actually time their nesting when yummy food is bursting everywhere for hungry chicks, not to avoid predators!

q: A decrease in which of the following would NOT result in a decrease in blood pressure?
e: Squeezing tiny blood vessels narrower actually raises blood pressure, just like pinching a garden hose makes water spray faster!

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of a current population that shows genetic drift due to the bottleneck effect?
e: Unlike cheetahs whose numbers shrank dangerously low, African elephants kept enough variety to avoid squeezing through a tiny genetic bottleneck.

q: Which of the following scenarios most closely resembles Hardy- Weinberg equilibrium [ee-kwuh-LIB-ree-uhm]?
a: Lizards on a large, isolated island with scarce, scattered food resources
Lizards on a large, isolated island with plentiful food resources
Birds on a small island that have highly selective mating behavior
Birds on a small island that fly frequently back and forth to the mainland
e: With a spacious island and snacks for everyone, these calm lizards live peacefully without evolutionary pressure changing their gene pool.

q: Which of the following is NOT a basis for assays to measure cell numbers or cell proliferation?
e: When cells divide, they carefully copy their DNA, not RNA, so measuring RNA replication cannot tell you how many cells grew.

q: Which of the following is NOT a way that monarch butterflies manage energy on their migrations?
e: Migrating monarchs glide on breezes and pack tummy fat, but they stick to regular flower nectar rather than switching foods.

q: Which of the following hormones causes plants to grow toward light?
e: Auxin sneaks over to the stem's shady side, stretching those cells longer so the plant happily bends toward the sunny warmth.

q: Which of the following organisms possesses a water-vascular system?
e: Squishy sea cucumbers stroll along the ocean floor by pumping seawater through their bodies like tiny hydraulic engines.

q: Which of the following types of epithelial tissue would most likely be found lining the lungs and blood vessels?
e: Super-flat, single-layer simple squamous cells line your lungs like smooth floor tiles, letting oxygen slip right through without delay.

q: What genes in Drosophila control pattern formation in the larva?
e: Homeotic genes act like master architects, telling a growing fly larva exactly where to build its head, tummy, and wings.

q: Which of the following describes the relationship between glucose and fructose?
e: Glucose and fructose share the exact same chemical blocks, but they are glued together in different patterns as structural isomers.

q: If a plant had a taproot, it would also most likely have:
a: two cotyledons in its seedling stage
diffusely arranged vascular bundles in its stem
no stomata on the upper surfaces of its leaves
e: Deep-digging taproots belong to dicot plants, which sprout into the world with two baby seed leaves called cotyledons.

q: Which of the following is most directly responsible for the colloid osmotic pressure in humans that acts to retain fluid in the vascular system:
e: Albumin is a hardworking protein sponge in your blood, soaking up fluid to keep it safely inside your blood vessels.

q: What disadvantage does the presence of introns and exons give eukaryotes [yoo-KAR-ee-ohts] when compared to other organisms?
a: The ability to produce more proteins from the same primary transcript
e: With extra puzzle pieces tucked inside their genes, eukaryotes have a much harder time detecting sneaky little mutations.

q: Which of the following marine microbe groups has a cell membrane mainly comprised of lipids?
e: Unlike tiny sea critters wearing hard mineral shells, fuzzy ciliates wrap their bodies in flexible membranes made of fatty lipids.

q: Which of the following are MOST often used to introduce foreign genes into mammalian genomes:
e: Plasmids act like tiny delivery wagons made of circular DNA, happily carrying foreign genes straight into mammalian cells.

q: Mycobacterium [MY-koh-bacterium] is a genus of slow-growing and difficult-to-eradicate bacteria responsible for what two human diseases?
e: Tough Mycobacterium germs hide behind a waxy shield, slowly causing two well-known diseases called leprosy and tuberculosis.

q: Which of the following best describes how a serine protease catalyzes amide-bond-breaking reactions?
a: The enzyme increases the activation energy
The enzyme provides a mechanism with lower-energy intermediates
e: Instead of climbing a steep chemical mountain, this enzyme provides a gentler path with lower-energy steps to snip bonds apart.

q: Which of the following visual disorders results in large pressure increases within the eye?
e: Glaucoma happens when extra fluid gets trapped inside the eye, building up pressure just like an overfilled water balloon.

q: Which of the following does not occur in the tertiary structure of a protein?
e: Proteins fold using electric charges and sulfur bridges, leaving sweet glycosidic bonds behind for building sugary carbohydrates instead.

q: The phase of the Plasmodium life cycle in which it lives in the salivary gland of the mosquito is called which of the following?
e: While resting inside mosquito saliva, this sneaky parasite takes its sporozoite form, waiting to wiggle into a new host.

q: In which of the following organ systems of the human body do chief cells primarily function:
e: Chief cells live right in your stomach lining, splashing out digestive juices to help break down your lunch.

q: Which of the following correctly describes why antifungal medications are often harder to design than antibacterials?
a: Both fungi and humans are eukaryotes [yoo-KAR-ee-ohts]
Bacteria and humans have similar cellular structures
Most antifungals target chitin building enzymes
e: Because fungi and humans are both eukaryotes, our cells share similar cozy parts, making it tricky for medicine to target them without bumping us!

q: A withdrawal reflex is initiated by skin receptors that detect external stimuli. The sensory neurons then pass the message on to the spinal cord, where the sensory nerve terminals synapse with which of the following?
e: Inside your spinal cord, speedy little interneurons act like postal workers, grabbing the hot message and rushing it straight to your muscles.

q: In which of the following cell processes would caspase activity most likely occur?
e: During apoptosis, a tired cell neatly packs its bags and bows out, using little worker enzymes called caspases to quietly take itself apart.

q: What type of creature is a Bonobo?
e: Bonobos are clever, playful apes swinging through the trees, and they happen to be our closest animal cousins!

q: Which of the following statements is true regarding the mechanism of infection in prion diseases?
a: Prions invade the cell nucleus, altering DNA transcription processes
Prions induce abnormal folding in normal protein molecules
Prions bind to specific sites on a ribosome [RY-buh-sohm], rendering them useless
Prions bind to mRNA, leaving the nucleus, inducing post-transcriptional changes before translation
e: A mischievous prion taps tidy, normal proteins on the shoulder and tricks them into folding into its own wonky, tangled shape.

q: Which of the following processes is MOST under the influence of prolactin?
a: Growth and maturation of the uterine lining [YOO-ter-in]
e: Prolactin acts like a caring kitchen bell, gently signaling a mother’s body that it is time for lactation, brewing up fresh milk for baby.

q: Which of these is a colony of polyps and not a jellyfish?
e: The Portuguese Man-of-War is secretly a whole bustling team of tiny polyps working together, disguised as one drifting jellyfish.

q: In humans, in addition to transferring antibodies, colostrum also stimulates the development of the neonatal gut through the transference of:
e: A mother's first milk brings special growth factors, tiny construction helpers that build and strengthen a newborn baby's brand-new tummy.

q: Human epidermis is mostly composed of which of the following basic animal tissues types:
e: Your skin's outer layer is made of epithelial tissue, packed tight like a neat suit of armor to keep the whole wide world out.

q: Which of the following could occur due to a mutation in a Hox gene in a human embryo?
e: Hox genes are master body architects, so a tiny blueprint hiccup can accidentally build extra bonus fingers or toes, causing polydactyly!

q: When you touch a hot object and quickly draw your hand away, this is known as:
e: That lightning-fast snap away from a hot pan is your withdrawal reflex, rescuing your fingers before your brain even has time to think!

q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between glucose and fructose?
e: Glucose and fructose share the exact same chemical blocks, but hooked together in different patterns, making them clever structural isomers.

q: If the ambient temperature drops 10 degrees Celsius, what would happen to the body temperature of a rabbit and a snake, respectively?
a: It would drop linearly for the rabbit and exponentially for the snake
It would stay the same for the rabbit and drop linearly for the snake
It would stay the same for the rabbit and drop exponentially for the snake
It would drop linearly for the rabbit and for the snake
e: A warm rabbit keeps its inner heater steady, while a cold-blooded snake chills down in a straight line with the cooler air.

q: In a double reciprocal plot of Michaelis-Menton kinetics, what is the effect of a competitive inhibitor:
a: change in the vertical axis intercept
change in the horizontal axis intercept only
change in both vertical and horizontal axes intercepts
e: A competitive blocker slows progress, changing only the line's steep slope while the vertical finish anchor stays right where it started.

q: Which of the following vitamin deficiencies causes the condition known as "Pellagra"?
e: Without enough Vitamin B3 fueling your cells, your body runs low on energy and catches a miserable, bumpy sickness called pellagra.

q: The basilar membrane in the cochlea [KOK-lee-uh] is differentially sensitive to which of the following aspects of sound?
e: Like a tiny, coiled piano, different spots along the basilar membrane ripple to high squeaks or low rumbles, sorting sounds by their frequency.

q: Some virus species can infect an individual host more than once because they change the shape of molecules exposed on the surface of their virions [VY-ree- ons] so that they are no longer recognized by the host's immunological memory. The influenza virus can make sudden and drastic changes in these molecules due to a phenomenon called reassortment. Which of the following contributes to the process of reassortment?
a: The diversity of animals infected by influenza
The segmented genome found in influenza
The lack of effective antivirals against influenza until recently
e: Because the flu carries its genome in separate segments, it can shuffle them like trading cards, quickly cooking up sneaky new disguises.

q: In elephant seals, sexual selection favors competition among males for female mates. Which of the following is a likely result of this phenomenon?
a: Directional selection toward large male size
e: Since only the biggest male seals win beach battles for mates, nature nudges evolution toward an ever-larger male body size.

q: Great Lakes coastal wetlands occur along the Great lakes shoreline and portions of the tributary rivers and streams. Which of the following are NOT abiotic factors that influence patterns of species co-occurrence and distributions:
a: Fluctuations in Great Lakes water levels
Physical and chemical characteristics of the bedrock
e: While rocks and water are non-living, vegetation zonation is made of growing green plants, making it lively and biotic instead of abiotic.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT correct regarding prions?
a: They can cause scrapie and Creutzfeldt-Jakob diseases [KROYTS-felt Jakob]
They infect the same taxa [TAK-suh] as viroids [VY-roids]
They can cause degenerative brain diseases
They are an infectious agent comprised entirely of protein
e: Prions make animals sick while viroids strictly bother plants, so they definitely do not infect the same living groups!

q: Which of the following organisms is characterized as a parazoan [para-ZOH-an]?
e: Meet the sponge, a simple sea critter happily living without true tissues or organs, making it a classic parazoan!

q: Which of the following is the adjective for a leaf arrangement in which two leaves are present at each node?
e: Picture two leaves sitting right across the stem from each other like best friends waving hello; that is an opposite arrangement.

q: If you lower the intracellular levels of fructose 2, 6 biphosphate, what will happen to the rate of gluconeogenesis [gloo-koh-nee-uh-JEN-uh-sis] and glycolysis [gly-KOL-uh-sis], respectively?
a: Gluconeogenesis speeds up, glycolysis slows down
Gluconeogenesis slows down, glycolysis speeds up
Gluconeogenesis and glycolysis both slow down
Glycolysis speeds up and gluconeogenesis halts
e: Without this tiny helper around, the cell stops burning sugar quickly and instead gets busy making fresh sugar!

q: Which of the following is NOT true of the most common form of DNA:
a: it has 3.4 nanometers between each successive nucleotide base of the same strand
each strand has a 3-prime phosphate and a 5-prime hydroxyl at opposite ends
e: DNA strands are twisted backwards here, because real strands always wear a phosphate hat at the five-prime end, not the three-prime!

q: All codon combinations specify a particular amino acid, with the EXCEPTION of which of the following?
e: Nonsense codons do not build anything; they act like little red stop signs telling the cell to finish building its protein.

q: The fat body of insects is an important organ for metabolism. Which of the following is NOT a function of the fat body?
a: Filter water from the hemolymph (read as: HEE-moh-lim(p)f)
e: An insect's fat body is a cozy pantry for storing energy, leaving the messy water-filtering chores to other organs!

q: What do the human appendix and the python pelvic spurs have in common?
e: Both are evolutionary leftovers, like tiny biological souvenirs that lost their main jobs over millions of years.

q: Which of the following was a technique invented by Meselson and Stahl in their classic experiments to support the theory of semiconservative replication:
e: These clever scientists spun DNA around like a dizzy carnival ride to separate the heavy strands from the light ones!

q: In which of the following areas of the human body is the zygomatic (read as: ZYE-go-MAT-ick) arch found:
e: Put a hand on your smiling cheek, and you will feel this sturdy arch right inside your head!

q: The Spotted Owl is considered an endangered species in the western United States, largely due to competition from the introduced Barred Owl. These two species are genetically similar and are believed to have speciated from a common ancestor after separation of the two populations on opposite coasts of the United States. This is an example of:
e: When geography separates owl cousins on opposite coasts, they slowly grow apart into different species through allopatric speciation.

q: Which of the following plants is NOT a succulent?
e: While succulents hoard water in plump, juicy leaves, eucalyptus is just a thirsty, woody tree loved by cuddly koalas.

q: Underwater mountains called seamounts provide a solid surface to cling to for many kinds of marine animals. Seamounts are important for all of the following reasons, except:
a: They are sustainable locations for deep-sea fishing
They support distinctive groups of animals, including corals
Their altitude they causes complex current patterns
e: Deep-sea fish around seamounts grow too slowly to handle heavy nets, making fishing there far from sustainable.

q: MRSA is an infection by which of the following?
e: Under a microscope, these pesky germs look like tiny, round spheres clustered together to cause trouble.

q: Which of the following tissues is MOST directly responsible for the increased diameter of a tree trunk from year to year:
e: This hidden ring of busy plant cells works all summer building new wood, helping tree trunks grow wider and wider!

q: What substance composes the frustule [FRUH-stool] of a diatom?
e: Diatoms are tiny ocean artists that build their sparkly outer shells entirely out of silica, just like real glass!

q: Which of the following is a carnivorous [kahr-NIV-or-uhs] plant?
e: Nepenthes plants lure hungry bugs into slippery, pitcher-shaped traps to dissolve them for a tasty, carnivorous snack!

q: If a protein contains a signal peptide, in which of the following locations would it LEAST likely be found?
e: A signal peptide is a special mailing label sending proteins into organelles, meaning they rarely stay in the cytosol.

q: Homologous structures in animals are evidence supporting evolutionary theory, because these structures:
a: Perform similar functions, but do not share the same basic structure
Can differ in appearance between animals, but are modifications of the same basic structure
Are produced by identical genes, which reside in all animals that share the homologous structure
Appear identical in all animals that share the homologous structure
e: Evolution remixes the same basic skeleton blueprint, turning shared bones into a human arm, a whale flipper, or a bat wing!

q: Kearns-Sayre Syndrome is caused by a mutation on a gene in the mitochondrial [my-tuh-KON-dree-uhl] DNA. Both males and females can have the disease, but the disease can only be transmitted to a child by the mother, never the father. Why is this so?
a: The gene is on the X chromosome, and females are XX
The sperm that fertilizes the egg contributes only its chromosomes and none of its mitochondria
The mutant protein is only active in the egg, not the sperm
e: The mother's egg supplies all the cell's tiny powerhouses, while the sperm only delivers chromosomes and zero mitochondria.

q: What is the name of the genus of the early hominid Lucy?
e: Lucy belongs to Australopithecus, a famous group of ancient relatives who took some of humanity's very first two-legged steps!

q: Cataracts occur in what part of the eye?
e: Think of your eye's lens as a clear little window. When a cataract moves in, it fogs up that lens like a steamy bathroom mirror.

q: Chlorophyll a and b most strongly absorb which of the following colors of light?
e: Plants love snacking on sunlight, and their green chlorophyll gobbles up energetic blue light most hungrily to make sweet food.

q: In the 1980s, Europeans began to be diagnosed with mad cow disease, a disease which affects the brain. What is the type of infectious agent that causes this disease?
e: Unlike sneaky viruses or bacteria, a prion is just a misfolded protein that mischievously bends healthy brain proteins out of shape.

q: Which of the following terms indicates centromere [SEN-truh- meer] placement at the end of the chromosome?
e: A telocentric chromosome wears its centromere right at the very tip, just like a bright pom-pom perched on a winter hat.

q: Chlorosis in plants can be caused by a deficiency in which of the following nutrients?
e: Plants need iron to brew rich green chlorophyll, so without it, their leafy smiles turn pale and yellow with chlorosis.

q: Glucose is an example of what class of sugars?
e: Glucose is known as a hexose sugar because its sweet little ring is built from six sturdy carbon atoms.

q: Which of the following segments of an mRNA molecule is not translated into protein?
e: Like a tiny red traffic light, the stop codon tells the cell factory to finish up, so it never gets built into protein.

q: Which of the following does not play a role in protein digestion?
e: While other enzymes slice up hearty proteins, dextrinase only has eyes for chopping up sweet, starchy carbs.

q: Which of the following cleavage patterns is characteristic of deuterostomes [doo-tuhr-oh-stohms]?
e: In deuterostome embryos, dividing cells use radial cleavage to neatly stack atop each other, like a tidy tower of tiny blocks.

q: Which of the following most closely approximates the number of protein-coding genes in the fruit fly genome?
e: Inside that tiny fruit fly buzzing around your kitchen, about 12,000 protein-coding genes work together to build its busy little life.

q: Which of the following is an example of a pair of homoplastic traits?
e: Bacteria and complex cells both invented swimming tails separately, making their flagella homoplastic traits that look alike without sharing family history.

q: Which of the following organic groups is NEVER bound to the central carbon atom of an amino acid?
e: Amino acids love hugging an amine and a carboxyl group, but a nitrile group is never invited to their central carbon party.

q: Folic acid is the synthetic form of which vitamin?
e: Folic acid is a handy, man-made version of folate, an energetic member of the busy Vitamin B family.

q: The drug colchicine [KOL-chuh-seen] inhibits polymerization [puh-lim-er-uh-ZAY-shuhn] of tubulin in microtubule assembly. Which of the following cell processes would be most severely impacted by colchicine activity?
e: Cells rely on tiny microtubule ropes to pull chromosomes apart during mitosis, so stopping those ropes halts cell division completely.

q: Bacteria are classified as Gram positive or Gram negative based on several characteristics, including which of the following?
e: Scientists sort bacteria by their cell wall structure, which acts like armor that either traps or lets go of colorful purple stain.

q: Which of the following is closest to the maximum ATP molecules generated from the complete oxidation of 1 mole of glucose in a typical eukaryotic cell:
e: Squeezing every drop of energy from a single glucose sugar can power up a grand maximum of 38 buzzing ATP battery packs.

q: Which of the following organisms possesses cnidocytes [NYE-doh-sites]?
e: Drifting gracefully through the ocean, a jellyfish arms its flowing tentacles with cnidocytes, which are spring-loaded stinging cells for snagging snacks.

q: An apple flower is hermaphroditic, it has both a pistil and a stamen, which means it is a type of:
e: Because an apple blossom houses both pollen-making and seed-making parts under one roof, the plant is happily monoecious.

q: A deficiency in which of the following vitamins causes pernicious anemia?
e: Cobalamin, also called vitamin B12, builds red blood cells, so without enough of it, the body gets tired with pernicious anemia.

q: In recent years, honey bee populations have been decreasing. What impact would the extinction of honey bees have on human agriculture?
a: Different types of pollinators could be used; there would be no impact on agriculture
All honey bee pollinated plants would go extinct
Plants would asexually reproduce instead; there would be no impact on agriculture
Some species are only pollinated by honey bees and would therefore need to be hand pollinated or face extinction
e: Some special flowers depend solely on honey bees, meaning gardeners would have to dust them by hand or watch them vanish.

q: Which of the following best describes a major role of the p53 protein in the cell?
a: Transitioning a cell into the G-naught phase after differentiation
Detecting DNA damage and halting cell division in the G-one phase
Triggering division in a cell with damaged DNA
Acting as a nuclease in the process of repairing DNA
e: Think of p53 as a tiny crossing guard, stopping cell division in G-one whenever it spots damaged DNA.

q: Which of the following phases of meiosis [my-OH-sis] is longest?
e: Prophase one takes the longest because chromosomes carefully hug and swap cozy little secrets before parting ways.

q: Which of the following is a major benefit of membrane-bound cells and organelles?
e: Membranes build tidy little rooms inside the cell so different chemical jobs can bubble away without making a giant mess!

q: An effective enzyme has a very high affinity for which of the following?
e: Helpful enzymes love catching molecules mid-somersault at their transition state, gently squeezing them until they transform.

q: You are walking in July when you come across a hedgehog. The animal does not stir when you pick it up; it is breathing and is not injured. What is the best explanation for the animal's lack of responsiveness?
a: It is in a state of torpor
It is in a state of suspended animation
e: On scorching summer days, this hedgehog is estivating, taking a deep, sleepy nap to stay cool and save energy.

q: One species resembles another species that is poisonous. What is this phenomenon called?
e: In Batesian mimicry, a harmless little creature wears a scary copycat costume to fool hungry bullies into staying away.

q: In newly-saturated soils, which of the following processes consumes oxygen more rapidly than it can be replenished by diffusion from the atmosphere?
e: Tiny soil microbes breathe so quickly through respiration that they gulp up every drop of oxygen underwater!

q: Unlike on most salamanders, this part of a newt is flat?
e: Unlike other salamanders, a newt sports a flat, paddle-like tail that works just like a rudder for swimming.

q: Which of the following pairs of terms referring to the life cycle of land plants is mismatched with the correct ploidy?
e: The integument is a protective coat made from the mother plant's diploid cells, so calling it haploid is totally backwards.

q: Which of the following is not true regarding mitosis?
a: Sister chromatids are held together by cohesion [coh-ee-sin] complexes
M-Cdk drives entry of the cell into mitosis
The mitotic spindle is built from actin filaments
The Golgi apparatus becomes less prominent during metaphase
e: Cells build their tug-of-war spindle using tubulin tubes, not actin filaments, to pull chromosomes apart!

q: Which of the following groups of organisms would contain the most biomass productivity in a trophic pyramid?
e: Sun-loving green plants, our primary producers, harvest tons of golden sunlight to make the biggest mountain of living food.

q: How do bacteria protect their own genomic DNA from being cut by their restriction endonucleases [en-duh-NOO-klee-ays-is]?
a: Genomic DNA of a bacterial species does not contain the recognition sequences for its own restriction endonucleases
Bacteria apply protective methyl groups to DNA at sites recognized by their restriction endonucleases
Bacteria have proteins associated with their genomic DNA, preventing the endonucleases from getting close enough to cut
Sequestration of chromosomal DNA in the nucleoid region of a bacterial cell protects it from being cut by restriction endonucleases
e: Clever bacteria stick tiny methyl tags onto their own DNA like name badges, warning their scissor-proteins not to snip!

q: In one form of the disease called macular degeneration, eyesight decreases due to overproduction of new blood vessels (angiogenesis [an-jee-oh-JEN-uh-sis]) in the eye. Inhibition of a gene involved in angiogenesis can be achieved by introducing which of the following forms of complementary RNA molecule into the eye?
e: Little bits of siRNA latch onto matching messages and silence them, politely telling runaway blood vessels to stop growing.

q: If you fluorescent-labeled the outsides of the trans-membrane proteins of one mammalian cell with a yellow label and another cell with a red label and fused them, which of the following would MOST likely occur over about 1 hour at 37C:
a: the labels would remain unevenly distributed on the outside of the cells
one color would show up in the inside of the cell and the other would remain on the outside
the labels would mix evenly on the outside of the cell
e: Like swimmers swirling in a warm pool, the red and yellow surface proteins drift around until they mix evenly!

q: If a person has consumed too much alcohol and is showing signs of ataxia [uh-TAK-see-uh], what portion of the brain is being inhibited?
e: The cerebellum is your inner gymnast; when alcohol makes it drowsy, staying balanced turns into a very wobbly adventure.

q: Which of the following statements about bacterial cell walls is NOT correct?
a: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan cell wall
Beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit cell wall synthesis
Lignin is the primary component of Gram-negative bacterial cell walls
The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria contains lipo-poly- saccharides
e: Lignin belongs in stiff wooden tree trunks, not bacteria, so it definitely is not part of a Gram-negative wall.

q: Through which of the following mechanisms do allosteric inhibitors typically operate:
a: binding to an enzyme's active site
binding to a site other than the active site and changing the shape of an enzyme
acting as a competitive inhibitor and overpowering the active sites of enzymes
e: An allosteric inhibitor nudges a secret side button on the enzyme, reshaping it so its active pocket cannot work.

q: Which of the following statements is true of plant cells, but not animal cells?
a: They use a cell plate to divide sister cells in cytokinesis
They use channels to allow transfer of ions between cells
They have specialized organelles that likely evolved through endosymbiosis
e: Because of their stiff jackets, dividing plant cells build a neat little cell plate right down the middle like a wall.

q: Which of the following amino acids is typically phosphorylated [faws-FOR-il-ated] by protein kinase A?
e: Protein kinase A loves giving sparkly phosphate gifts to serine, snapping them right onto that specific friendly amino acid.

q: The size of most mammalian cells is closest to which of the following?
e: Mammalian cells are microscopic wonders, measuring around one micrometer across, far too tiny for our eyes to spot alone.

q: The common dandelion, which is fluorescent under UV light, is pollinated by what?
e: To busy little bees, that glowing dandelion shines like a bright landing strip, inviting them right in for a sweet sip of nectar!

q: Which of the following types of signaling best describes cellular communication via hormones?
e: Endocrine glands act like tiny post offices, sending hormone letters floating through your bloodstream to deliver messages far away.

q: In dragons, the alleles [uh-LEELS] for yellow flame color and blue flame color are incompletely dominant. If a homozygous [hoh-muh-ZY-guhs] yellow-flame dragon mates with a homozygous blue-flame dragon, all of the brood will have green flame. Which of the following choices represents an expected probability for a brood produced by two green-flame dragons?
e: When two green-flame dragons mix their magic, each egg has a one-in-four chance of getting two yellow genes for yellow fire.

q: Which of the following forms of nitrogen cannot be directly utilized by plants?
e: Even with nitrogen gas floating all around, plants cannot grab it from the air until soil bacteria turn it into plant food.

q: Which of the following is NOT true regarding aquatic biomes?
a: Much of the photosynthesis occurring in a coral reef is performed by corals
Intertidal zones are characterized by high levels of oxygen and nutrients
Oceanic pelagic zones are the largest biome on Earth
Phytoplankton are the dominant photosynthesizers in pelagic zones
e: Corals are actually tiny animal builders, so they leave all the sun-powered food making to their microscopic algae roommates!

q: Topoisomerases [toh-poh-eye-SAW-mer-aces] are involved in which of the following processes?
e: Topoisomerases act like gentle detanglers, smoothing out tight twists in DNA so cells can safely copy it during replication.

q: Euglena are unicellular organisms classified into the Kingdom Protista. Which of the following characteristics is NOT true of euglena?
a: They can make their own food by photosynthesis
They can absorb food from their environment
They move by the motion of their flagella
e: These spunky little swimmers actually love splashing around in quiet freshwater ponds, not salty ocean waves.

q: In which of the following populations would you expect genetic drift to show the strongest effect?
e: In a tiny zoo colony, random chance makes a huge splash, easily changing genetic traits because there are so few penguins.

q: The common shore ragworm only leaves its sandy tube to feed. If a shadow passes overhead, it will quickly return to the safety of its burrow. If the shadow passes overheard repeatedly and nothing happens, the worm will eventually ignore the shadow. This type of learning is called:
e: Through habituation, the clever worm learns that harmless shadows are not scary monsters, so it calmly stops ducking into its burrow.

q: Which of the following is not true regarding arthropods?
a: Arthropods have an open circulatory system
Molting occurs because arthropods cannot grow without shedding their exoskeleton
Book lungs are found in arachnids
Cheliceriformes [kuh-liss-er-uh-forms] are characterized by 5 pairs of legs and two pairs of antennae
e: Spiders and their kin walk on four pairs of legs and have zero antennae, making that five-legged description totally wrong.
