q: Which of the following is NOT a biogenic amine?
e: While the others are tiny chemical messengers made from single amino bits, dynorphin is actually a bigger protein-like peptide.

q: In which of the following organisms would one most likely find nematocysts?
e: Jellyfish carry these spring-loaded stinging harpoons in their floaty tentacles to catch dinner with a quick zap!

q: Which species of Brown Bear is not extinct?
e: While other brown bears sadly vanished, the Syrian brown bear is still plodding happily through mountain forests today!

q: Which of the following methods of dissemination of bacterial genetic material is mismatched to its description?
a: Transduction: viral transfer of one cell's DNA to another
Conjugation: through physical interaction, a donor cell transfers genetic material to a recipient cell
Transformation: one bacteria engulfs another to integrate its DNA
e: In transformation, bacteria do not gobble each other up; they just scoop up loose bits of floating DNA like sunken treasure.

q: Oswald Avery found that an "infectious principle" could be transferred from dead, virulent streptococcus bacteria to living, avirulent bacteria, causing them to become virulent. Which of the following is NOT true of this infectious principle?
a: This material can be separated from protein in an ultracentrifuge [ultra-SEN-trih-fyooj]
RNA-digesting enzymes have no effect on the activity of this material
Performing a hydrophobic [high-droh-FOH-bik] extraction removes the material from water
DNAse [D.N. ace] destroys all activity of this material
e: DNA loves water way too much to vanish into oil, so an oily extraction leaves this magic recipe right behind.

q: You suspect that Cylon, an alien, may be the parent of a human- alien hybrid baby. The alien's blood type happens to be homozygous [hoh-muh-ZY-guhs] for blood type P for purple, the allele of which is symbolized by IP [eye superscript P]. As with other blood types, the P protein is co-dominant. If the human parent's blood type is A with a homozygous genotype, what blood phenotype would the baby have to be in order to be a confirmed human-alien hybrid baby?
e: By getting an A tag from one parent and a P tag from the other, this cosmic baby proudly displays both as type AP.

q: Which of the following animal respiratory pigments does not contain iron?
e: Hemocyanin uses shiny blue copper instead of iron to grab oxygen, giving creatures like octopuses cool blue blood.

q: Which of the following BEST describes the syndrome that manifests itself in starving children as swollen distended abdomens, spindly arms, and edema in the face, hands, and feet resulting from the catabolism of muscle and blood proteins?
e: Kwashiorkor happens when a child misses vital protein, causing fluid to gather in their belly while their muscles struggle.

q: Which of the following is a constituent of blood plasma but NOT of blood serum?
e: Fibrinogen is the sticky protein that weaves nets for blood clots, so it gets completely used up when serum forms.

q: At a 4th of July picnic, Uncle Vernon was munching down on his ear of yellow corn when he exclaimed, "Why do some of these corn kernels have purple spots? Is the corn toxic?" You quickly explain that the corn is not toxic and that the spots were caused by what?
e: Playful jumping genes hop right into a kernel's color recipe mid-growth, switching on purple spots like bursts of confetti.

q: In humans, the cerebellum is primarily responsible for which of the following functions?
e: Your cerebellum acts like a tiny tightrope walker in your brain, keeping you upright so you can zoom around without tipping over!

q: What scientific suborder does the family Hyaenidae belong to?
e: Hyenas might laugh like rowdy dogs, but science places them into Feliformia, meaning they are actually secret cousins to cats.

q: Which of the following best describes the repressor protein in the lac (read as: LACK) operon:
e: This little repressor protein is like a polite traffic cop, regulating when the cell's food-digesting machine turns on or takes a nap.

q: Which of the following insects has a unique muscle arrangement that allows them to power their flight directly?
e: Dragonflies have flight muscles hooked directly to their wings, letting them steer like acrobatic little helicopters dancing through the summer air.

q: What is the first place in the breakdown of glucose, starting in glycolysis and through the Krebs cycle, where CO2 is released:
e: As pyruvate turns into Acetyl Co-A, it happily pops off a little puff of carbon dioxide, the very first one released from your sugar snack!

q: In which of the following locations would a spliceosome [SPLY- see-uh-sohm] be found?
e: Tucked safe inside the cozy nucleus, the spliceosome snips messy message ribbons into neat, tidy instructions for building things.

q: An ecologist uses seven foot tall mist nets to capture birds. In which of these habitats would the number of captures most likely underestimate the actual number of birds present?
e: In a tall temperate forest, feathered friends party way up in the leafy canopy, soaring right over seven-foot nets hidden below!

q: Which of the following forms of nitrogenous [nye-TRAW-jen-us] waste excretion is most energetically costly to produce?
e: Making uric acid takes a mountain of energy, but animals gladly spend it to save every last precious drop of water.

q: If you needed to find a sample of simple cuboidal epithelium [eh- pih-THEEL-ee-um] in the human body, you would want tissue from which of the following organs?
e: Your kidneys are packed with cheerful, cube-shaped cells lined up in little tubes to wash your blood clean all day long.

q: Which of the following are NOT found in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast?
e: Busy Rubisco doesn't sit in that membrane; it floats freely in the chloroplast's soupy liquid, catching carbon from the air.

q: The mechanisms involved in aligning homologous chromosomes in meiosis are also useful for which of the following?
e: The same clever tool that matches chromosomes also glues DNA back together when both of its spiraling strands snap clean in half!

q: Which of the following diseases is caused by a virus?
e: Shingles happens when the sneaky chickenpox virus wakes up from a long, quiet nap inside your nerves to cause mischief.

q: The organisms that form truffles are predominantly part of what group of fungi?
e: Yummy truffles belong to the ascomycetes, clever fungi that pack their secret spores into microscopic little sleeping bags underground.

q: Which of the following types of cells could one find surrounding a stomatal pore?
e: Guard cells hug leaf pores like friendly doormen, puffing up to let fresh air in or closing tight to save water!

q: Which of the following ecosystems typically has the lowest net primary productivity per unit area?
e: The freezing tundra grows the least plant life of all, shivering through long, dark winters under a thick blanket of frost.

q: Monocytes in the blood are precursors to which of the following cell types found in tissues?
e: Wandering monocytes slip out of the blood and grow up into big, hungry macrophages, ready to gobble up pesky germs!

q: Which of the following best describes what will occur to a tadpole if it is fed pieces of a thyroid gland?
a: It will be unable to undergo metamorphosis
It will begin to suffer from adrenal [Ah-DREE-nul] insufficiency
e: Munching on thyroid tissue gives a tadpole a rush of growth signals, rushing it to sprout frog legs right away!

q: Which of the following BEST describes the problem that torsion creates for gastropods?
a: More energy is needed to develop a coiled shell
Waste is expelled above the organism's head and mouth
It limits the amount of space the organism has for growth
To eat, an organism must extend its body outside of its protective shell
e: When a snail twists its body around, its plumbing twists too, awkwardly dropping waste right above its own head and mouth!

q: Which of the following is NOT true of nucleated mammalian cells:
a: mast cells contain large amounts of histamine
the golgi apparatus processes proteins for exocytosis
all the DNA in a nucleated cell is in the nucleus
e: Not all DNA lives in the nucleus, because busy little mitochondria keep their own secret loops of DNA, too!

q: In the famous experiment by Hershey and Chase that showed DNA was the genetic material, what did they use to transmit the DNA into E. coli:
e: Scientists used bacteriophages, tiny virus landing pods, to inject their DNA blueprints straight into unsuspecting bacteria.

q: Which of the following best describes the reason for the similarity between the wing of a bird and the wing of an insect?
e: Birds and bugs are not close cousins, but convergent evolution gave them both wings because flying is just that awesome!

q: Which of the following characteristics of plants is absent in charophyte algae?
e: Unlike algae, land plants alternate multicellular generations, playing a clever tag-team game between two different grown-up body forms.

q: Female insects usually lay their eggs near which of the following?
e: Caring insect moms lay eggs right beside yummy food so their hungry babies can wake up to an all-you-can-eat breakfast!

q: Which of the following best describes the type of RNA that codes for a complete gene on the sense strand of a DNA molecule?
e: Pre-messenger RNA is the cell's fresh, unedited recipe copy straight from the DNA, before any pieces get trimmed away.

q: Which of the following types of genes violates Mendel's principle of independent assortment?
e: Linked genes sit so close together on a chromosome that they hold hands and travel together, breaking Mendel's shuffling rule.

q: Which of the following statements best describes the sex chromosome content of female and male cells in birds?
a: Females are ZW, males are ZZ
Females are WW, males are ZW
Females are ZZ, males are ZW
Females are ZZ, males are WW
e: In the bird world, girl birds carry mismatched ZW chromosomes, while boy birds get a matching pair of ZZ chromosomes.

q: Which of the following is a characteristic of monocots, but NOT eudicots [yoo-dy-KOTS]?
a: Flower parts in multiples of four or five
e: Instead of neat tidy rings, monocot stems sprinkle their water pipes all over the place in scattered vascular bundles.

q: Professional antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages and dendritic [den-DRIH-dik] cells typically present foreign antigens to which of the following types of cells?
e: Scout cells show captured invader pieces directly to helper T cells, who then rally the whole immune team into action!

q: What specific part of the human brain has the most influence on heart rate, sleep, body temperature, and metabolism, and is a large part of the ventral portion of the diencephalon (read as: die-en-SEFF-ah-lon):
e: Your tiny hypothalamus acts like your body's master control dial, gently balancing your temperature, heartbeat, and sleepy bedtime rhythms.

q: Which of the following organisms is the primary infection target of the virus T2?
e: The little T2 virus acts like a tiny lunar spaceship built specifically to land on and invade E. coli bacteria.

q: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of most insecticides?
e: Most bug sprays protect plants by scrambling insect nerves, shutting down the electrical messages their little bodies need to move.

q: If you are doing a western blot, what kind of macromolecule are you trying to detect?
e: A western blot acts like a super-sleuth that hunts through a messy cell soup to spot one specific protein.

q: Which of the following is most likely a descendent of dinosaurs?
e: That cheerful robin hopping on your lawn is actually a real, feathered dinosaur who swapped giant teeth for flight and song!

q: Which of the following is a primary consequence of histone acetylation:
a: increased access of transcriptional factors to DNA
decreased access of transcriptional factors to DNA
increased rate of cells entering mitosis
e: Histone acetylation unspools tightly wrapped DNA like a cozy scarf, letting cell helpers easily reach inside to read the genes.

q: What is the name of the enzyme that catalyzes the formation of bicarbonate and hydronium ions from CO2 and H2O [C-O two and H two O]?
e: Carbonic anhydrase is a super-fast enzyme that instantly snaps water and bubbly carbon dioxide together into bicarbonate.

q: Which of the following genes would initially establish the axes of the Drosophila body?
e: Fly mothers pack their eggs with maternal effect genes first, handing the tiny embryo its very first head-to-tail roadmap.

q: Which of the following is NOT considered to be a tumor suppressor protein?
e: While tumor suppressors act like brakes, HER2/neu is an eager gas pedal that actually pushes cells to divide and grow.

q: In an indirect immunofluorescence experiment, which of the following would be most useful for imaging a protein that is first probed with a rabbit antibody?
e: A glowing goat-anti-rabbit RFP antibody happily sticks onto the first rabbit antibody, lighting up the target protein like a red beacon.

q: As the average temperature dropped during the last glacial period, a species of cave bears evolved a layer of thicker fur. What kind of selection is this an example of?
e: As the world froze, directional selection pushed the bear population in one clear direction, favoring super-shaggy coats for staying warm.

q: Assume that genes A and B are not linked. If an organism is heterozygous [het-er-uh-ZY-guhs] for both genes, what is the probability that the organism will produce a gamete [GAM-eet] with both the dominant A and B alleles [uh-LEELS]?
e: Because the gene pairs shuffle independently like rolling dice, dominant A and B have a one-in-four chance of teaming up!

q: Which of the following statements does NOT accurately describe allosteric regulation of enzyme activity?
a: An allosteric regulator binds covalently at an enzyme's catalytic site
Allosteric regulation can increase or decrease protein activity
Binding of an allosteric regulator induces a conformational change in a protein
The binding of hemoglobin to oxygen is an example of positive allosteric regulation
e: These little helpers do not glue themselves to the main workbench; they gently nudge a secret back door instead!

q: Which of the following regulate development in animals, plants and fungi, and were first discovered in Drosophila:
e: Homeobox genes are like master architects, holding the secret blueprints that tell tiny fly bodies and growing plants where every part belongs!

q: Which of the following organisms stores major food reserves as laminarin and oil instead of starch?
e: While other plants hoard sugary starch, giant brown algae drift in ocean currents, happily packing lunchboxes filled with special laminarin and droplets of oil!

q: Mineral salts participate in enzymatic activity as which of the following?
e: Mineral salts act as trusty co-factors, rushing in like cheerful sidekicks to hand enzymes the missing tools they need to get working!

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about the G protein hormone receptor system?
a: It is an example of membrane-based signal transduction
It results in an amplification of the original signal
The hormone is a ligand for the G protein
The G protein must be able to move along the membrane
e: The messenger hormone never hugs the G protein directly. It knocks on an outer receptor door, which then passes the secret whisper inside!

q: In accessory fruits, the majority of the fruit tissue is derived from outside the floral ovary. Which of the following fruits is an example of an accessory fruit?
e: Sweet red strawberries are playful tricksters because their juicy flesh actually puffs up from the flower's stem base, not from the ovary!

q: Which of the following organelles within the eukaryotic [yoo- KAR-ee-oh-tik] cell functions as the digestive system of the cell, serving both to degrade material taken up from outside the cell and to digest obsolete components of the cell itself?
e: Lysosomes are the cell's tidy recycling bins, happily gobbling up worn-out parts and melting down trash with powerful tummy juices!

q: Which of the following types of tissue do monocot roots possess at their center that dicot roots do not?
e: Monocot roots hide a soft, spongy core called pith right in their centers, tucked away like a cozy pillow that dicot roots skip!

q: Which of the following is NOT true regarding ribosomes:
a: they are about 20 nanometers in diameter
eukaryotic ribosomes are slightly larger than prokaryotic ribosomes
mitochondrial ribosomes have 40S (read as: forty S) small subunits
e: Mitochondria carry ancient little ribosomes, but their tiny building blocks are much smaller than the standard forty S pieces found elsewhere.

q: Which of the following best exemplifies secondary endosymbiosis [en-doh-sim-bee-OH-sis]?
a: Human white blood cell phagocytosis [fag-uh-sy-TOH-sis] of a pathogenic bacterium
Cyanobacterium [sy-uh-noh-bak-TEER-ee-uhm] is engulfed by a heterotrophic eukaryote [het-er-uh-TROF-ik yoo-KAR-ee-oht]
A heterotrophic eukaryote engulfs a green algal eukaryote
e: Secondary endosymbiosis happens when one hungry cell swallows another cell that already carries a sun-loving green alga inside it!

q: Which of the following is NOT a direct requirement for dinoflagellates [din-uh-FLAJ-uh-layts] to carry out bioluminescence?
e: To create their glowing ocean sparkle, these tiny critters crave oxygen and fuel, but leave sleepy carbon dioxide out of the light show entirely!

q: Which of the following compounds would one use to detect the presence of DNA in an agarose gel?
e: Ethidium bromide sneaks right between the rungs of hidden DNA ladders, lighting them up like glowing neon signs under ultraviolet light!

q: Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase [kahr-BOK-suh- layz]/oxygenase[OK-si-juh-nays], also known as RuBisCO, is an enzyme present in photosynthetic plants and is thought to be the most abundant protein on earth. Which of the following is NOT a reason that plants produce such large quantities of RuBisCO?
a: RuBisCO is inhibited by carbon dioxide
Plants build large aggregate complexes of RuBisCO
e: Slow RuBisCO actually adores carbon dioxide as tasty food, so saying it stops or slows down around it is completely backward!

q: Fruits primarily function in order to entice animals to eat them. In what way does this benefit the fruiting plant?
a: Animals pollinate while eating the fruits
Animals eat the fruit instead of other parts of the plant
There is no benefit to the plant
e: Plants bake sweet, juicy snacks so wandering critters carry their tucked-away seeds on marvelous journeys, planting them far from home!

q: Which of the following is an incorrect descriptor of DNA replication?
a: Discontinuous on the lagging strand and continuous on the leading strand
e: Copying life's precious recipe book is careful and precise, not a mindless, broken record repeating the same page over and over!

q: Which one of these is scientific term for "Brain Freeze"?
e: Gulping icy treats too fast triggers sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia, a gigantic medical name for an ordinary brain freeze.

q: Which of the following organelles is the location of post-translation modifications to proteins?
e: The bustling Golgi body acts like a cheerful shipping center, adding fancy ribbons, tags, and final touches to brand-new proteins!

q: In humans, in addition to transferring antibodies, colostrum also stimulates the development of the neonatal gut through the transference of which of the following?
e: Colostrum carries loving growth factors that act like tiny cheerleaders, encouraging a newborn baby's tummy lining to grow strong and healthy!

q: The lambdoid suture is found in which of the following parts of the human body:
e: The lambdoid suture stitches bony plates together like a neat seam in the back of your skull, protecting your brilliant brain!

q: Which chamber in the heart has the highest systolic pressure?
e: The mighty left ventricle flexes with supreme muscle power, blasting fresh blood on a thrilling roller-coaster ride across your whole body!

q: Which of the following molecules catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids?
e: A ribosome acts like a cozy little factory, carefully snapping amino acids together to build brand-new proteins.

q: In a gel electrophoresis [i-lek-troh-fuh-REE-sis] experiment, in which of the following directions will a DNA sample move, and why?
a: Toward the negative electrode because DNA has a positive charge
Toward the negative electrode because DNA has a negative charge
Toward the positive electrode because DNA has a positive charge
Toward the positive electrode because DNA has a negative charge
e: Because DNA carries a negative charge, it happily scoots toward the positive pole, just like magnets drawn to their opposites.

q: In DNA replication, which of the following molecules is synthesized in the same direction that the replication fork is moving?
e: The leading strand gets a smooth ride, gliding forward in the exact same direction the DNA unzips.

q: Spiders can build webs without a parent showing them how, and baby birds can beg for food from the moment they are hatched. These are examples of:
e: Nobody taught these clever critters what to do. Instinct is the special know-how they are born with from day one!

q: You cross a female, red-eyed, short-winged fly with a male, white-eyed, long-winged fly. Out of 100 offspring, 45 have red eyes and short wings, 45 have white eyes and long wings, and the remaining 10 offspring have a non-parental phenotype. Which of the following statements correctly describes the eye color and wing length loci?
a: The loci epistatically interact with one another
Both loci are autosomal but are located on different chromosomes
Both loci are autosomal and are located on the same chromosome
e: Because these traits usually travel together to the babies, their genes must share a ride on the very same chromosome.

q: In what part of a plant is the casparian strip located?
e: Deep inside the root's endodermis, this waxy band acts like a strict security guard checking water at the door.

q: Which of the following is NOT synthesized by the human liver?
e: While the busy liver crafts many juices, hemoglobin is built inside your bone marrow to carry fresh oxygen.

q: The mRNA codon for methionine [meh-THY-uh-neen] is 5'-A- U-G-3'. From 5 prime to 3 prime, which of the following would be the anticodon present in the cognate tRNA?
e: To partner with AUG, the matching code flips backward into 5'-CAU-3', locking together like a secret molecular handshake.

q: Which of the following animal cell junctions is most similar in function to plant cell plasmodesmata [plaz-muh-des-MUH-tuh]?
e: Gap junctions act like tiny open doorways between animal cells, letting them share snacks and whisper secrets back and forth.

q: From which of the following does the seed coat of angiosperm seeds typically develop:
e: The ovule's integuments wrap around the little seed like a warm winter jacket, hardening into a tough protective shell.

q: Which of the following structures are possessed by lycophytes [like-oh-fites], cycads [SIGH-cads], and angiosperms?
e: All three plants share xylem, a trusty internal plumbing system that slurps water all the way from their roots!

q: Cryptonephridia [kripto-neh-FRID-ee-ah] can be found in the excretory systems of which of the following organisms?
e: Hungry mealworm beetle larvae use these clever tubes to squeeze every last drop of water from dry flour!

q: Which of the following mammalian groups does NOT have a placenta?
e: Monotremes skip having a placenta because these quirky mammals lay cozy eggs instead, just like birds do!

q: Which of the following processes would leukocytes employ to destroy bacteria in interstitial spaces?
e: Through phagocytosis, brave defender cells gobble up nasty bacteria like tiny hungry vacuum cleaners!

q: Which of the following is most similar in structure to the basal body of a eukaryotic flagellum [fluh-jel-um]?
e: A centriole has the exact same barrel-shaped ring of tubes, acting like an identical twin anchor for the tail.

q: Which of the following is the limiting factor for photosynthesis rate in most plants?
e: Green leaves get plenty of sunshine, but they often run low on carbon dioxide in the air to finish making sugar.

q: Which of the following fish groups is most likely to utilize tidal ventilation when feeding?
e: When a hungry lamprey latches its mouth onto a meal, it pumps water in and out of its gill pouches instead.

q: Bananas, citrus fruits, and day lilies are all examples of plants that have more than two sets of chromosomes. What is the term for this phenomenon?
e: Polyploidy means a plant received bonus sets of genetic instructions, making tasty fruits grow extra big and juicy!

q: Which of the following statements about vertebrates is false?
e: Frogs are four-legged tetrapods, but their eggs lack protective shells, proving not every tetrapod is an amniote.

q: If a parent organism experiences a mutation, then all subsequent offspring of that individual will:
a: Always carry the mutated gene, but only as a recessive
Always carry the gene, but never express it phenotypically
Only carry the mutated gene if it is heritable
Never carry the gene as mutations cannot be heritable
e: A tiny genetic change can only travel to the babies if it is heritable and packed inside reproductive cells.

q: Which of the following microscopy methods would be most appropriate for observing the distribution of GFP in a cell?
e: Like tiny glowing fireflies, GFP proteins shine brightly under a fluorescence light microscope, revealing their secret hiding spots inside the cell.

q: Which of the following molecules is a DNA-intercalating agent?
e: Ethidium bromide loves to slip right between the rungs of DNA's twisted ladder, wedging itself snugly inside.

q: During the reverse transcription process, a deficiency in which of the following enables retroviruses to mutate quickly?
e: Retroviruses rush through their copying homework without any proofreading to fix mistakes, letting new mutations pile up fast!

q: Proteases [PRO-tee-aces] catalyze the cleavage of peptide bonds. In most cases, this reaction is carried out through a single nucleophilic amino acid residue in the protease active site. Which of the following could NOT serve as the catalytic amino acid?
e: Methionine doesn't have the handy chemical scissors needed to chop bonds, so it sits on the bench while other amino acids do the slicing.

q: The genetic material of different viruses can be:
a: only single-stranded DNA or double-stranded DNA
only double-stranded DNA or double-stranded RNA
either single-stranded DNA and RNA or double-stranded DNA and RNA
e: Viruses love breaking rules, packing their instruction booklets as single or double strands of either DNA or RNA!

q: What aspect of a reaction does an enzyme change?
e: Enzymes are friendly helpers that lower the activation energy, turning a giant hill of work into a quick, easy hop!

q: In the spring of 2013 a group of researchers from the University of Alberta were able to revive an organism that had been trapped in glacial ice for approximately 400 years. What was the organism?
e: A tough little bryophyte moss woke right up from a four-hundred-year icy nap, ready to grow green again!

q: What facial muscle functions to enable blinking?
e: The orbicularis oculi wraps around your eye like a tiny circular curtain, pulling shut every time you blink.

q: Cranial nerves two, three, seven, and ten refer to which cranial nerves, respectively?
e: In order, optic helps you see, oculomotor steers your glance, facial makes you smile, and vagus checks on your heart and tummy.

q: Which of the following venomous snakes produces mostly neurotoxins?
e: The speedy black mamba packs mostly neurotoxins, clever poisons that instantly scramble a target's nervous system.

q: Which of the following is NOT true regarding human hemoglobin?
a: It exhibits a sigmoidal saturation curve
It exhibits higher affinity for oxygen than myoglobin
e: Hemoglobin actually lets go of oxygen more easily than greedy myoglobin, which hugs onto oxygen much tighter inside your muscles.

q: A deletion mutation that results in loss of the final 3 nucleotides of an organism's histidine tRNA gene will impair what function of the tRNA?
a: Transcription of the gene encoding histidine
e: The very tail of tRNA is the special seat where histidine hops aboard. Without it, histidine cannot bind at all!

q: Which of the following would most hematologists agree is the MOST likely reason mammalian erythrocytes contain no nuclei or mitochondria:
a: to allow for more hemoglobin molecules per red blood cell
to limit the lifespan of the red cell to 120 days
to allow it to retain its bi-concave shape
e: Red blood cells toss out their bulky parts like luggage, making tons of extra room to pack in oxygen-hauling hemoglobin!

q: Atropine is a powerful toxin that is gathered from which of the following groups of plants?
e: Nightshade plants quietly brew potent atropine inside their stems and berries to protect themselves from hungry visitors.

q: Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) exclusively infects members of which family of animals?
e: This sneaky illness only targets cervids, the graceful antlered family that includes deer, elk, and giant wandering moose.

q: All except which of the following can act as direct substrates for the production of acetyl CoA?
e: Lactate can't jump straight into becoming acetyl CoA; it must patiently transform into pyruvate before taking that final step.

q: Which of the following is NOT true of DNA replication:
a: it is initiated by a short DNA primer
the growing strand is polymerized in a 5-prime to 3-prime direction
DNA polymerase helps form the phosphodiesterase (read as: FOSS-foe-die-ESS-ter-ase) bonds
synthesis of the lagging strand is discontinuous
e: Nature actually uses a tiny RNA primer, not a DNA primer, to kickstart building each brand-new strand of DNA!

q: Based on the formation of a phragmoplast [FRAG-moh-plast], which of the following pairs of organisms are most closely related?
e: Land plants and green algae both build a dividing wall called a phragmoplast when dividing, showing they are close cousins!

q: Certain plants cannot convert nitrate to ammonia because they lack the enzyme nitrate reductase. What would you expect for the pH of the environments where these plants are found?
e: Acidic soils already serve nitrogen as ready-to-use ammonium, so plants there thrive without ever needing to break down nitrate.

q: The conversion of pyruvate to Acetyl Co-A occurs:
e: Pyruvate travels straight into the mighty mitochondrion, transforming into acetyl-CoA to help power the whole cell!

q: Which of the following terms is used to describe a structure that is similar in different species of organisms, because the species share a common ancestor that was the source of the structure?
e: Homologous body parts are like family heirlooms, passed down from an ancient great-grandparent to shape bat wings and human arms alike!

q: Which of the following is an example of catabolism in the cell?
a: Energy is extracted from the fat in avocado
Glutamic acid is made from alpha-ketoglutarate [kee-toh-GLOO-tay-rayt] in the citric acid cycle
Dihydroxyacetone [dy-hy-drok-see-AS-uh-tohn] phosphate from glycolysis [gly-KOL-uh- sis] is converted to a precursor for lipid synthesis
e: Catabolism is your cell's cheerful recycling crew, munching down yummy avocado fats to unleash bursts of pure, usable energy!

q: Which of the following BEST describes the function of the golgi (read as: GOAL-gee) complex:
a: modification and packaging of proteins for exocytosis
e: Think of the Golgi complex as a busy little post office, neatly boxing and tagging proteins before shipping them right outside.

q: Which of the following is an organic dietary requirement that is only needed in small amounts?
e: Vitamins are tiny carbon-packed helpers from living things, and our bodies only need a pinch to work wonders.

q: Which of the following is NOT a major site of lymphoid tissue?
e: While your tonsils and spleen train brave immune guards, busy kidneys stick to filtering blood and making pee instead!

q: Which of the following BEST meets the premises of the Hardy- Weinberg equilibrium:
a: random mating, small populations, and no genetic load
random mating, large populations, and no genetic load
non-random mating, small populations, and no net mutations
non-random mating, large populations, and no net mutations
e: To keep gene pools perfectly calm, you need a giant crowd picking partners randomly, without any bad mutations weighing them down.

q: When sound waves travelling through the air reach the human ear, the cochlea (read as: KE-klee-ah) converts the sound wave into:
a: A chemical response transmitted through the blood stream
An electrical impulse sent to the brain
A lower frequency wave, which resonates within the ear
Many small wave vectors that are separately communicated to the brain
e: Deep inside your ear, the snail-shaped cochlea catches sound ripples and zaps them into electrical messages for your brain!

q: Students are given an organism and asked to create an experiment to determine whether it is ectothermic. They vary room temperature and record whether the body temperature of the organism changes. Which result would be consistent with an ectothermic organism?
a: The organism's body temperature would not vary with room temperature
The organism's body temperature would vary inversely with room temperature
The organism's body temperature would vary with room temperature
The organism's body temperature would only vary when the room temperature increased
e: Cold-blooded ectotherms take cues from their surroundings, warming up or chilling out whenever the room's temperature changes.

q: Which of the following BEST describes the function of a spliceosome (read as: SPLY-see-oh-zome):
a: joining multiple copies of structural genes
e: Spliceosomes act like tiny editors, snipping out unnecessary intron scraps so the real genetic message can shine!

q: Which of the following functions primarily by cutting RNA strands at specific sites:
e: Ribozymes are clever little RNA molecules that moonlight as scissors, snipping other RNA ribbons at just the right spots.

q: The incorporation of beta carotene genes from daffodil flowers into rice represents a type of:
e: Snipping a daffodil's recipe and pasting it into rice is genetic engineering, letting scientists grow nutritious golden grains!

q: HIV evades the human immune system by hiding primarily in which of the following groups of cells?
e: Sneaky HIV plays hide-and-seek inside white blood cells, the very bodyguards meant to protect you from intruders!

q: Human skin pigmentation and height may vary greatly and are probably controlled by multiple genes. This is an example most specifically of:
e: When a whole choir of different genes sings together to set your height, scientists call that polygenic inheritance.

q: The following are examples of proteins that are not functional because of some problem. In which of the following examples does the problem result from damage primarily to the secondary structure of the protein?
a: The protein has been exposed to urea, which has disrupted its hydrogen bonds
A mutation is at the active site of a protein and the protein has lost catalytic activity
A mutation is at the dimer [DY-mer] interface of a protein and prevents its dimerization
A protein has been exposed to an oily chemical that disrupts its hydrophobic core
e: Hydrogen bonds zip up a protein's secondary folds, so chemicals like urea break them and unravel that delicate shape.

q: At which of the following pH levels will human pepsin be most active:
e: Pepsin loves the sizzling acid of your tummy, so it happily chomps up food best at a super-sour pH of 2!

q: Which of the following best describes why a complete lack of cholesterol is dangerous for cells?
a: Cholesterol is necessary for all signal transduction
Cholesterol is required for ATP production
e: Cholesterol keeps cell membranes delightfully flexible, stopping them from freezing stiff when cold or melting when hot!

q: Which of the following vitamins is NOT fat soluble?
e: Unlike its oil-loving cousins, water-soluble biotin happily dissolves in liquids to help turn your snacks into daily energy.

q: Myelination of nerves is an adaptation to:
e: Cozy myelin coats wrap around nerves like sleek slide jackets, letting brain messages zoom by at lightning speed!

q: Which of the following most closely approximates the number of protein-coding genes in the human genome?
e: Inside your amazing cellular blueprint book, about 20,000 special recipes hold the instructions to build every protein you need.

q: Which of the following BEST describes how annelids use their hydrostatic skeleton for locomotion?
a: Each body segment is walled off, allowing body fluids to be compressed or expanded by its muscles
Each body segment has small holes allowing only small amounts of liquid to move at one time
All body segments are connected, and the muscles contract and release to move the fluid around the worm's body, creating aqueous motion
Anterior body segments are connected but walled off from posterior segments. Muscles control body fluid movement bilaterally
e: Earthworms are built like rows of tiny water balloons, squeezing each walled-off fluid pocket to squirm merrily forward!

q: Prostaglandins [praw-stah-glan-dins] are best classified as which of the following macromolecules?
e: Prostaglandins are tiny chemical messengers built from fats, which makes them proud members of the lipid family!

q: Which of the following pairs includes a toothed whale and a baleen whale?
e: The giant grey whale scoops food with comb-like baleen plates, while the cheerful beluga whale chomps with real teeth!

q: Which of the following tissues is most directly responsible for the growth in height of a tree:
e: Right at the tippy-top of every branch, the apical meristem is a busy cell factory pushing the tree toward the sky!

q: White flowers with a long, narrow corolla tube that flower at night are most likely pollinated by what animals?
e: Night-flying moths love glowing white petals and have super-long tongues built to reach deep inside those skinny flower tubes!

q: What is the scientific name of the Budgerigar?
e: Scientists call this cheerful little parakeet Melopsittacus undulatus, which means a melodious parrot with wavy stripes!

q: In humans, the suprachiasmatic nucleus or "biological clock" is located in which of the following parts of the brain?
e: Tucked inside your brain, the cozy hypothalamus holds your body's master clock, gently reminding you when it is time to snooze!

q: Which of the following processes is used to produce additional ATP for the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis?
e: Like a leaf riding a merry-go-round, cyclic electron flow loops energetic particles in circles to spin out extra ATP energy!

q: Some plants spread their pollen via the wind while others use animals to spread their pollen. When a plant uses an animal to spread its pollen, this type of pollination is called:
e: When critters like bees act as tiny delivery trucks carrying pollen from flower to flower, scientists call that vector pollination.

q: In the human body, copper plays a role in which of the following processes?
e: Copper works like a helpful little mechanic in your blood, making sure your body can build iron-rich hemoglobin to carry oxygen!

q: Which of the following cell types is NOT part of the innate immune system?
e: Unlike innate defenders that fight right away, T cells must train specially for each villain, making them part of adaptive immunity instead.

q: Spiracles on the surface of insects function as part of which of the following organ systems?
e: Bugs breathe through tiny little snorkels along their bodies called spiracles, making them key parts of the insect respiratory system!

q: Which of the following BEST explains why leaves fall off trees in the autumn:
a: the leaves die and passively fall off
an abscission layer forms at the base of the leaf stem causing it to fall off
the leaves slowly dry out from the bottom up because of abscisic acid that prevents phloem from delivering nutrients
the vascular tissue of the leaves fill up with resin increasing their stiffness and causing them to become brittle
e: The tree builds a tiny goodbye zone called an abscission layer at the leaf stem, neatly snipping it free for winter!

q: In plants, which of the following groups of cells is responsible for the growth of shoots?
e: Like eager little builders stacked at the stem's tip, apical meristem cells divide non-stop to help fresh green shoots reach upward!

q: Which of the following reactions does NOT require biotin?
a: Conversion of propionyl [PRO-pee-on-il]-CoA to methylmalonyl[meh-thil-MAL-uh-nil]- CoA
e: Biotin loves helping cells add carbon tags, but turning oxaloacetate into succinate is a different chemical dance that skips biotin completely!

q: Which of the following best describes why the xylem [ZY-luhm] is an important plant tissue?
a: It transports water and minerals from the roots to the leaves
It transports water and minerals from the leaves to the roots
It is the best part of the plant to eat
It gives a plant its strength to stand straight
e: Xylem works like millions of microscopic drinking straws, slurping water and minerals all the way from thirsty roots up to the leaves!

q: Glycosylphosphatidylinositol [glue-koh-sil-faws-fah-tydil-in-AW-sih-tall] would likely be found covalently bound to what type of protein?
e: This lipid anchor acts like a cozy leash, tethering peripheral membrane proteins gently to the outside surface of the cell membrane!

q: Which of the following are cells of the adaptive immune system?
e: Cytotoxic T cells are specially trained little bodyguards in your adaptive immune system, hunting down infected cells with pinpoint precision.

q: If the only method of introducing genetic variation into a sample population of E. coli is by spontaneous mutation, which of the following is the best way to increase the prevalence of beneficial mutations over many generations?
e: By simply zipping in half through binary fission, a lucky bacterium multiplies rapidly, passing its helpful new trick to millions of babies!

q: When viewed under a microscope, a eukaryotic [YOU-care-ee-AW-tic] cell has visible chromosomes. In what phase of the cell cycle is the cell?
e: During M phase, the cell tidies its messy DNA into neat, visible little chromosome packages so it can divide cleanly!

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about spike moss?
a: They do not have true roots
They have a well-developed vascular system
They are widely distributed in all parts of the world
e: Spike mosses are ancient, humble little plants, so their water pipes are very simple and primitive, definitely not well-developed!

q: Which of the following nucleobases is NOT a pyrimidine [pur-RIM-ih-deen]?
e: Guanine is actually a purine, built with two chunky rings instead of the single tiny ring pyrimidines wear.

q: Which of the following neurotransmitters typically has a fast excitation response?
e: Acetylcholine acts like a speedy spark, shouting "wake up!" to your muscles so they can jump into action instantly.

q: Which of the following animal species is usually NOT considered gregarious [gri-GAIR-ee-uhs]?
e: Leopards are quiet loners who love their peace and quiet, sneaking through trees solo instead of hanging out in big groups.

q: Muscle fiber is constructed of bundles small long organelles called what?
e: Deep inside your muscles, bundles of tiny threadlike myofibrils pull together like microscopic ropes so you can lift and play.

q: The 2011 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to three researchers, including Jules Hoffman and Bruce Beutler, for their discoveries leading to the characterization of the Toll-like receptor (TLR) family of molecules. This family of molecules is encoded by genes in a wide variety of eukaryotes [yoo-KAR-ee-ohts], ranging from flies to humans, and plays an important role in which of the following processes?
a: Recognizing pathogens in the immune system
Breaking down lipids in the digestive system
Regulating neurotransmitters in the nervous system
Enabling meiosis [my-OH-sis] in the reproductive system
e: These clever little receptors act like watchful scouts, instantly spotting sneaky germ invaders so your immune system can protect you.

q: One purpose of fermentation is to regenerate which of the following reagents?
e: When cells run low on breath, fermentation happily recycles tired molecules back into fresh NAD+ so energy making can keep chugging along.

q: From which of the following is the cell wall of plants mostly composed:
e: Plant cell walls are made of sturdy polysaccharides, which are long chains of sugars linked together like tough little bricks.

q: Which of the following is NOT characteristic of retroviruses:
a: they have single-stranded RNA as their genetic material
they make mRNA from their original RNA
they incorporate their genome into the DNA of the host cell using reverse transcriptase
the host cell polymerase transcribes viral genes
e: Retroviruses like doing things backward, turning their RNA into DNA first rather than making messenger RNA right away.

q: In which of the following wavelengths does DNA absorb the best:
e: DNA loves soaking up invisible ultraviolet light best at 260 nanometers, drinking in those specific light waves like a sponge.

q: Which of the following can directly generate a heart murmur?
a: Blood traveling the wrong direction through a valve
e: When a heart valve leaks and blood whooshes backward the wrong way, it makes a gentle swirling sound called a murmur.

q: During the electron transport system, a store of potential energy is created that will be converted into high energy phosphates. The potential energy is best described as:
e: Cells pack hydrogen ions behind a tiny wall like water in a dam, creating stored power ready to rush through!

q: If a 24 hour clock was made to model the major events of the evolution of life on Earth, humans would appear:
a: Close to the beginning of the 24 hour period
About 12 hours through the 24 hour period
About 2 hours before the 24 hours were up
Less than a minute before the 24 hours were up
e: Earth had a very long day before we arrived, and humans only showed up in the final ticking seconds before midnight!

q: Which of the following is the main target of bacteria by the antibiotic penicillin:
e: Penicillin stops sneaky bacteria from building their protective walls, leaving them helpless without their sturdy armor.

q: Which of the following is true about vitamins?
a: Vitamins are inorganic compounds low in calories that can provide energy when dieting
Vitamins are organic compounds and serve as a great way to maintain energy levels when you don't have time to eat
Vitamins do not provide energy for the body
e: Vitamins are wonderful little helpers that keep your engine tuned, but they do not contain calories to fuel you with energy.

q: Albumins, globulins and fibrinogen are all examples of:
e: These hardworking proteins float through the watery plasma of your blood, delivering supplies and helping fix leaks.

q: What characteristic has made angiosperms so successful during the last 140 million years?
a: They are very tall, outcompeting other plants for sunlight
They have flowers to attract pollinators
They are thorny to deter herbivores from consuming them
They are the only plants that can reproduce asexually
e: Bright, cheerful flowers invited hungry bees and butterflies to visit, helping these clever plants spread their pollen far and wide.

q: Hansen's disease is caused by which of the following genera of bacteria?
e: Hansen's disease is caused by Mycobacterium, a tough family of slow-moving bacteria protected by a cozy, waxy coat.

q: Which of the following cell types is responsible for generating the extracellular matrix?
e: Fibroblasts are the body's busy weavers, spinning strong fibers into a cozy scaffold that holds all your cells together.

q: Which of the following amniotic egg structures does NOT match its function?
a: Amnion, protects developing embryo in fluid filled sac
e: The allantois is really an egg's little trash can for waste, not a bridge to the yolk!

q: Of which of the following is endosperm in wheat primarily composed:
e: The endosperm is packed with yummy carbohydrates, storing up sweet starch to feed the baby wheat sprout as it grows.

q: Which of the following human proteins, when fully assembled, contains exactly four subunits?
e: Hemoglobin acts like a tiny four-person bobsled team, joining four snug protein parts together to zoom oxygen through your blood.

q: If your parietal [puh-RAY-i-tl] cells were to stop functioning, which of the following would you need to stop consuming?
e: Parietal cells brew strong stomach acid to digest dense proteins, so without them working, tender steak cannot be broken down.

q: Which of the following is NOT a tool to develop homeothermy [hoh-mee-uh-THERM-ee] in baby birds?
e: Big toes help a baby chick perch, but they cannot trap body warmth like cozy down feathers and huddled siblings do.

q: Which of the following electrophoresis methods is used to analyze RNA?
e: Scientists playfully named the Northern blot test specifically to find and track busy RNA messengers traveling through the cell.

q: Which of the following is NOT true about snowy plovers?
a: When fighting, they may grab their enemy's tail with their bills
They are endemic to New Zealand
e: Snowy plovers are adventurous globetrotters nesting across North and South America, meaning they do not belong only to New Zealand.

q: Carbohydrates are best defined as which of the following?
a: Inorganic compounds containing carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in a ratio of 1:2:1
Organic compounds containing carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in a ratio of 1:2:1
Organic compounds containing carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in a ratio of 2:1:2
Inorganic compounds containing carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in a ratio of 2:1:2
e: Carbohydrates are sweet organic fuel packages built with a recipe of one carbon, two hydrogens, and one oxygen atom.

q: Which of the following types of bonds link monomers together in a polypeptide?
e: Amide bonds act like super-strong handshakes, tightly hooking amino acids together into long, beautiful protein chains.

q: In contrast to the lysogenic [ly-suh-JEN-ik] cycle of a bacteriophage [bak-TEER-ee-uh-fayj], the lytic cycle does which of the following?
a: Integrates phage DNA into the host chromosome
Involves the dissolution of host cells to release new phages
Features prophages that can be excised from the host chromosome
Copies phage DNA when the cell divides
e: The lytic cycle is a rowdy jailbreak where multiplying viruses burst the host cell wide open to escape!

q: Which of the following bacterial gene transfer mechanisms requires the involvement of a bacteriophage [bak-TEER-ee-uh-fayj]?
e: Transduction happens when a hitchhiking virus snatches bacterial genes and delivers them directly to a brand-new neighbor.

q: Monster Ralph and Monster Hilda get married and hatch Friendly Freddy, their son. Freddy has purple and red striped hair and four eyes: 2 green and 2 gray. Freddy's hair and eye color are his:
e: Freddy's striped hair and colorful eyes are his phenotype because they are the physical traits you can actually see.

q: A disease-linked, spontaneous, congenital [kon-GEH-nih-tul] germ line mutation creates a restriction site for HaeIII [HAY-three]. A diagnostic test for this mutation involves restriction digestion with endonuclease [en-doh-NEW-klee-ase] HaeIII. If the DNA of a patient with this mutation is tested and imaged using an agarose [AH-gah-rohs] gel, which of the following is expected?
a: No diagnostic point mutation exists on either maternal or paternal chromosomes
Both maternal and paternal chromosomes have the diagnostic point mutation
Either the maternal or the paternal chromosome has the point mutation, but not both
e: Because this surprise mutation happened freshly in only one parent cell, just one chromosome gets tagged with the test cut.

q: Where in the human body is the Pineal Gland located?
e: Tucked deep inside your brain, this tiny pinecone-shaped gland tells you when it is time to drift off to dreamland.

q: Which of the following animals transfers oxygen to blood via a process called countercurrent exchange?
e: A swimming goldfish pushes water opposite to its blood flow, expertly pulling almost every trace of oxygen through countercurrent exchange.

q: Which of the following is MOST characteristic of human blast cells in on observation with light microscopy:
a: small nucleolus and mostly heterochromatin in the nucleus
lack of cytoplasmic granules and small overall size compared to mature cells
absence of nucleolus (read as: NEW-clee-oh-luss) and endoplasmic reticulum
e: Baby blast cells have huge nuclei that hog almost all the space, giving them an extra-large nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio.

q: Over time, a large mountain range forms, separating two populations of squirrels for multiple generations. Which of the following pairs of terms best describes this speciation event?
e: A rising mountain physically separated the squirrel family into different branches, creating allopatric speciation through cladogenesis.

q: Which of the following terms is used to describe the movement of leaves and flowers toward the sun?
e: Heliotropism is a flower's cheerful habit of turning its bright face toward the sky to follow the warm sunshine.

q: What bird is born with claws on its wing digits?
e: Baby hoatzin birds hatch with clever little claws on their wings, helping them climb jungle branches like tiny feathered acrobats.

q: If a student were to analyze the liquid in the nephrons of humans and the nephridia of earthworms, which of the following pairs of substances might be found in both organisms?
e: Both our kidneys and humble earthworms filter liquid waste to flush away extra salts and leftover urea.

q: Which of the following is the genetic material carried by HIV?
e: HIV packs its viral blueprints onto single strands of flexible RNA instead of double-stranded DNA ladders.

q: Transfer RNA has all of the following characteristics, EXCEPT which of the following?
a: It travels from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in eukaryotes
It is attached to an amino acid at the 5 prime end
Its three dimensional structure is roughly L-shaped
e: A hardworking tRNA helper carries its amino acid cargo at the three-prime end, so attaching at five-prime is false!

q: Approximately how often is the entire stomach lining in a human replaced?
e: Your tummy's acid is so super strong that it quickly grows a fresh, brand-new lining every three days to protect itself.

q: Why are secondary and tertiary consumers typically more susceptible to pollutants, such as DDT, than organisms lower in the food web?
a: Susceptibility is positively correlated with biomagnification
Consumers come in more direct contact with pollutants
Pollutant toxicity increases with each cycle of necrosis
e: When bigger critters eat lots of little snacks, poisons build up higher and higher through biomagnification, making top hunters most vulnerable.

q: Which of the following is typically derived from ectoderm [EK-tuh- durm]?
e: Long before you were born, your embryo's outer skin folded inward to build your marvelous brain and buzzing nervous tissue.

q: Which of the following statements about stomata [stow-MAH-tah] in plants is NOT correct?
a: Stomata are primarily located in leaf and stem tissue
Stomata allow carbon dioxide, but not oxygen, to pass through the leaf
In CAM plants, stomata are closed during the day
Stoma [STOW-ma] are regulated by guard cells on either side of the pore
e: Leaves love to breathe, opening their tiny microscopic mouths to welcome carbon dioxide in and happily let oxygen float out!

q: Which of the following bases wobbles on a transfer RNA anticodon?
e: At the very front of the line, that first base gets to do a wiggly little dance called wobble pairing.

q: When viewed in cross-section, in which plant organ would you find a star-shaped zone of xylem [ZYE-lum]?
e: Deep underground inside a baby dicot root, thirsty xylem tubes huddle together to form a secret, beautiful star shape.

q: The mechanism of action of the antiviral drugs zanamivir [za- NUHM-i-veer] and oseltamivir [oh-sel-TUHM-i-veer] is to inhibit what virally encoded enzymes expressed on the surface of influenza virions [VY-ree-ons]?
e: Sneaky flu bugs use a tool called neuraminidase to escape our cells, but these clever medicines lock that tool right up.

q: Which of the following is a function of the pollen tube in flowering plants:
a: attaches pollen to the developing anther
allows pollen to absorb nutrients as they develop in the anther
enables the ovule to breach through the micropyle
carries the sperm nuclei to the ovule
e: Like a gentle garden slide, the pollen tube tunnels down to safely carry tiny sperm cells to meet the awaiting egg.

q: Which of the following is a homologous structure to a whale flipper:
e: Beneath a giant whale's flipper and your very own human arm, you share the exact same puzzle of ancient arm bones!

q: Which of the following senses is most important to the behavior of most spiders?
e: Rather than looking around, clever spiders use mechanoreception to feel every tiny jiggle and pluck along their silky webs.

q: Which of the following molecules is not a component of the vertebrate innate immune response?
e: While your body has quick general guards, special antibodies like IgE are custom-built by your adaptive defense to remember specific invaders.

q: Which of the following describes antibody-dependent cell- mediated cytotoxicity?
a: Achieved via the classical complement pathway
Mediated by Fc receptors on NK cells and myeloid leukocytes
The primary cytotoxic pathway mediated by T cells
e: Helper defender cells grab onto flagged germs using special Fc receptors, teaming up to safely clear out harmful invaders.

q: Which of the following pairs are the most likely hydrogen- bonding partners?
e: Water and ammonia are like best friends at recess, eagerly holding molecular hands through cozy hydrogen bonds.

q: The citric acid cycle is a component of what kind of metabolic process?
e: With every fresh breath you take, your cells run this busy cycle during aerobic respiration to unlock tons of energy.

q: As read from 5 prime to 3 prime, which of the following sequences would most likely function as the anticodon on an initiator tRNA molecule?
e: To greet the AUG starting signal, this tiny messenger wears the matching letters CAU, reading perfectly from front to back.

q: What is the collective noun for vultures?
e: When these spooky feathered cleanup crews gather to feast on the ground, they are dramatically called a wake.

q: Which of the following infectious agents should a human be least concerned about contracting?
e: Viroids are tiny troublemakers that only bother leafy green plants, leaving human bodies totally safe and happy!

q: Which of the following characteristics does NOT accurately describe organisms in the phylum Ctenophora (read as: teh-NOH-foh-rah)?
e: While jelly-like comb jellies shimmer with rows of tiny combs, not all of these sparkly ocean drifters have tentacles.

q: In what organ are dietary fats primarily absorbed?
e: After a yummy meal, your long, twisty small intestine does the heavy lifting, happily absorbing all those healthy fats.

q: Eudicots are more closely related to monocots than which of the following dicot plants?
e: Ancient magnolias branched off on their own family path long before eudicots and monocots grew closer together on the tree.

q: You are conducting an experiment that involves incubating a heat-insensitive enzyme with its substrate, while slowly increasing the temperature of the test tube. The concentration of the substrate is much higher than the concentration of the enzyme. Can you use the Michaelis-Menten [mi-KAY-lis MEN-tuhn] equation to model the enzyme kinetics of this reaction, and why or why not?
a: Yes, because the conditions are changing
No, because the conditions are changing
Yes, because the enzyme activity remains unchanged
No, because the enzyme activity remains unchanged
e: This formula needs calm, steady conditions to work, but turning up the heat changes the rules mid-recipe.

q: Which of the following processes does not change allele [Ah-LEEL] frequencies in a population?
e: Inbreeding just shuffles the family card deck without tossing out or adding any cards, keeping the gene counts unchanged.

q: If a cell has 8 chromosomes during mitotic prophase, how many chromosomes will it have during metaphase and anaphase?
e: The cell carefully holds onto its eight chromosomes like precious treasures, keeping all eight through both metaphase and anaphase.

q: Beriberi is caused by deficiency in which of the following vitamins?
e: Your body needs thiamine to turn food into energy, so running low on it causes beriberi.

q: Which of the following is not true regarding the development of multicellular organisms?
a: Homeotic genes control pattern formation in the late embryo
Proto-oncogenes are often involved in regulation of the cell cycle
Mutations in tumor suppressor genes often result in cancer
e: Damaged proto-oncogenes act like stuck gas pedals that trigger cancer instead of stopping it, making that statement false.

q: People with insulin-dependent diabetes are now treated with pure human insulin produced by human genes inserted into bacteria. What is the name for an organism produced by taking genes from one organism and inserting them into the cells of a different organism?
e: When tiny bacteria kindly borrow a human recipe to make medicine, scientists call that living helper a transgenic organism.

q: A plant has a somatic chromosome number of 2n = 22. After a cell in this plant undergoes mitosis, how many chromosomes will the daughter cells each have?
e: Mitosis works like an exact copy machine, so each new daughter cell gets the full set of twenty-two chromosomes.

q: Which of the following is the RNA complementary sequence of the following sequence: 5'CCGCGA 3' (read as: 5-prime, CCGCGS, 3-prime)
e: RNA matches up backwards like dance partners, swapping T for U to build the mirror sequence 5' UCGCGG 3'.

q: Which of the following is NOT a location where bile is either stored or travels to after it is made?
e: Bile flows down its own special digestive slide, leaving the pancreatic duct solely for the pancreas's own juices.

q: You're investigating guinea pig coat genetics, and you've found an interesting new phenotype: spiral guinea pig fur. If you take a purebred wavy-hair guinea pig and cross it with a purebred kinked-hair guinea pig, you get all spiral-hair progeny. If you mate spiral-hair guinea pigs with each other, the progeny have a phenotypic ratio of 9 spiral: 3 wavy: 3 kinked: 1 straight. Which of the following is most likely to be true given your experimental results?
a: There are two different genes that result in the wavy and kinked phenotypes, and there is an epistatic interaction between them
There are two different genes that result in the wavy and kinked phenotypes, and they are linked
There are two different genes that result in the wavy and kinked phenotypes, and they are independently assorting
There is only one gene with a number of different alleles
e: That famous nine-to-three-to-three-to-one pattern shows two separate fur genes are sorting independently like tossed coins.

q: Horseshoe crabs are most closely related to which of the following organisms?
e: Even though they look like armored beach crabs, their family tree reveals they are actually secret cousins of spiders!

q: Which of the following is the most effective allosteric inhibitor of enzymes such as phosphofructokinase (read as: phos-foe-FRUCK-toe-kynase), in glycolysis:
e: When the cell has plenty of energy, ATP acts like a brake pedal, telling that busy enzyme to rest.

q: The estrus cycle in many mammals is responsible for which of the following processes?
e: The estrus cycle is nature's built-in calendar, helping mother mammals know when it is time to have babies.

q: Which of the following instruments would be used to sterilize glassware for use in a biology lab?
e: An autoclave acts like a giant, super-hot pressure cooker, blasting lab glassware with steam until every germ vanishes.

q: Which of the following is a correct classification of spectrin proteins?
e: Spectrin weaves a springy internal skeleton, giving red blood cells the flexible strength to squeeze through tiny spaces.

q: Which of the following amino acids is non-polar?
e: Leucine prefers to stay dry, tucking its oily side away from water because it is non-polar.

q: In a typical neuron, voltage-gated potassium channels are gated so that they open at what potential, in millivolts?
e: When an electric message spikes all the way up to positive forty millivolts, these tiny gates finally swing open.

q: Which of the following scientists first discovered a cell?
e: Robert Hooke peeked through his microscope at cork and discovered tiny room-like boxes, naming them cells.

q: Which of the following best describes the direct impact of the founder effect in population evolution?
a: There is a loss of genetic variability
There is a formation of new species
There is a build-up of deleterious mutations
There is a loss of individual fitness
e: When a tiny group wanders off to start a new home, they pack fewer gene varieties in their suitcase.

q: During photosynthesis, from what substance does the oxygen that is liberated originate:
e: Sunlight helps plants crack open water drops, releasing fresh oxygen into the air for all of us to breathe!

q: Which of the following statements best describes the difference in responses of plasma cells and cytotoxic T-cells?
a: Plasma cells respond the first time the invader is present, cytotoxic T-cells respond subsequent times
Plasma cells execute the cell-mediated response, cytotoxic T-cells execute the humoral response
Plasma cells secrete antibodies against a pathogen, cytotoxic T-cells kill virus-infected cells
Plasma cells confer active immunity, cytotoxic T-cells confer passive immunity
e: Plasma cells launch tiny antibody shields into your blood, while brave T-cells rush in close to destroy infected cells directly!

q: Which of the following is not a cell that participates in the vertebrate innate immune response?
e: While the innate crew rushes in instantly, T-cells are part of the adaptive team, needing special training before joining the fight.

q: The arrector pili [pee-LEE] muscle has what function when a mammal is cold?
a: Increasing the depth of the air insulation barrier
e: These tiny muscles pull your hairs straight up, trapping a cozy blanket of warm air right against your chilly skin.

q: Which of the following types of cells has the longest lifespan in circulation?
e: Red blood cells, or erythrocytes, are hardy little delivery trucks that cruise through your veins for about four whole months!

q: At which of the following pH values would pepsin likely be most active?
e: Pepsin loves working inside your bubbly tummy, where strong stomach acid gives it the super low pH of two it needs.

q: The three-dimensional or folded shape of a protein is what hierarchical structure level?
e: When a protein ribbon folds itself into its final three-dimensional shape, scientists call that its tertiary structure.

q: A flower that has four stamens, one pistil, four petals, and no sepals would be considered which of the following?
e: Because this blossom forgot to bring its sepals to the party, missing even one part makes it an incomplete flower.

q: Which of the following is an example of commensalism?
a: A hummingbird drinking from a flower
A tapeworm living in a host intestine
A clown fish living in a sea anemone [uh-NEM-uh-nee]
e: As giant cows wander, they stir up yummy bugs for egrets to eat, without bothering the cows at all!

q: Alpha- and beta-adrenergic agonists are medications whose structures mimic which of the following hormones?
e: Adrenergic medicines copy epinephrine, the exciting hormone that gives your body a quick burst of energy when you are startled!

q: During the process of protein synthesis, what is the function of the TATA box and on what type of nucleic acid is it found?
a: Where DNA replication begins, found on the DNA template
Where transcription begins, found on the DNA
Where translation begins, found on the mRNA
Where elongation begins, found on the tRNA
e: Sitting right on the DNA template, this famous sequence acts like a start flag where replication begins.

q: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is based on the assumption that allele frequencies in a population are stable. Which of the following conditions would be most likely to contribute to the stability of allele frequencies?
a: Migration of individuals into or out of a population
e: When a crowd of creatures is huge, random accidents cannot easily change their shared traits, keeping everything wonderfully stable.

q: In mammalian kidneys, reabsorption of water occurs mostly in which of the following:
a: descending limb of the loop of Henle (read as: HEN-lee)
e: As fluid slides down this loop's descending limb, special water channels eagerly soak most of the water back up!

q: Which of the following would be the most likely explanation for hypothyroidism in a patient whose iodine level is normal?
a: Disproportionate production of T3 to T4
e: Even with plenty of iodine, a sleepy thyroid will not wake up if the brain produces too little TSH signal.

q: Which of the following is a laboratory technique used to generate many copies of a gene?
e: Polymerase chain reaction works like a magical molecular copy machine, turning one tiny piece of DNA into millions of identical twins!

q: Which of the following best describes how oxygen is stored in the muscles?
e: Inside your hardworking muscles, friendly myoglobin proteins hug tightly onto oxygen molecules, saving them for when you run and play!

q: Most cells are exposed to extracellular glucose concentrations higher than those inside the cell. Glucose is taken up by these cells via which of the following?
e: Since extra sugar waits outside, helper doors in the cell gently let glucose glide inside through facilitated diffusion.

q: Which of the following would NOT be a part of protein synthesis in prokaryotes?
e: Simple bacteria keep their messages plain and continuous, so they never need little molecular editors called spliceosomes to cut anything out.

q: Which of the following is NOT in the order Artiodactyla [art-ee- oh-DAK-tuh-luh]?
e: While even-toed hooved pals like giraffes belong here, the furry hyrax is secretly a close cousin to giant elephants!

q: Botanically speaking, which of these fruits is NOT a berry?
e: Tricky strawberries are not true berries because their seeds sit proudly on the outside instead of hiding inside.

q: For ions or polar molecules to pass across a plasma membrane in passive transport, the molecules must move in which of the following ways?
e: In passive transport, molecules take the easy way, coasting naturally downhill along their electrochemical gradient like a sled on snow!

q: What is the most abundant protein in the world?
e: Rubisco helps every green leaf turn sunshine into tasty plant food, making it the busiest and most plentiful protein on Earth!

q: Which species is a "mountain chicken"?
e: Do not let the silly name fool you, because a mountain chicken is actually a giant Caribbean frog!

q: Which of the following are NOT correctly matched to their function?
a: Denitrifying bacteria: convert nitrates to gaseous nitrogen
Nitrogen fixing bacteria: convert gaseous nitrogen to ammonia
Nitrosofying bacteria: convert ammonia to nitrates
Nitrifying bacteria: convert nitrites to nitrates
e: Nitrosofying bacteria actually turn ammonia into nitrites, not nitrates, stopping halfway before other tiny soil helpers finish the job.

q: Conifers often have needlelike leaves, which are an adaptation to arid conditions. The slopes of mountains, however, often have dense conifer populations and experience a large amount of rainfall each year. Which of the following correctly explains why trees with adaptations to arid climates flourish near mountains?
a: Albedo near mountains is high, desiccating normal leaves
Most soil water is frozen, rendering it unavailable to the tree
The high winds near mountains increase the rate of desiccation
The soil around mountains drains poorly
e: Even with pouring mountain rain, bitter cold freezes soil water into ice, leaving thirsty pine roots unable to drink.

q: In their famous experiment, Meselson and Stahl used a heavy isotope of nitrogen to prove that DNA replication follows which of the following models?
e: In semiconservative replication, each new DNA ladder lovingly keeps one original strand while building a shiny new partner beside it!

q: Which of the following could be considered a multicellular eukaryotic (read as: yew-KEHR-ee-otic) heterotroph whose cells lack cell walls?
e: Animals are multicellular eaters without plant cell walls, and the creepy-crawly whip scorpion is the only true animal on this list.

q: Which of the following plants belong to the phylum [FY-luhm] Pterophyta [ter-uh-FY-tuh]?
e: Horsetails and ferns are plant cousins in Pterophyta that unfurl feathery green fronds instead of making seeds or flowers.

q: The amino acid sequence of a protein represents the translation of which of the following?
a: The reverse-complement of the mRNA strand
e: The nontemplate DNA strand shares the exact same code letters as the messenger RNA, directly spelling out the protein's final chain.

q: Which of the following biological molecules most directly enables the structural compartmentalization required for cellular respiration and photosynthesis [foh- tuh-SIN-thuh-sis]?
e: Phospholipids huddle together to build snug bubble-like walls, creating separate little rooms inside cells for busy chemical kitchens.

q: Which of the following is NOT true of the platypus?
a: They are one of the few venomous mammals
e: Platypus eggs are packed with thick yolk and divide incompletely, which makes them meroblastic instead of holoblastic.

q: Which of the following organ systems is responsible for the secretion of hormones?
e: The endocrine system acts like your body's post office, sending tiny chemical messenger hormones everywhere to keep you running smoothly.

q: Which of the following does NOT belong to the Arthropoda:
e: Nematodes are smooth, squishy roundworms that completely lack the jointed legs and crunchy suits of armor that arthropods wear.

q: Which of the following BEST explains why water molds are NOT classified as fungi?
a: They have cell walls of cellulose and produce motile spores
They have cell walls of chitin (read as: KY-tin) and when aggregated function like a multicellular organism
e: True fungi have chitin walls, but water molds build plant-like cellulose walls and swim through puddles with wiggly spores.

q: Which of the following best describes features observed in two or more species that were inherited from a common ancestor?
e: Orthologous traits are like cherished family heirlooms, passed down directly from a single shared ancestor into different cousin species.

q: What osteichthyes [os-tee-IK-thee-eez] was known from the fossil record for nearly 100 years before a living specimen was discovered?
e: Scientists thought the chunky, deep-sea coelacanth was long extinct until a living one surprisingly turned up in a fishing net!

q: Which of the following organelles would likely contain a high concentration of catalase [CAT-ah-lace]?
e: Peroxisomes pack lots of catalase inside to safely turn harsh, bubbling hydrogen peroxide into gentle water and friendly oxygen.

q: Some bacteria have the ability to form endospores to survive in extreme environments. Which of the following is true of endospores?
a: They are sensitive to ultraviolet radiation
e: A tough endospore stays completely dehydrated, squeezing out its water so sleeping bacteria can safely survive boiling heat and drought.

q: Which of the following hormones is most pronouncedly elevated in a woman undergoing menopause?
e: When ovaries slow down during menopause, the brain pumps out extra follicle-stimulating hormone, shouting louder to wake them up.

q: Which of the following statements is true regarding fungal mutualism?
a: Many species of ants culture fungi inside of their bodies
Lichens are capable of nitrogen fixation
Plants can generally grow normally without endophytes
e: Lichens can fix nitrogen from thin air because fungi team up with clever blue-green bacteria buddies to share nutritious meals.

q: In insects, larval imaginal discs typically produce all of the following adult structures, EXCEPT:
e: Imaginal discs build fancy adult parts like wings and legs, while an insect's abdomen forms from humble larval cells instead.

q: A scientist isolates a small amount of DNA from a Tyrannosaur fossil. Which of the following would be most useful for increasing the amount of DNA with which the scientist has to work?
e: Polymerase chain reaction works like a tiny, magical copy machine, turning one whisper of fossil DNA into millions of copies scientists can actually study.

q: During meiosis [my-OH-sis], when a cell has lost both members of a homologous [huh-MOL-uh-guhs] pair of chromosomes, which of the following types of aneuploidy [an-yoo-PLOI-dee] would apply to the cell?
e: Nullisomy means zero, so when a cell completely loses both buddy chromosomes from a matching pair, none are left at all.

q: Which of the following is the primary determinant of secondary protein structure?
e: Tiny hydrogen bonds act like friendly little handshakes along the protein ribbon, neatly snapping it into lovely spirals and folded sheets.

q: SDS is a detergent. Which of the following explains how SDS denatures proteins?
a: Interferes with the hydrophobic interactions that normally stabilize the proteins
Interferes with the hydrophillic interactions that normally stabilize the proteins
Interferes with the amphiphillic [amfih-FILL-ic] interactions that normally stabilize the proteins
e: Soapy SDS sneaks inside folded proteins and breaks up the cozy, water-fearing huddles that normally hold them in shape.

q: Which of the following techniques would one use to separate proteins based on size?
e: In SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, proteins race through an obstacle course of gel where tiny runners easily slip past the big, clumsy ones.

q: Which of the following percentages is the closest to the fraction of the human genome that codes for proteins?
e: Amazingly, only about one percent of your body's giant recipe book actually gives instructions for building proteins.

q: During DNA replication, which of the following enzymes is mismatched to its function?
a: DNA primase: creates DNA primer to start replication
Single strand binding protein: prevents parental DNA strands from re-annealing
e: DNA primase actually builds starting flags out of RNA, not DNA, so claiming it makes a DNA primer is a little mix-up.
